1.name: THE CREATIVE
1.title: Hexagram 1 乾 - Qián / THE CREATIVE
1.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 1 (Qián) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
1.intro:
The hexagram consists of six undivided lines. The undivided lines correspond to the light, strong, spiritual, and active primal power. The character of the hexagram is entirely uniform and strong in its nature. Since no weakness adheres to it, its essential quality is power. Its image is heaven. This power is represented as unbound by specific spatial conditions; therefore, it is conceived as movement. Time is considered the foundation of this movement. Thus, the power of time and the power of perseverance in time - duration - are also comprised within this hexagram.

In the explanation of the hexagram, a dual interpretation must be consistently taken into account: the macrocosmic aspect and its effect on the human world. Applied to cosmic events, the hexagram expresses the strong creative action of the deity. Applied to the human world, it designates the creative action of the saint and sage, the ruler and leader of humanity, who awakens and develops their higher nature through his power.

dictamen.text: The Creative works sublime success, Furthering through perseverance.
dictamen.commentary:
According to their original meaning, these attributes belong together in pairs. For the one who receives this oracle, it signifies that success will be granted from the primal depths of cosmic events, and everything depends on seeking one's own happiness and that of others solely through perseverance in what is right.

From very early times, philosophical reflection turned toward the specific meanings of these four attributes. The Chinese word translated as "sublime" means "head, origin, great." Therefore, Confucius explains in the commentary: "Great indeed is the originating power of the Creative; all beings owe their beginning to it. And this power permeates the entire heaven." For this first attribute also runs through the other three.

The beginning of all things lies, so to speak, in the beyond, in the form of ideas that have yet to achieve realization. But within the Creative also lies the power to give form to these archetypes of ideas. This is designated by the word "success." This process is illustrated by an image from nature.

The clouds pass, and the rain does its work, and all individual beings flow into their forms.

Applied to the human sphere, these attributes show the great man the path to immense success: "By perceiving causes and effects with great clarity, he completes the six stages at the right time and mounts them at the right time like six dragons to ascend into heaven." The six stages are the six individual positions of the hexagram, which are represented below through the imagery of dragons. The way to success is defined here as recognizing and realizing the cosmic meaning, which, as an all-pervading law, causes all time-bound phenomena through its end and beginning. Thus, every stage reached becomes simultaneously the preparation for the next, and time is no longer an obstacle but the means to realize what is possible.

After the act of creation is expressed through the two attributes of sublimity and success, the work of preservation is shown as a continuously unfolding development, linked to the terms "furthering" - literally "creating what corresponds to one's nature" - and "persevering" - literally "correct and firm." "The course of the Creative alters and shapes all beings until each attains its true, destined nature, then it preserves them in harmony with the great harmony. Thus it shows itself furthering through perseverance."

When transferred to the human realm, this reveals how the great man brings peace and security to the world through his organizing activity: "By raising his head above the multitude of beings, all lands unite in peace."

Another line of speculation goes even further in separating the words "sublime, success, furthering, persevering" and aligns them with the four human cardinal virtues: Love is assigned to "sublimity," which also includes all other attributes as a foundational principle. Custom is assigned to the attribute of "success," which orders, organizes, and thereby makes the expressions of love successful. Justice is assigned to the attribute of "furthering," which creates conditions where everyone receives what corresponds to their nature, what is due to them, and what constitutes their happiness. Wisdom is assigned to the attribute of "perseverance," which recognizes the fixed laws of all events and is therefore capable of creating lasting conditions.

These speculations, which were already suggested in the Wen Yan commentary in the second part of the Book of Changes, formed the bridge by which the philosophy of the five stages of change (elements) - anchored in the Book of Documents - was combined with the philosophy of the Book of Changes, which relies purely on the polar duality of positive and negative principles. Over time, this opened the door to an ever-expanding numerical symbolism.

imagen.text: The movement of heaven is full of power. Thus the superior man makes himself strong and untiring.
imagen.commentary:
The doubling of the hexagram Qián, whose image is heaven, points to the movement of heaven, since there is only one heaven. A complete circular motion of heaven constitutes a day. The doubling of the sign implies that one day follows another. This generates the concept of time and, since it is the same heaven moving with untiring strength, the powerful endurance in and over time - a movement that never stops or flags, just as day follows day continuously. This duration in time is the image of the power inherent in the Creative.

The wise man draws from this the model for how to develop himself for lasting impact. He must make himself completely strong by consciously eliminating everything that drags him down or is base. In this way, he gains the untiring resilience that comes from complete cycles of activity.

1.text: Hidden dragon. Do not act.
1.commentary:
In China, the dragon has a completely different meaning than in Western conception. The dragon is the symbol of the mobile-electrical, powerful, inspiring force that manifests in a thunderstorm. This force withdraws into the earth during winter, becomes active again in early summer, and appears in the sky as lightning and thunder. As a consequence, the creative forces stir again on earth.

Here, this creative force is still hidden beneath the earth and therefore has no effect yet. Transferred to human affairs, this means that an eminent person is still unrecognized. Nevertheless, he remains true to himself. He does not allow himself to be influenced by external success or failure, but waits for his time, strong and unconcerned.

Thus, for the one who draws this line, it is important to wait with calm, strong patience. Time will fulfill itself. One does not need to fear that a strong will fail to assert itself. Yet, it is vital not to expend one's strength prematurely or try to force something that is not yet ripe.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Dragon appearing in the field. It is furthering to see the great man.
2.commentary: Here, the effects of the light force begin to show. Applied to human situations, this means that the great man appears in the field of his activity. He does not yet hold a ruling position but is still among his peers. However, what distinguishes him from others is his seriousness, his absolute reliability, and the influence he exerts on his surroundings without conscious effort. Such a person is destined to gain great influence and set the world in order. Therefore, it is furthering to see him.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: The superior man is creatively active all day long. Even in the evening, he is still full of inner care. Danger. No blame.
3.commentary: A sphere of activity opens up for the important man. His fame begins to spread. The masses flock to him. His inner strength is equal to the increased external activity. There is plenty of work to do, and even in the evening, when others rest, plans and anxieties crowd in. A danger exists here at the place of transition from lowliness to height. Many a great man has been ruined because the masses rushed to him and swept him into their courses. Ambition spoiled the inner purity. But true greatness is not impaired by temptations. If one remains in touch with the seeds of the new time and its demands, one possesses sufficient prudence to guard against straying and remains without blame.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: A wavering flight over the depths. No blame.
4.commentary: Here, the place of transition is reached where freedom can exercise itself. A double possibility lies before the important man: either to soar upward and play a decisive role in public life, or to withdraw and cultivate his personality in silence - the path of the hero or the hidden sage. There is no general law as to which is correct. Anyone in such a position must decide freely according to the innermost laws of his being. If he acts completely truthfully and consistently, he will find the path that corresponds to him, and this path is right for him and without blame.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Flying dragon in the heavens. It is furthering to see the great man.
5.commentary: Here, the great man has arrived in the celestial sphere. His influence extends visibly across the entire world. Everyone who sees him can count themselves blessed. Confucius says about this: "Things that accord in tone vibrate together. Things that are kindred in their innermost essence seek each other. Water flows toward the wet; fire turns toward the dry. The clouds (heaven's breath) follow the dragon; the wind (earth's breath) follows the tiger. Thus the sage arises, and all beings look toward him. What comes from heaven feels related to what is above. What comes from earth feels related to what is below. Each follows its kind."
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Arrogant dragon will have cause to repent.
6.commentary: If one wishes to climb so high as to lose touch with other people, one becomes isolated, and this necessarily leads to failure. Here lies a warning against a titanic striving that exceeds one's strength. A fall to the depths would be the consequence.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

all.text: There appears a flight of dragons without a head. Good fortune.
all.commentary: When all lines are nines, the entire hexagram comes into motion and changes into the hexagram Kūn, the Receptive, whose character is devotion. The strength of the Creative and the mildness of the Receptive unite. Strength is indicated by the flight of dragons, mildness by the circumstance that their heads are hidden. This means: mildness in conduct combined with strength of decision brings good fortune.
all.title: When all lines are nines, it means:

2.name: THE RECEPTIVE
2.title: Hexagram 2 坤 - Kūn / THE RECEPTIVE
2.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 2 (Kūn) of the I Ching, featuring Unicode characters and Pinyin.
2.intro:
This hexagram consists entirely of yielded (divided) lines. The divided line represents the dark, soft, receptive primal power of Yin. The primary attribute of the hexagram is devotion, and its symbol is the Earth. It serves as the perfect counterpart to The Creative - a complement, not an opposite; a completion, not a conflict. It represents Nature in contrast to Spirit, Earth to Heaven, space to time, and the feminine-maternal to the masculine-paternal. When applied to human affairs, this principle of partnership is found not only in the relationship between man and woman, but also between ruler and minister, or father and son. Even within the individual, this duality manifests as the coexistence of the spiritual and the sensory.

However, this does not imply a true dualism, because a clear hierarchy exists between the two hexagrams. In itself, The Receptive is just as important as The Creative. Yet, its inherent quality of devotion defines its position relative to The Creative. It must act under the guidance and inspiration of The Creative to bring about beneficial results. It becomes harmful only if it abandons this position and tries to stand as an equal partner alongside The Creative. This leads to opposition and conflict, which proves disastrous for both sides.

dictamen.text: THE RECEPTIVE brings sublime success, Furthering through the perseverance of a mare. If the superior man has an undertaking and tries to lead, He goes astray; but if he follows, he finds guidance. It is favorable to find friends in the west and south, And to forego friends in the east and north. Quiet perseverance brings good fortune.
dictamen.commentary:
The four fundamental attributes of The Creative - "sublime success, furthering through perseverance" - are also found here to describe The Receptive. However, this perseverance is specifically defined as the perseverance of a mare. The Receptive represents spatial reality, standing in contrast to the spiritual potential of The Creative. When potential becomes actualized and the spiritual takes on spatial form, it always occurs through a limiting, individualizing definition. This is why the term "perseverance" is further qualified by "of a mare." The horse belongs to the earth just as the dragon belongs to heaven. Its boundless movement across the plains symbolizes the vast expanses of the earth. The term "mare" is chosen because it combines the strength and speed of a horse with the gentleness and devotion of a cow.

Nature can actualize the impulses of The Creative only because it matches its essential nature. Its wealth lies in nourishing all living things, and its greatness lies in beautifying and glorifying everything. In this way, it brings prosperity to all life. While The Creative generates things, they are born from The Receptive.

Applied to human affairs, the lesson is to act in accordance with one's situation. One is not in an independent position but is working as an assistant. The task here is to accomplish something, not to lead. Trying to lead would only cause one to go astray; the true objective is to let oneself be guided. By learning to remain devoted in the face of fate, one is certain to find proper guidance. The superior man allows himself to be led. He does not advance blindly; instead, he assesses what the circumstances demand of him and follows this guidance of destiny.

Since there is work to be done, one needs helpers and friends during times of labor and effort, once the ideas to be executed are already established. This period of work and effort is symbolized by the west and south. The south and west represent the place where The Receptive works on behalf of The Creative - just as nature does in summer and autumn. If one does not gather all available strength during this time, the task at hand will remain unfinished. Therefore, finding friends here means securing cooperation and productivity. However, besides work and effort, there is also a time for planning and organizing, which requires solitude. The east symbolizes the place where one receives orders from their master, and the north represents where one reports on what has been accomplished. In these moments, one must stand alone and objective. In this sacred hour, one must forego companions so that the purity of thought is not clouded by partisan hatred or favoritism.

imagen.text: The condition of the earth is receptive devotion. Thus the superior man, of broad character, carries the outer world.
imagen.commentary: Just as there is only one heaven, there is only one earth. While the doubling of the hexagram for heaven implies temporal duration, for the earth it signifies spatial expansion and the stability with which it carries and sustains all living things. In its devotion, the earth sustains both good and evil without exception. Likewise, the superior man makes his character broad, solid, and enduring, so that he is capable of supporting and tolerating both people and things.

1.text: When there is hoarfrost underfoot, solid ice is near.
1.commentary:
Just as the light power represents life, the dark power represents death. In autumn, when the first hoarfrost falls, the power of darkness and cold is only beginning to unfold. Following these initial traces, the manifestations of death will gradually multiply according to fixed laws, until the rigid winter arrives with its ice.

This is exactly how it works in life. When faint, barely noticeable signs of decay appear, they continue to progress until destruction finally arrives. In life, however, one can take preventive measures by paying attention to the signs of decay and confronting them in time.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Straight, square, great. Without purpose, yet nothing remains unadvanced.
2.commentary:
Heaven is symbolized by a circle, while the earth is symbolized by a right-angled square. Thus, squareness is an inherent attribute of the earth. On the other hand, straight movement is originally a quality of The Creative, as is greatness. Yet all square things have their roots in the straight line and, in turn, form physical dimensions. In mathematics, lines, planes, and solids are distinct; straight lines produce square planes, and square planes produce cubic volumes. The Receptive aligns itself with the attributes of The Creative and makes them its own. Thus, a straight line becomes a square, and a square becomes a cube. This represents simple devotion to the laws of The Creative without adding or subtracting anything. Therefore, The Receptive requires no special purpose or effort, and everything turns out right.

Nature produces all beings without deceit, which is its straightness; it is calm and still, which is its squareness; it does not refuse to tolerate any creature, which is its greatness. Consequently, it achieves what is right for all things without external contrivance or special purposes. For human beings, the highest wisdom lies in making their actions as spontaneous and natural as nature itself.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Hidden lines; one is able to remain persevering. If you should serve a king, Seek not works, but bring completion!
3.commentary: If one is free from vanity, they can conceal their merits so that they do not prematurely draw public attention. This allows one to mature in quiet isolation. If circumstances require it, one may also step into the public eye, but even then, with restraint. The wise person gladly leaves the glory to others. They do not seek finished achievements to be credited to their name; rather, they hope to set active causes in motion - meaning they complete works in such a way that they bear fruit for the future.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: A tied-up sack. No blame, no praise.
4.commentary: The dark power opens when it moves and closes when it rests. Here, the strictest reserve is indicated. The times are dangerous: any forward step leads either to the hostility of overwhelming opponents if one tries to fight them, or to misunderstood recognition if one is too compliant. Therefore, it is necessary to keep oneself enclosed, whether in solitude or in the turmoil of the world; even there, one can conceal themselves so well that no one knows them.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: A yellow lower garment brings sublime good fortune.
5.commentary: Yellow is the color of the earth and of the center, symbolizing what is reliable and genuine. The lower garment is inconspicuously adorned, symbolizing noble restraint. When someone is called to act in a prominent yet dependent position, true success relies on the utmost discretion. Authenticity and refinement should not manifest directly, but should express themselves indirectly as an inner influence working outward.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Dragons fight in the meadow. Their blood is black and yellow.
6.commentary:
In the highest position, the dark power should give way to the light. If it attempts to maintain itself in a position that does not belong to it, and rules instead of serving, it incurs the wrath of the strong. A struggle ensues in which it is overthrown, though both sides suffer harm.

The dragon, symbol of heaven, arrives and fights the false dragon, whose image the earthly power has assumed here. Dark blue is the color of heaven; yellow is the color of the earth. Therefore, when black and yellow blood flows, it is a sign that both fundamental forces suffer damage through this unnatural conflict.
6.title: Six at the top means:

all.commentary:
When all the lines are sixes, the hexagram of The Receptive transforms into the hexagram of The Creative. It thus gains the power of endurance by holding fast to what is right. While there is no progress, there is also no regression.

Thus gaze with modest eyes upon
The eternal weaver's masterpiece,
How a single treadle moves a thousand threads;
The shuttles dart from side to side,
The threads flow invisibly to meet,
One strike a thousand links unites;
She did not gather this by begging,
She ordered it from eternity,
So that the eternal master mind
Securely may the woof design.
all.title: When all the lines are sixes, it means:

3.name: DIFFICULTY AT THE BEGINNING
3.title: Hexagram 3 屯 - ZHŪN / DIFFICULTY AT THE BEGINNING
3.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 3 (ZHŪN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
3.intro: The name of the hexagram, Zhūn, originally represents a blade of grass pushing up against an obstacle as it sprouts from the earth. From this arises the meaning of difficulty at the beginning. The hexagram indicates how heaven and earth bring forth individual beings. It is their first encounter, which is inherently accompanied by difficulties. The lower trigram, Zhèn, is the Arousing; its movement is directed upward, and its image is thunder. The upper trigram, Kǎn, is the Abysmal, the dangerous; its movement is directed downward, and its image is rain. The situation therefore points to a dense, chaotic abundance. Thunder and rain fill the air. However, the chaos eventually clears. The upward movement, even as the abysmal element descends, finally breaks free from danger. The built-up tensions release during the thunderstorm, and everything breathes a sigh of relief.

dictamen.text: Difficulty at the beginning brings supreme success. Perseverance furthers. One should not undertake anything. It is advantageous to appoint helpers.
dictamen.commentary: Times of growth are filled with difficulties. It is like a first birth. Yet these difficulties arise from the sheer abundance of what is striving for form. Everything is in motion; therefore, despite the inherent danger, there is a prospect of great success if one maintains perseverance. When such times of beginning come as a destiny, everything is still unformed and dark. For this reason, one must wait, as any premature action could bring failure. It is equally critical not to remain isolated. One needs helpers to master the chaos together. This does not mean watching the events unfold passively; rather, one must join in, offering encouragement and guidance throughout.

imagen.text: Clouds and thunder: the image of difficulty at the beginning. Thus the superior person sorts out and brings order.
imagen.commentary: Clouds and thunder are represented by specific structural lines, which implies that order is already inherent within the chaos of early difficulties. Thus, during such times of beginning, the superior person must organize and structure the confusing abundance, much like unraveling silk threads from a tangled skein and binding them into strands. To find one's way within the infinite, one must learn both to distinguish and to connect.

1.text: Hesitation and hindrance. It furthers to remain persevering. It furthers to appoint helpers.
1.commentary: When encountering a hindrance at the start of an enterprise, one must not attempt to force progress, but should instead pause cautiously. However, one must not allow oneself to be destabilized, but must steadfastly keep the goal in mind. It is essential to seek the right assistance. Such helpers are found only by interacting with people with humility and avoiding arrogance. Only in this way do people willingly align with you, allowing you to tackle the difficulties together.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Difficulties pile up. Horse and wagon separate. He is no robber, He comes to woo in due time. The maiden is chaste, she does not pledge herself. Ten years, then she pledges herself.
2.commentary:
One finds oneself in difficulty and restraint. Then suddenly a turn occurs, as if someone arrived with a horse and wagon and unhitched them. This event comes so unexpectedly that one suspects the newcomer to be a robber. Gradually it becomes clear that he has no evil intentions, but seeks a friendly alliance and offers relief. Yet the offer is rejected because it does not come from the right source; instead, one waits until the time is fulfilled - ten years signify a completed cycle, a fulfilled time. Then normal conditions naturally return, and one can unite with the intended partner.

Under the image of a bride who remains faithful to her beloved during severe conflicts, advice is offered for a specific life situation: when sudden relief is offered by an unrelated party during times of difficulty and hindrance, one must remain cautious and avoid taking on obligations that such assistance would entail, as this would compromise freedom of decision. By waiting for the right time, peaceful conditions will return, and what was hoped for will be achieved.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Whoever hunts the deer without the forester only loses his way in the forest. The superior person understands the signs of the time and prefers to desist. To go on brings humiliation.
3.commentary: Hunting in an unfamiliar forest without a guide leads to getting lost. One must not attempt to break out of current difficulties blindly and without guidance. Fate cannot be deceived. Premature striving without the necessary direction leads to failure and shame. Therefore, the superior person, recognizing the seeds of what is to come, prefers to renounce a desire rather than bring about failure and humiliation by trying to force it.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Horse and wagon separate. Strive for union. To go brings good fortune. Everything acts to further.
4.commentary: One is in a position where action is required, yet one's own strength is insufficient. However, an opportunity to connect presents itself. It is crucial to seize it. One must not be held back by false pride or misplaced reluctance. It is a sign of inner clarity when one overcomes inertia to take the first step, even if it involves a certain degree of self-denial. In a difficult situation, there is no shame in accepting help. If the right helper is found, everything turns out well.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Difficulties in granting blessings. Small perseverance brings good fortune, Great perseverance brings misfortune.
5.commentary: One finds oneself in a situation where it is impossible to express good intentions in a way that makes them manifest and understood. Others interpose themselves and distort everything one does. Under these circumstances, one must proceed cautiously and gradually. One should not attempt to force grand designs, as such things succeed only when general trust is already established. Only through quiet, faithful, and conscientious work can one gradually clear up the situation and dissolve the hindrances.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Horse and wagon separate. Bloody tears pour forth.
6.commentary:
Some people find the initial difficulties too overwhelming. They get stuck and cannot find their way through. They drop their hands and give up the struggle. Such a resignation is among the saddest of outcomes. Therefore, Confucius remarks on this: "Bloody tears pour forth: one should not do this continuously."

Difficulties pile up. Horse and wagon turn around.
Were the robber not there, the wooer would surely come.
The maiden is faithful, she does not pledge herself.
Ten years, then she pledges herself.
6.title: Six at the top means:

4.name: YOUTHFUL FOLLY
4.title: Hexagram 4 蒙 - MENG / YOUTHFUL FOLLY
4.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 4 (MENG) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
4.intro:
This hexagram points to youth and folly in two distinct ways. The upper trigram, Gèn, has the mountain as its image, while the lower, Kǎn, is represented by water. A spring emerging at the foot of a mountain serves as a clear image of inexperienced youth. Furthermore, the attribute of the upper trigram is keeping still, while that of the lower is the abyss or danger. Halting in hesitation before a dangerous abyss symbolizes the helpless folly of youth. 

However, both trigrams also contain the exact pathway to overcoming this initial ignorance. Water is an element that flows onward by inherent necessity. When a spring gushes forth, it does not know where it will ultimately go. Yet, through its steady, persistent flow, it completely fills up every deep hollow that blocks its progress, and success is achieved.

dictamen.text: Youthful Folly has success. It is not I who seek the young fool, The young fool seeks me. At the first oracle I give an answer. If he asks two or three times, it is importunity. If he importunes, I give no answer. Perseverance furthers.
dictamen.commentary:
Folly is nothing terrible in youth; it can still achieve success. However, one must find an experienced teacher and approach them in the correct manner. This requires, first of all, that the youth recognizes their own inexperience and actively seeks out a master. Only this humility and genuine interest guarantee the openness needed to learn, which shows itself in respectful recognition of the teacher.

Therefore, the teacher must wait quietly until approached. They should not offer instruction uninvited; only in this way can teaching occur at the right time and in the right manner.

The answer a teacher provides to a student's questions must be clear and definite, like the answer an oracle-seeker wishes to receive. It must be accepted as a resolution of doubt and a final decision. Distrustful or thoughtless further questioning merely importunes the teacher and is best met with silence, just as the oracle gives only one answer and fails when faced with testing, doubtful questions.

When perseverance is added, not letting up until everything is mastered step by step, a beautiful success is assured. The hexagram thus provides counsel for both the teacher and the student.

imagen.text: A spring wells up at the foot of the mountain: The image of Youth. Thus the superior man fosters his character by thoroughness in all his actions.
imagen.commentary: The spring begins to flow and overcomes stagnation by filling up all the hollow spaces in its path. In the same way, the path to building character lies in thoroughness, which skips nothing but fills all gaps gradually and steadily like water, thus moving forward.

1.text: To develop the fool, It is furthering to apply discipline to the person. The fetters should be removed. To go on thus brings humiliation.
1.commentary: Law stands at the beginning of education. Inexperienced youth tends to treat everything casually and playfully at first. Therefore, the seriousness of life must be shown to them. A certain self-discipline, enforced through strict training, is beneficial. Those who play with life never find their way. However, discipline must not degenerate into mere drill. Continuous drill humiliates and paralyzes one's inner strength.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Bearing fools in mildness brings good fortune. Knowing how to treat women brings good fortune. The son is equal to the tasks of the household.
2.commentary: This represents a person who has no external power but possesses the necessary spiritual strength to bear the responsibility resting upon them. They have the inner superiority and strength to tolerate the shortcomings of human folly with mildness. This same attitude applies to women, historically regarded as the weaker sex; one must know how to accommodate and acknowledge them with a certain chivalrous forbearance.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: You must not choose a maiden Who, when she sees a man of bronze, Loses control of herself. Nothing is furthering.
3.commentary: A weak, inexperienced person striving upward easily loses their individuality when they encounter a strong personality in a high position whom they slavishly imitate. They resemble a maiden who throws herself away upon meeting a strong man. One should not be welcoming toward such a dependent approach; responsiveness would benefit neither the youth nor the educator. It is due to a maiden's dignity to wait until she is courted. In both cases, it is undignified to offer oneself, and it is unwise to accept such an offer.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Entangled folly brings humiliation.
4.commentary: For youthful folly, nothing is more hopeless than getting entangled in empty illusions. The more stubbornly it clings to such unrealistic fantasies, the more certainly it brings humiliation upon itself. Confronted with this narrow-minded folly, an educator often has no choice but to leave the youth to their own devices for a time, not sparing them the humiliation that arises from their behavior. This is often the only way to save them.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Childlike folly brings good fortune.
5.commentary: An inexperienced person who seeks instruction with childlike humility and lack of pretension is on the right path. For anyone who submits to a teacher free from pride will surely find advancement.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: In punishing folly, it does not further to commit excesses. It furthers only to prevent excesses.
6.commentary:
Under certain circumstances, an incorrigible fool must be punished. Those who will not listen must feel the consequences. This punishment differs from the initial shock or discipline applied at the beginning. However, punishment must never be inflicted in anger; it must be restricted to an objective defense against unjust violations. It is never an end in itself but serves only to restore orderly conditions. 

This applies both to education and to governmental measures against a population guilty of excesses.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

5.name: WAITING (NOURISHMENT)
5.title: Hexagram 5 需 - XŪ / WAITING (NOURISHMENT)
5.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 5 (XŪ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
5.intro: All beings require nourishment from above. However, the dispensing of food has its own proper time, which must be awaited. The hexagram depicts clouds rising into the sky, preparing to shed the rain that refreshes all living things and provides humanity with food and drink. This rain will come in due time. It cannot be forced; one must wait for it. The concept of waiting is further illustrated by the attributes of the two primal trigrams: inner strength faced with danger ahead. Strength in the face of danger does not act precipitously but knows how to wait, whereas weakness in the face of danger grows agitated, lacking the patience to endure the delay.

dictamen.text: Waiting. If you are sincere, you have light and success. Perseverance brings good fortune. It furthers one to cross the great water.
dictamen.commentary:
Waiting is not empty hoping; it carries the inner certainty of reaching its goal. Only this inner certainty brings the light that leads to success. This leads to perseverance, which brings good fortune and grants the strength to cross the great water.

A danger lies ahead that must be overcome. Weakness and impatience can accomplish nothing. Only the strong can cope with their fate, because their inner security allows them to endure. This strength manifests as unyielding sincerity. Only when we can look at things exactly as they are, free from self-deception and illusion, does a light emerge from events that reveals the path to success. This realization must be followed by resolute and persistent action; for only by resolutely facing one's fate can it be mastered. Then one can cross the great water - that is, make the decision and endure the danger.

imagen.text: Clouds rise up to heaven: the image of Waiting. Thus the superior man eats and drinks, and remains cheerful and of good heart.
imagen.commentary: When clouds rise into the sky, it is a sign that it will rain. There is nothing to be done but wait for the rain to fall. It is the same in life when destiny is preparing itself. As long as the time is not yet ripe, one should not worry or try to shape the future through personal contrivance and intervention. Instead, one should quietly gather strength - nourishing the body with food and drink, and sustaining the spirit with cheerfulness and goodwill. Destiny unfolds entirely on its own, and when it arrives, one is ready.

1.text: Waiting in the meadow. It furthers one to abide in what is permanent. No blame.
1.commentary: The danger is still far away. One is still waiting in the open plain. Conditions are still simple. There is merely something in the air that is bound to come. In such times, it is essential to maintain the regular routines of life for as long as possible. Only in this way does one prevent the premature waste of energy, remaining free from blame and errors that would cause weakness later on.
1.title: Nine at the beginning

2.text: Waiting on the sand. There is some gossip. The end brings good fortune.
2.commentary: Danger is gradually drawing closer. The sand is near the bank of the river, which represents the danger. Inconveniences begin to manifest. During such times, general unrest easily arises, and people blame one another. He who remains calm will succeed in making everything turn out well in the end. All slander must eventually fall silent if one does not grant it the satisfaction of an offended counterargument.
2.title: Nine in the second place

3.text: Waiting in the mud brings the approach of the enemy.
3.commentary: The mud, already washed by the water of the river, is no favorable place for waiting. Instead of gathering strength to cross the water in one bound, a premature advance was made, whose momentum led only as far as the mud. Such an unfavorable position invites enemies from the outside, who naturally exploit the situation. Only through seriousness and caution is it possible to safeguard oneself from harm.
3.title: Nine in the third place

4.text: Waiting in blood. Get out of the pit.
4.commentary: The situation is extremely dangerous. It has become a matter of utmost gravity, a question of life and death. Bloodshed is imminently expected. One can move neither forward nor backward, cut off as if in a pit. Here, one must simply endure and let fate take its course. This composure, which refrains from worsening the damage through impulsive actions, is the only way to escape the dangerous pit.
4.title: Six in the fourth place

5.text: Waiting with wine and food. Perseverance brings good fortune.
5.commentary:
Even in the midst of danger, there are intervals of peace when things go relatively well. If one possesses the right inner strength, one will utilize these breathers to fortify oneself for the coming struggle. One can enjoy the moment without being deflected from the goal, for perseverance is required to remain victorious.

This also applies to public life. Everything cannot be achieved at once. It is the highest wisdom to grant people such periods of rest, which revitalize their joy in work and help carry the task to completion. Here lies the hidden secret of the entire hexagram. It differs from Hexagram 39 (Obstruction) because in Waiting, one is certain of one's cause and therefore does not allow the peace of inner cheerfulness to be taken away.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place

6.text: One falls into the pit. Three uninvited guests arrive. Honor them, and in the end, good fortune comes.
6.commentary: The waiting is over; the danger can no longer be averted. One falls into the pit and must resign oneself to the inevitable. At that moment, all efforts seem to have been in vain. Yet, precisely in this extremity, an unforeseen turn of events occurs. From the outside, an intervention takes place without one's own doing, leaving one initially uncertain whether it brings rescue or destruction. In this situation, it is crucial to remain inwardly flexible. The correct response is not a defiant, defensive closing-off, but a respectful welcoming of the new turn. Thus, one ultimately escapes the danger, and everything turns out well. Even fortunate turnarounds often arrive in a guise that initially seems foreign to us.
6.title: Six at the top

6.name: CONFLICT
6.title: Hexagram 6 訟 - SÒNG / CONFLICT
6.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 6 (SÒNG) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
6.intro:
The upper primary trigram, whose image is heaven, has an upward direction of movement; the lower primary trigram, water, is by its nature directed downward. The directions of movement of the two halves diverge, which gives rise to the idea of conflict.

The attribute of the Creative is strength; that of the Abysmal is danger, craftiness. Where cunning faces force, conflict arises.

A third interpretation is suggested within the character by the combination of inward craftiness and outward strength and determination. Such a character will certainly be prone to conflict.

dictamen.text: Conflict: You are sincere and are being obstructed. A cautious halt halfway brings good fortune. Carrying things through to the end brings misfortune. It furthers one to see the great man. It does not further one to cross the great water.
dictamen.commentary:
Conflict develops when someone encounters opposition while feeling they are in the right. Without the conviction of being right, opposition leads to craftiness or violent encroachment, but not to open conflict.

If one is involved in a conflict, a powerful moderation that is ready at any moment to settle the matter and compromise halfway is the only thing that brings good fortune. Pursuing a conflict to the bitter end brings evil, even if one is in the right, because it perpetuates enmity. It is important to see the great man,

imagen.text: Heaven and water move in opposite directions: the image of Conflict. Thus the superior man, in all his transactions, considers the beginning.
imagen.commentary: The image indicates that the causes of conflict lie in the pre-existing, opposing directions of both parties. Once such conflicting tendencies are present, conflict follows of necessity. It follows from this that in order to prevent conflict, everything must be carefully considered at the very beginning. If rights and duties are precisely defined, or if the spiritual directions of people are aligned when they form an association, the cause of conflict is eliminated in advance.

1.text: If one does not perpetuate the matter, there is a little gossip. In the end, good fortune comes.
1.commentary: As long as a conflict is still in its earliest stages, it is best to drop it. Especially when facing a stronger opponent, it is not advisable to let things come to a showdown. This may lead to a slight exchange of words, but in the end, everything turns out well.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: One cannot conflict; one returns home and gives way. The people of his town, three hundred households, remain free from blame.
2.commentary: In a struggle against a superior adversary, retreat carries no shame. Withdrawing in time avoids evil consequences. If one were to provoke an unequal conflict out of a false sense of honor, one would bring disaster upon oneself. A wise compliance in such a case benefits the entire community, which is thereby spared from being dragged into the dispute.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: To nourish oneself on ancient virtue brings perseverance. Danger. In the end, good fortune comes. If you should happen to serve a king, seek no achievements.
3.commentary: This warns against the danger brought on by an ambitious or encroaching disposition. Only what is honestly earned through past merit remains a permanent possession. Such a possession may be challenged at times, but because it is real property, it cannot be stolen. For one cannot lose what belongs to them by virtue of their own nature. When entering the service of a superior, conflict can only be avoided by not seeking achievements for oneself. It is enough that the work is done; let the honor remain with the other.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: One cannot conflict; one turns back and submits to fate, changes one's mind and finds peace in perseverance. Good fortune!
4.commentary: The inner disposition is initially restless. One feels uncomfortable with their situation and wishes to improve it through conflict. Since one is dealing with a weaker opponent, this would be entirely possible - marking a contrast with the Nine in the second place - yet one cannot carry on the conflict because one lacks inner justification and a clear conscience. Therefore, one turns back and submits to fate. One changes their mind and thus finds lasting peace in alignment with eternal law. This brings good fortune.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: To litigate before him brings supreme good fortune.
5.commentary: This refers to the arbiter of the conflict, who is powerful, just, and possesses the authority to give weight to the right. One can safely submit a case to him. If one is in the right, supreme good fortune is attained.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Even if a leather belt is bestowed upon someone, by the end of a single morning it will be snatched away three times.
6.commentary: This depicts someone who has carried a conflict to its bitter end and won. He receives a decoration, but his good fortune is not lasting. It is repeatedly challenged, resulting in endless conflict.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

7.name: The Army
7.title: Hexagram 7 師 - Shī / The Army
7.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 7 (Shī) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
7.intro:
This hexagram consists of the trigrams Kǎn (Water) below and Kūn (Earth) above. It symbolizes groundwater accumulating within the earth. In the same way, military power gathers within the masses of the people: invisible during peacetime, yet always available as a source of power. The attributes of these trigrams are danger within and obedience without. This points to the essence of an army, which is inherently dangerous, while discipline and obedience must prevail externally.

Looking at the individual lines, the ruler of the hexagram is the strong nine in the second place, to which the other yielding lines subordinate themselves. This line signifies the commander because it occupies the center of the lower trigram. However, because it rests in the lower rather than the upper trigram, it does not represent the ruler, but rather the capable general who maintains obedience within the army through his authority.

dictamen.text: The army needs perseverance and a strong man. Good fortune without blame.
dictamen.commentary:
An army is a mass that requires organization to become a cohesive force. Nothing can be achieved without firm discipline. However, this discipline cannot be forced through coercion alone; it requires a strong leader who wins the hearts of the people and inspires enthusiasm. To fully develop his capabilities, he needs the absolute trust of his ruler, who must grant him full responsibility for the duration of the war. 

Yet war is always a dangerous endeavor that brings destruction and devastation. Therefore, it should never be undertaken lightly, but rather used like a poisonous medicine as a last resort. An experienced leader must clarify the just cause and a clear, understandable objective to the people. Only when a specific goal exists - one for which the people can consciously dedicate themselves - does the unity and strength of conviction emerge that leads to victory. Furthermore, the commander must ensure that nothing unjust occurs during the passion of war or the euphoria of victory, lest it fail to win general approval. Justice and perseverance are the fundamental requirements for a successful outcome.

imagen.text: Groundwater is in the midst of the earth: the image of the Army. Thus the superior man increases his masses by generosity toward the people.
imagen.commentary:
Groundwater is invisibly present within the earth. In the same way, the military power of a nation is invisibly present within its masses. When danger threatens, every peasant becomes a soldier, returning to his plow once the war ends. 

Whoever shows generosity toward the people wins their affection, and a population living under a benevolent government becomes strong and resilient. Only an economically robust nation can be significant as a military power. Therefore, one must cultivate this power by fostering the economic well-being of the people and maintaining a humane government. Only when this invisible bond exists between the government and the people - where the people feel as secure under it as groundwater within the earth - is it possible to wage a war successfully.

1.text: An army must march out in good order. If order is lacking, misfortune threatens.
1.commentary: At the beginning of a military campaign, order must prevail. There must be a just and compelling cause, and the obedience and coordination of the troops must be well-organized; otherwise, failure is the inevitable consequence.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: In the midst of the army! Good fortune! No blame. The king confers a threefold decoration.
2.commentary: The commander must be in the midst of his army. He must maintain a close connection with it and share both good fortune and hardship with the masses he leads. Only in this way can he meet the heavy demands placed upon him. He also requires the recognition of the ruler. The honors he receives are justified because they do not represent personal favoritism; instead, the entire army is honored through the leader who dwells in its midst.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: The army carries corpses in the wagon, perhaps. Misfortune!
3.commentary: One explanation points to a defeat caused by someone other than the chosen leader interfering in command. Another explanation aligns with this meaning but interprets the expression "carrying corpses in the wagon" differently.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: The army retreats. No blame.
4.commentary: When facing a superior enemy against whom conflict is hopeless, an orderly retreat is the only correct course of action, as it preserves the army from defeat and dissolution. It is by no means a sign of courage or strength to insist on fighting a hopeless battle under any circumstances.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: There is game in the field. It furthers one to catch it. No blame. Let the eldest lead the army. The younger carries corpses; then perseverance brings misfortune.
5.commentary: The game is in the field, meaning it has left its habitat in the forest and invaded the fields, causing devastation. This indicates an enemy invasion. In such a case, energetic combat and defense are entirely justified. However, the fight must be conducted according to established rules. It must not degenerate into a wild, chaotic free-for-all where everyone fights on their own initiative; that would lead to disaster despite the greatest perseverance and bravery. Instead, the army must be guided by an experienced commander. War must be conducted systematically; the multitude must not simply slaughter whatever comes to hand, otherwise defeat is suffered, and despite all persistence, misfortune threatens.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: The great prince issues commands, founds states, vests families with fiefs. Inferior people should not be employed.
6.commentary: The war has ended in victory. With the triumph achieved, the king distributes fiefs and family estates among his loyal followers. However, it is crucial that inferior people are not allowed to attain power. If they have assisted, they may be compensated with money, but they must not be granted territories or sovereign rights, preventing any abuse of authority.
6.title: Six at the top means:

8.name: HOLDING TOGETHER (UNION)
8.title: Hexagram 8 比 - Bǐ / HOLDING TOGETHER (UNION)
8.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 8 (Bǐ) of the I Ching, featuring Unicode characters and Pinyin.
8.intro: Water over the earth flows together wherever it can, just as all rivers naturally gather in the sea. This symbol illustrates the concept of holding together and its inherent laws. The same idea is suggested by the structure of the hexagram: all lines are yielding except for the single firm line in the fifth place, which occupies the ruler's position. The yielding lines hold together because they are guided by the strong-willed leader who serves as their center of union. Yet this powerful, leading personality also maintains a bond with the others, finding in them a vital complement to his own nature.

dictamen.text: Holding together brings good fortune. Inquire of the oracle once again whether you possess sublimity, constancy, and perseverance; if so, there is no blame. Those who are uncertain gradually join. Whoever arrives too late meets with misfortune.
dictamen.commentary:
This hexagram concerns joining with others to complement and support one another through mutual solidarity. For such a union to endure, there must be a central point around which the others rally. Becoming the center of unity for people is a grave task carrying immense responsibility. It demands inner greatness, consistency, and strength. Therefore, anyone who wishes to gather others around themselves must first examine whether they are equal to the challenge. Attempting to unite people without a true inner calling causes more confusion than if no union had been formed at all.

Where a true rallying point exists, those who hesitate at first will gradually come forward on their own. Those who delay will suffer the consequences, because timing is vital when holding together. Relationships form and strengthen according to deep inner laws. Shared experiences cement them, and anyone who comes too late to share in these foundational moments will find the door closed.

On the other hand, someone who recognizes the need for union but lacks the inner strength to act as its center has a duty to join an existing organic community.

imagen.text: Water on the earth: the image of Holding Together. Thus the kings of antiquity granted the individual states as fiefs and maintained friendly relations with the feudal lords.
imagen.commentary: Water on the earth fills every crevice and clings tightly to the soil. The social organization of antiquity was founded on this very principle of solidarity between the ruler and his dependents. Water flows together naturally because all its parts are subject to the same laws. In the same way, human society must hold together through a community of shared interests that makes every individual feel like a member of a greater whole. The central power of any social organism must ensure that every member finds their true interest in holding together, just as it was in the paternal relationship between the high king and his feudal lords in ancient China.

1.text: Hold to him truly and faithfully: this is no blame. Truth like a full earthen bowl: Thus, in the end, good fortune comes from without.
1.commentary: When establishing relationships, absolute sincerity is the only proper foundation. This mindset is represented by a filled earthen bowl, where everything is substance and nothing is empty form. Such a disposition does not express itself in clever words, but through an inner power so potent that it naturally attracts good fortune from the outside.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Hold to him inwardly. Perseverance brings good fortune.
2.commentary: When a person responds uprightly and perseveringly to a call from above requesting their cooperation, the resulting relationship remains primarily internal, allowing them to retain their autonomy. Conversely, anyone who desperately clings to others for social advancement fails to follow the path of the superior man. Instead of maintaining his dignity, he compromises himself.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: You hold together with people who are not the right ones.
3.commentary: We often find ourselves surrounded by people who do not belong to our own sphere. In these situations, we must not let habit betray us into a false familiarity. It goes without saying that this would lead to trouble. Maintaining courtesy without intimacy is the only correct approach toward such people; only by keeping our distance do we remain free for future relationships with our true peers.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Hold to him outwardly as well. Perseverance brings good fortune.
4.commentary: Here, the relationship with the person who serves as the center of unity is already firmly established. In this position, one can and should openly show allegiance. It is simply a matter of remaining steadfast and refusing to be led astray.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Manifestation of holding together. In the royal hunt, the king allows beating from three sides only and relinquishes the game that turns away in front. The citizens need no warning. Good fortune!
5.commentary:
During the royal driven hunts in ancient China, it was customary to herd the game from three sides only, leaving the fourth side open for the animals to escape. Those that did not turn away ran toward a gate where the king stood ready. Only the animals that entered this enclosure were taken; those that broke away in front were allowed to run free. This custom reflected the royal mindset: the king refused to turn the hunt into a slaughter, taking only the game that had, so to speak, voluntarily surrendered itself.

This line depicts a ruler or an influential leader who naturally attracts people. He welcomes those who come to him and allows those who choose otherwise to go their own way. He neither begs nor flatters; everyone comes of their own accord. This creates a voluntary allegiance among his followers. People do not need to constrain themselves artificially; they can express their true dispositions without fear. No restrictive measures or policing are required, as they are naturally devoted to their leader. This same freedom applies to life in general. We should never court the favor of others through sycophancy. If we cultivate the inner purity and strength necessary to become a focal point, the people destined to be with us will gather naturally.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: He finds no head for holding together. Misfortune.
6.commentary: The head signifies the beginning. Without a proper beginning, there can be no proper end. If someone misses the opportunity to unite and continually hesitates, shrinking from wholehearted devotion, they will live to regret their mistake when it is too late.
6.title: Six at the top means:

9.name: THE TAMING POWER OF THE SMALL
9.title: Hexagram 9 小畜 - XIǍO CHÙ / THE TAMING POWER OF THE SMALL
9.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 9 (XIǍO CHÙ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
9.intro: The hexagram signifies the small, representing the power of the dark element that restrains, tames, or inhibits. A weak line occupies the fourth place, the position of the minister, holding all the remaining strong lines in check. Viewed as an image, it shows the wind blowing across the sky. It restrains the ascending breath of the Creative, causing the clouds to condense, though it is not yet strong enough to bring rain. The hexagram presents a configuration where the weak temporarily restrains the strong. This can only lead to success if it is achieved through gentleness.

dictamen.text: The Taming Power of the Small has success. Dense clouds, no rain from our western region.
dictamen.commentary: This imagery arises from the historical circumstances in China during the reign of King Wen.

imagen.text: The wind drives across the heavens: The image of the Taming Power of the Small. Thus the superior man refines the outward expression of his being.
imagen.commentary: While the wind gathers the clouds in the sky, it produces no massive or lasting effects because it is merely air without a solid body. Similarly, during times when a grand outward impact is impossible, an individual can only refine the minor details and outward expressions of their character.

1.text: Return to the way. How could this be a blame? Good fortune!
1.commentary: It is in the nature of a strong character to press forward. In doing so, however, one enters a sphere of restraint. Therefore, he returns to the path appropriate for his situation, where he remains free to advance or retreat. It is both wise and reasonable not to force anything by violence, which naturally brings good fortune.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Allowing oneself to be drawn into returning. Good fortune!
2.commentary: One naturally wishes to advance. Yet, before moving further, the example of other like-minded individuals reveals that the path is blocked. In such a situation, a reasonable and resolute person does not wait to face a personal rebuff. Instead, they choose to retreat alongside their peers when pushing forward does not suit the times. This brings good fortune, as it prevents them from compromising themselves.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: The spokes burst from the wagon wheels. Husband and wife roll their eyes.
3.commentary: An attempt is made here to press forward by force, under the assumption that the restraining power is weak. However, since circumstances actually grant power to the weak element, this attempt at a surprise advance is bound to fail. External conditions stall progress, much like a wagon that cannot move when its spokes break. Yet, this hint from fate is ignored, leading to bitter arguments akin to disputes between a husband and wife. This is clearly an unfavorable state of affairs; even if the weaker party manages to hold their ground due to the situation, the friction involved prevents any positive outcome. Consequently, the strong character cannot properly exert their influence on their surroundings. Having suffered a rebuff where an easy victory was expected, they have compromised their own position.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: If you are sincere, blood vanishes and anxiety gives way. No blame.
4.commentary: Occupying a difficult, highly responsible position, one must guide and restrain the ruler or powerful figure to ensure that justice is done. This carries a great danger, even raising the dread of bloodshed. However, the power of selfless truth outweighs these obstacles. It commands such respect that one's efforts are brought to a successful conclusion, causing all danger of bloodshed and anxiety to dissipate.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: If you are sincere and loyally bound, you are rich in your neighbor.
5.commentary: Loyalty leads to a firm bond because it relies on mutual completion. For the weaker element, loyalty manifests as devotion; for the stronger, it shows as reliability. This reciprocal completion generates genuine wealth, which shines brightest when it is shared with one's neighbor rather than kept to oneself. Shared joy is double joy.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: The rain comes, rest is attained. This is due to the lasting effect of character. Perseverance brings danger to the woman. The moon is nearly full. If the superior man persists, misfortune comes.
6.commentary: Success has been achieved. The wind has finally gathered the rain, and a firm standpoint is reached. This outcome is the result of a gradual accumulation of small effects born out of respect for a superior character. However, a success built up piece by piece demands extreme caution. It would be dangerous to indulge in the illusion that one can exploit or boast about it. The feminine, weak element that has won this victory must never stubbornly presume upon it, as that would invite danger. The dark power of the moon is at its peak when it is nearly full. Once it faces the sun directly as a full moon, its decline becomes inevitable. Under these circumstances, one must remain content with what has been achieved. Advancing further before the proper time has arrived would bring misfortune.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

10.name: TREADING
10.title: Hexagram 10 履 - Lǚ / TREADING
10.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 10 (Lǚ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
10.intro: Treading signifies the correct way of conducting oneself. Heaven, the father, resides above, while the lake, the youngest daughter, rests below. This arrangement demonstrates the natural distinction between high and low, which forms the foundation of orderly social conduct. Treading literally means "stepping upon something." The small, Joyous element treads upon the great, Strong element. The direction of movement for both primary trigrams is upward. That the strong treads upon the weak is a natural order, which is why the Book of Changes does not explicitly mention it. The weak treading upon the strong carries no danger because it occurs in good humor and without presumption, ensuring the strong is not provoked and tolerates it with good nature.

dictamen.text: Treading upon the tail of the tiger. It does not bite the man. Success.
dictamen.commentary:
The situation is inherently difficult, as the strongest and the weakest stand in direct proximity. The weak follows behind the strong and interacts with it. Yet the strong tolerates this and inflicts no harm, because the contact is cheerful and non-threatening.

In human terms, this represents dealing with wild, unapproachable people. In such cases, one achieves their purpose by adhering to proper decorum and good manners. Maintaining pleasant, courteous conduct ensures success, even when facing highly irritable individuals.

imagen.text: Heaven above, the lake below: the image of Treading. Thus the superior man distinguishes between high and low and thereby establishes the resolve of the people.
imagen.commentary: Heaven and the lake exhibit a difference in height that arises naturally from their very essence, completely free from envy. Similarly, differences in rank must exist within human society; absolute equality is impossible to achieve. However, the crucial factor is that social distinctions must not be arbitrary or unjust, as that format inevitably leads to envy and class struggle. Conversely, when external rank corresponds to inner worth, and merit serves as the measure of social standing, people find contentment and society achieves harmony.

1.text: Simple treading. Progress without blame.
1.commentary: One is in a position not yet bound by the obligations of social intercourse. By conducting oneself with simplicity, one remains free from societal constraints and can peacefully follow the inclinations of the heart, making no demands on others and remaining content. Here, treading does not mean standing still, but rather moving forward. Although one starts from a very humble baseline, they possess the inner strength that guarantees progress. Contentment with simplicity allows one to advance without blame. If someone cannot find peace in modest circumstances, they become restless and ambitious, seeking advancement merely to escape poverty and low status rather than to achieve something meaningful. Once such a person attains their goal, they inevitably become arrogant and extravagant, making their progress blameworthy. The capable person, by contrast, remains content in simple conduct; they wish to advance in order to accomplish something of value. When they reach their goal, they perform meaningful work, and all is well.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Treading a smooth, level path. The perseverance of a quiet man brings good fortune.
2.commentary: This portrays the situation of a solitary sage. He stays far from the hustle and bustle of the world, seeks nothing, desires nothing from anyone, and refuses to be dazzled by alluring goals. True to himself, he walks a level road, passing through life unassailed. Because he is self-sufficient and does not challenge fate, he remains free from complications.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: A one-eyed man can see, a lame man can tread. He treads upon the tail of the tiger. It bites the man. Misfortune! Thus does a warrior act for his great prince.
3.commentary: A one-eyed man can see, but not clearly enough for true vision. A lame man can tread, but not well enough to make real progress. If someone with such deficiencies nevertheless considers himself strong and rushes into danger, he brings misfortune upon himself by attempting something far beyond his strength. This reckless way of plunging ahead without regard for one's own limitations might, at most, be acceptable for a warrior fighting on behalf of his great prince.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: He treads upon the tail of the tiger. Caution and circumspection lead ultimately to good fortune.
4.commentary: This denotes a dangerous enterprise. The inner strength required to endure it is present, but it combines externally with a hesitant caution. This stands in sharp contrast to the previous line, which is inwardly weak but aggressively pushes forward. Consequently, ultimate success is assured, allowing one to achieve their will and overcome danger by stepping forward carefully.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Resolute treading. Perseverance with awareness of danger.
5.commentary: This refers to the ruler of the entire hexagram. One finds oneself compelled to act with absolute resolution. However, one must remain acutely aware of the danger inherent in such a decisive stance, especially if one persists in it. Only by maintaining this awareness of danger can success be achieved.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Look at your conduct and examine the favorable signs. If everything is complete, supreme good fortune comes.
6.commentary: The work is completed. If one wishes to know whether good fortune will follow, one must look back at their past conduct and its consequences. If the effects are good, good fortune is certain. No one truly knows themselves completely; it is only by looking at the consequences of one's actions and the fruits of one's labor that one can gauge what to expect.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

11.name: PEACE
11.title: Hexagram 11 泰 - TÀI / PEACE
11.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 11 (TAI) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
11.intro: The Receptive, whose movement is downward, is above; the Creative, whose movement is upward, is below. Their influences therefore meet and are in deep harmony, so that all living things bloom and prosper. This sign is associated with the first month (February-March), in which the forces of nature prepare for the arrival of a new spring.

dictamen.text: Peace. The small departs, the great approaches. Good fortune! Success!
dictamen.commentary:
In nature, this hexagram indicates a time when heaven is on earth, so to speak. Heaven has placed itself beneath the earth. Thus, their forces unite in deep harmony, giving rise to peace and blessings for all living beings.

In the human world, it signifies a period of social concord. Those in high positions humble themselves before the lowly, and the humble are well-disposed toward the great, bringing an end to all feuds.

Within, at the center, in the decisive position, is the light principle; the dark principle is outside. Thus, the light has a powerful effect, and the dark is yielding. In this way, both sides receive their due. When the good elements of society occupy central positions and hold the reins of power, the bad elements also come under their influence and improve. When the spirit derived from heaven rules within man, his physical nature also comes under its influence and finds its appropriate place.

The individual lines enter the hexagram from below and leave it at the top. Therefore, the small, the weak, and the negative are on the way out, while the great, the strong, and the good are on the rise. This brings good fortune and success.

imagen.text: Heaven and earth unite: the image of Peace. Thus the ruler divides and completes the course of heaven and earth, furthers and regulates the gifts of heaven and earth, and so aids the people.
imagen.commentary: Heaven and earth are in communion and combine their effects. This brings a general time of blossoming and prosperity. This stream of energy must be regulated by the ruler of men, which is accomplished through division. Thus, the undifferentiated flow of time is divided by man into seasons according to the succession of its phenomena, and all-encompassing space is distinguished into cardinal directions through human definitions. In this manner, nature, with its overwhelming abundance of phenomena, is restricted and harnessed. On the other hand, nature must be furthered in its products. This happens when its yields are adapted to the right time and the right place, increasing the natural harvest. This restricting and frustrating activity toward nature is the work done upon nature that benefits mankind. [

1.text: When ribbon-grass is pulled up, the sod comes with it. Each according to its kind. Undertakings bring good fortune.
1.commentary: In times of prosperity, every able man who is called to an office immediately draws other like-minded people after him, just as when pulling up ribbon-grass, one always pulls up several stalks connected by their roots. In such times, when widespread effectiveness is possible, the mind of the capable man is set on going forth into life to accomplish something meaningful.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Bearing the uncultured with gentleness, crossing the river with resolution, not neglecting what is distant, not regarding one's companions: thus one may manage to walk in the middle.
2.commentary: In times of prosperity, it is crucial above all to possess the inner greatness to tolerate even the imperfect. A great master knows no sterile material; he can make something out of anything. This broad-mindedness, however, is by no means negligence or weakness. Precisely in times of blossom, one must always be ready to venture even dangerous undertakings, such as crossing a river, if they are necessary. Likewise, one must not neglect what is distant, but attend to everything with punctuality. One must be particularly on guard against factions and clique-building. For even though like-minded individuals come forward together, they must not form a party through mutual collusion; instead, everyone must do his duty. These four things are the means by which one can overcome the hidden danger of gradual slackening that lurks in every time of peace, and in this way, one finds the right middle course of action.
2.title: Nine at the second place means:

3.text: No plain without a slope, no departure without a return. He who remains persevering in danger is without blame. Do not complain about this truth; enjoy the happiness you still possess.
3.commentary: Everything earthly is subject to change. Decline follows prosperity. This is the eternal law on earth. Evil can indeed be held back, but it cannot be permanently eliminated; it returns. This conviction could make one melancholy, but it should not. It should only prevent one from falling into delusion during times of good fortune. If one remains mindful of danger, one stays persevering and makes no mistake. As long as a person's inner being remains stronger and richer than their external fortune, as long as we remain inwardly superior to fate, good fortune will remain true to us.
3.title: Nine at the third place means:

4.text: He flutters down, not boasting of his wealth, together with his neighbor, guileless and sincere.
4.commentary: In times of mutual trust, those of high rank come to the lowly quite simply and without boasting of their wealth. This is not due to the compulsion of circumstances, but corresponds to their innermost disposition. Then the approach occurs quite naturally, because it rests on inner conviction.
4.title: Six at the fourth place means:

5.text: The Sovereign Yi gives his daughter in marriage. This brings blessing and supreme good fortune.
5.commentary: The Sovereign Yi is Tang, the Completer. He decreed that the imperial princesses, although higher in rank than the husbands to whom they were wed, should obey their husbands just like other wives. Here too, a truly humble union of high and low is pointed out, which brings happiness and blessing.
5.title: Six at the fifth place means:

6.text: The rampart falls back into the moat. Use no armies now. In your own city, proclaim your commands. Perseverance brings humiliation.
6.commentary: The change already indicated in the middle of the hexagram has come to pass. The city wall sinks back into the moat from which it was dug. Doom breaks in. In this case, it is necessary to submit to fate and not try to halt it through violent resistance. The only thing left to do is to maintain oneself within the narrowest circle. If one wished to stubbornly resist evil in the usual way, the collapse would only worsen, and humiliation would be the consequence.
6.title: Six at the top means:

12.name: STANDSTILL
12.title: Hexagram 12 否 - PǏ / STANDSTILL
12.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 12 (PǏ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
12.intro: This hexagram is the exact opposite of the preceding one. Heaven above withdraws further and further, while Earth below sinks deeper into the abyss. The creative forces are out of relation. It is a time of standstill and decline. This hexagram is linked to the seventh month (August-September), when the year has passed its peak and autumnal decay prepares its approach.

dictamen.text: Evil people do not further The perseverance of the superior man. The great departs, the small approaches.
dictamen.commentary: Heaven and earth are out of communion, and all things become rigid. High and low are out of relation, and confusion and disorder prevail on earth.
