Within is the dark, and without is the light. Within is weakness, without is hardness; within are the inferior men, and without are the superior men. The way of the inferior man is ascending, while the way of the superior man is declining. Yet the superior men do not allow themselves to be turned from their principles. If they can no longer act effectively, they remain true to these principles and withdraw into concealment.

imagen.text: Heaven and earth do not unite: The image of Standstill. Thus the superior man falls back upon his inner worth In order to escape the difficulties. He does not permit himself to be honored by revenues.
imagen.commentary: When mutual distrust prevails in public life due to the influence of inferior men, fruitful activity becomes impossible because the foundation is wrong. Therefore, the superior man knows what to do under such circumstances. He does not allow himself to be tempted by brilliant offers to participate in public life, which would only be dangerous for him since he cannot join in the baseness of others. Thus, he hides his worth and withdraws into concealment.

1.text: When ribbon-grass is pulled up, the sod comes with it. Each according to its kind. Perseverance brings good fortune and success.
1.commentary: The text is almost identical to the first line of the preceding hexagram, but in the opposite sense. There, one person draws another along into an official career. Here, one draws another along into retirement from public life. Therefore, instead of saying "Undertakings bring good fortune," it says here, "Perseverance brings good fortune and success." Only by understanding when the opportunities for action are gone and withdrawing in time does one spare oneself humiliation and achieve success in a higher sense, knowing how to safeguard the value of one's personality.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: They bear and endure, This means good fortune for the inferior men. The standstill serves the great man for success.
2.commentary: Inferior men are ready to flatter their superiors in a fawning manner. They would even tolerate the superior man if he helped them resolve the confusion. This brings good fortune to them. But the great man quietly bears the consequences of the standstill. He does not mix with the crowd of inferior men; that is not his place. By accepting personal suffering, he ensures the ultimate success of his principles.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: They bear shame.
3.commentary: Inferior men who have risen to power illegitimately feel unequal to the responsibility they have assumed. They begin, at first without showing it outwardly, to feel ashamed in secret. This marks the beginning of a turn for the better.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: He who acts at the command of the Highest remains without blame. Those of like mind share in the blessing.
4.commentary: The time of standstill approaches its turning point. Whoever wishes to restore order must be called to do so and possess the necessary authority. Anyone attempting to set things right according to their own whim would bring about errors and failure. But he who is called is favored by the conditions of the time, and his blessing extends to all those of like mind.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: The standstill comes to an end. Good fortune to the great man! "What if it should fail, what if it should fail!" Thereby he binds it to a cluster of mulberry shoots.
5.commentary: The times are changing. The right man has arrived who can restore order. Therefore, good fortune! But precisely during such periods of transition, fear and trembling are necessary. Only through the utmost anxiety, constantly thinking, "What if it should fail," is success secured. When a mulberry bush is cut down, a series of exceptionally firm shoots sprout from the root. Therefore, the consolidation of success is symbolized by tying it to a cluster of mulberry shoots. [
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: The standstill ceases. First standstill, then good fortune.
6.commentary: The standstill does not last forever. However, it does not end by itself; it requires the right man to put an end to it. This marks the difference between peace and standstill. Peace requires continuous effort to be maintained. Left to itself, it would turn into standstill and decline. A period of decline does not turn back into peace and prosperity on its own; it requires effort to be overcome. This highlights the creative role of man, which is necessary to bring order to the world.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

13.name: Fellowship with Men
13.title: Hexagram 13 同人 - Tóng Rén / Fellowship with Men
13.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 13 (Tóng Rén) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
13.intro: The image of the upper primary trigram, Qián, is heaven; that of the lower, Lí, is flame. It is the nature of fire to flame up to heaven. This gives the idea of fellowship. It is the second line that, through its central character, unites the five strong lines around it. This hexagram is the counterpart of Hexagram 7, The Army. There, danger is within and obedience without-the essence of a warlike army, which needs one strong line among many weak ones to hold it together. Here, clarity is within and strength without-the essence of a peaceful union of mankind, which needs one yielding line among many firm ones to maintain cohesion.

dictamen.text: Fellowship with Men in the Open: Success. It furthers one to cross the great water. The perseverance of the superior man furthers.
dictamen.commentary: True fellowship among men must rest upon a cosmic basis. It is not the private ends of the ego, but the goals of humanity that bring about enduring fellowship among men; hence it is said: "Fellowship with men in the open brings success." When such unity prevails, even difficult and dangerous tasks, such as crossing the great water, can be accomplished. But to bring about such fellowship, a persevering and enlightened leader is needed, one who possesses clear, convincing, and inspiring goals and knows how to carry them out with strength.

imagen.text: Heaven together with fire: The image of Fellowship with Men. Thus the superior man organizes the clans and distinguishes things.
imagen.commentary: Heaven has the same direction of movement as fire, yet it is distinct from it. Just as the luminous bodies in the heaven serve to organize and divide time, so human society and all things that truly belong together must be organically structured. Fellowship should not be a mere blending of individuals or a blurring of distinctions-that would be chaos, not fellowship. Instead, it requires an organized diversity to lead to true order.

1.text: Fellowship with men at the gate. No blame.
1.commentary: The beginning of a gathering of men should take place before the door. All are equally close to one another. No factional interests exist as yet. Thus, no mistake is made. The foundations of any union must be equally accessible to all participants. Secret agreements bring misfortune.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Fellowship with men in the clan. Humiliation.
2.commentary: Here lies the danger of a separate faction based on personal and selfish interests. Such factions, which are exclusive and do not leave room for everyone-obliged to condemn one part of humanity in order to rally the rest-arise from base motives and therefore lead to humiliation in the long run.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: He hides weapons in the thicket, He climbs the high hill in front of it. For three years he does not rise.
3.commentary: Here fellowship has turned into mistrust. Men distrust one another, lay secret ambushes, and seek to spy on the other from afar. One is dealing with a tough opponent who cannot be overcome in this manner. Obstacles are shown here that stand in the way of fellowship with others. One has ulterior motives oneself and seeks to take the other by surprise. But this very behavior breeds suspicion; one imagines the same trickeries in the opponent and tries to spy them out. As a result, one moves further and further away from true fellowship. The longer this lasts, the more alienated one becomes.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: He climbs up on his wall; he cannot attack. Good fortune!
4.commentary: Here, reconciliation draws nearer after alienation. To be sure, there are still dividing walls upon which men stand facing each other. But the difficulties are too great. One falls into distress, and through distress, one comes to one's senses. One cannot fight, and it is precisely upon this that good fortune rests.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Men bound in fellowship first weep and lament, But afterward they laugh. After great struggles they succeed in meeting.
5.commentary:
Two people are outwardly separated but united in their hearts. They are kept apart by their positions in life. Many obstacles and inhibitions rise between them, causing them grief. But they allow no obstacle to sever their bond; they remain true to each other instead. And although overcoming these obstacles demands severe struggles, they will ultimately triumph, and then their sadness will turn to joy when they find each other.

Confucius says concerning this:
Life leads the earnest man through a complex, winding path.
Often the power of its course is checked, then it goes straight again.
Here an eloquent mind may pour itself out freely in words,
There the heavy burden of knowledge must lock itself in silence.
But where two people are at one in their inmost hearts,
They break even the strength of iron or bronze.
And where two people completely understand each other in their inmost hearts,
Their words are sweet and strong like the fragrance of orchids.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Fellowship with men in the pasture. No remorse.
6.commentary: The warm attachment of the heart is lacking here. One actually stands outside the fellowship with others. Yet one joins them. The fellowship does not embrace everyone, but only those living outwardly together. The pasture is the meadow outside the city. The ultimate goal of the union of mankind is not yet attained here. However, one need not reproach oneself. One joins society without separate, selfish aims.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

14.name: Possession in Great Measure
14.title: Hexagram 14 大有 - Dà Yǒu / Possession in Great Measure
14.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 14 (Dà Yǒu) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
14.intro: The fire in heaven above shines far, causing all things to come into the light and manifest themselves. The weak fifth line occupies the place of honor, and all the strong lines correspond to it. He who is humble and mild in a high position wins all things.

dictamen.text: Possession in Great Measure: Supreme success.
dictamen.commentary: The two primary trigrams indicate that strength and clarity unite. Possession in great measure is determined by destiny and accords with the time. How is it possible that the weak line has the power to hold fast and possess the strong lines? Through its selfless humility. It is a favorable time. Strength within, clarity and culture without. Power expresses itself in a refined and controlled way. This brings supreme success and wealth.

imagen.text: Fire in heaven above: the image of Possession in Great Measure. Thus the superior man curbs evil and furthers good, and thereby obeys the benevolent will of heaven.
imagen.commentary: The sun high in heaven, shining upon everything on earth, is the image of possession in great measure. But such possession must be properly managed. The sun brings both evil and good to light. Man must combat and curb evil, and further and favor good. Only in this way does one respond to the benevolent will of God, who wills only good and not evil.

1.text: No relationship with what is harmful; there is no blame. If one remains conscious of difficulty, one remains without blame.
1.commentary: Great possession that is still in its initial stage and has not yet experienced any challenge is without blame, for there is as yet no opportunity to make mistakes. But there are still many difficulties to overcome. Only by remaining conscious of these difficulties does one remain truly free inside from the possibility of pride and extravagance, and has fundamentally overcome every blame.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: A large wagon to load. One may undertake something. No blame.
2.commentary: Great possession consists not only in the quantity of goods at one's disposal, but above all in their mobility and utility. Then one may use them for undertakings and remain free from embarrassment and mistakes. The large wagon, which can be heavily loaded and driven far, signifies capable helpers who stand at one's side and are equal to their task. One can load great responsibility onto such people, which is necessary for important undertakings.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: A prince offers it to the Son of Heaven. A petty man cannot do this.
3.commentary: It is the way of a magnanimous, open-minded person not to view his possessions as his exclusive personal property, but to place them at the disposal of the ruler or the community. By doing so, he takes the correct attitude toward wealth, which can never endure as private property. A narrow-minded person, of course, is incapable of this. For him, great possession turns to his detriment because, instead of sacrificing, he wishes to keep it.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: He makes a distinction between himself and his neighbor. No blame.
4.commentary: A position is characterized that stands between rich and powerful neighbors. This brings danger. In such a case, one must look neither to the right nor to the left, remaining free from envy and the temptation to equal others. Thus one remains free from blame.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: He whose sincerity is accessible and yet dignified has good fortune.
5.commentary: The situation is very favorable. Without external compulsion, simply as a result of uncalculated sincerity, one wins people over so that they are attached in true sincerity as well. Yet in the time of Possession in Great Measure, mildness alone is not enough. Otherwise, insolence could easily creep in. This rise of insolence must be kept in check by dignity; then good fortune is assured.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: He is blessed from heaven. Good fortune! Nothing that is not advantageous.
6.commentary:
In the fullness of possession and power, one remains humble and honors the wise man who stands outside the worldly bustle. Thereby one places oneself under the blissful influence from heaven, and everything goes well.

Confucius says of this line:

"To bless means to help. Heaven helps the devoted; people help the truthful. He who walks in truthfulness and is devoted in his thinking, and furthermore holds the worthy in high esteem, is blessed from heaven. He finds good fortune, and there is nothing that is not advantageous."
6.title: Nine at the top means:

15.name: MODESTY
15.title: Hexagram 15 謙 - QIĀN / MODESTY
15.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 15 (QIÁN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
15.intro: The hexagram is composed of Gèn, Keeping Still, the Mountain, and Kūn, the Receptive, Earth. The mountain is the youngest son of the Creative, the representative of heaven on earth. It dispenses the blessings of heaven, the clouds and rain that gather around its peak, downward, and then shines transfigured in heavenly light. This demonstrates modesty and its effect in high and strong people. Above stands Kūn, the Earth. The quality of the earth is lowliness, but for this very reason, it is represented as exalted in this hexagram by being placed above the mountain. This shows the effect of modesty in low, simple people: they are exalted by it.

dictamen.text: Modesty creates success. The superior man carries through to the end.
dictamen.commentary:
The law of heaven empties the full and fills the modest. When the sun is at its highest, it must move toward its setting according to heavenly law; when it is at its deepest below the earth, it moves toward a new rising. When the moon is full, it wanes according to the same law, and when it is empty, it waxes again. This heavenly law also operates in the destinies of human beings. The law of earth is to change the full and flow toward the modest: high mountains are worn down by waters, and valleys are filled up. The law of destiny's powers is to harm the full and dispense good fortune to the modest. Humans, too, hate the full and love the modest.

Destinies follow fixed laws that act with necessity. Yet human beings have it in their power to shape their own destiny, depending on whether they expose themselves to the influence of blessing or destructive forces through their behavior. When a person holds a high position and shows modesty, they shine in the light of wisdom. When they are low and show modesty, they cannot be overlooked. Thus, the superior man succeeds in carrying his work through to the end without boasting of his achievement.

imagen.text: Within the earth, there is a mountain: The image of Modesty. Thus the superior man diminishes what is too much, And increases what is too little. He weighs things and makes them equal.
imagen.commentary: The wealth of the earth hiding a mountain within is not apparent from the outside, for the height of the mountain serves to balance the depressions. Thus high and low complement each other, and the result is a plain. This provides the image of modesty: that which required long-lasting effort appears natural and easy. This is how the superior man acts when establishing order on earth. He balances social extremes, which are the source of unrest, and thereby creates just and level conditions.

1.text: A modest-modest superior man may cross the great water. Good fortune!
1.commentary: A dangerous undertaking, such as crossing a great water, is made very difficult if many demands and considerations must be taken into account. On the other hand, it becomes easy if it is handled quickly and simply. Therefore, the completely unpretentious mindset of modesty is well-suited to accomplish even difficult undertakings, because it makes no demands or preconditions, but dispatches the matter nimbly and easily. Where no claims are made, no resistances arise.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Modesty that expresses itself. Perseverance brings good fortune. Out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.
2.commentary: When someone is so inwardly modest that this attitude shows in their outward behavior, it turns out to their good fortune. In this way, they naturally possess the possibility of persistent influence, which no one can displace.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: A meritorious and modest superior man carries through to the end. Good fortune!
3.commentary: Here is the center of the hexagram, where its secret is voiced. Through great achievements, one soon acquires a significant name. If one allows oneself to be blinded by fame, criticism will very soon set in, and difficulties will arise. If, on the other hand, one remains modest despite one's merits, one makes oneself beloved and wins the helper forces needed to carry the work one has undertaken through to the end.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Nothing that would not be furthering For modesty in movement.
4.commentary: Everything has its measure. Even modesty in behavior can be exaggerated. Here it is in place, since the position between a meritorious assistant below and a kindly ruler above carries a very great responsibility. The trust of the superior must not be abused, and the merits of the subordinate must not be obscured. There are indeed officials who do not distinguish themselves; they shelter behind the letter of regulations, reject all responsibility, accept pay without rendering a corresponding service, and carry titles given no meaning by reality. The modesty mentioned here is the exact opposite of that. Modesty in such a position shows itself precisely by being engaged with interest in the work.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Not boasting of wealth to one's neighbor. It is furthering to attack with force. Nothing that would not be furthering.
5.commentary: Modesty is different from weak good-nature that lets everything slide. When occupying a responsible post, one must occasionally take energetic action. But for this, it is necessary not to seek to influence by personally boasting of one's superiority; rather, one must be certain of one's surroundings. The intervention must be purely objective and must contain nothing personally offensive. In this, modesty shows itself even in severity.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Modesty that expresses itself. It is furthering to set armies marching To chastise one's own city and one's own country.
6.commentary: Anyone who is truly earnest about their modesty must ensure that it manifests in reality. They must proceed with great energy. When hostility arises, nothing is easier than to look for the blame in others. A weak person might then withdraw into themselves, feeling offended and taking pity on themselves, believing it to be modesty that they do not fight back. True modesty shows itself in vigorously setting about creating order, beginning the chastisement with one's own self and one's closest circle. Something truly powerful is accomplished only when one has the courage to let one's armies march against oneself.
6.title: Six at the top means:

16.name: ENTHUSIASM
16.title: Hexagram 16 豫 - YÙ / ENTHUSIASM
16.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete translation and analysis of Hexagram 16 (YÙ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
16.intro: The strong line in the fourth place, the position of the leading official, finds cooperation and obedience from all the other weak lines. The upper primary trigram, Zhèn, has movement as its characteristic, while the lower, Kūn, represents obedience and devotion. Thus, a movement is initiated that meets with devotion, resulting in a sweeping, enthusiastic effect. Furthermore, the law of movement along the line of least resistance is of great importance, expressed in this hexagram as a law for both natural phenomena and human life.

dictamen.text: Enthusiasm. It is favorable to appoint assistants and set armies marching.
dictamen.commentary:
The time of enthusiasm relies on the presence of a prominent man who is in touch with the soul of the people and acts in harmony with it. Therefore, he finds universal, willing obedience. To awaken enthusiasm, it is necessary to adjust one's regulations to the nature of those being led. The inviolability of natural laws rests upon this rule of movement along the line of least resistance. These laws are not external to things, but rather the immanent harmony of movement within them. This is why heavenly bodies do not deviate from their orbits, and all natural processes unfold with strict regularity.

A similar principle applies to human society. Here, too, only those laws deeply rooted in popular sentiment can be successfully implemented, whereas laws opposing this sentiment only arouse bitterness.

Enthusiasm also makes it possible to appoint assistants to carry out tasks without fearing hidden opposition. It is enthusiasm that unifies mass movements, as in war, enabling them to achieve victory.

imagen.text: Thunder comes sounding forth from the earth: the image of Enthusiasm. Thus the ancient kings made music to honor merit, and offered it magnificently to the Supreme God, inviting their ancestors to be present.
imagen.commentary:
When thunder, the electrical force, bursts forth again from the earth at the beginning of summer and the first thunderstorm refreshes nature, a long-held tension breaks. Relief and joy take its place. Similarly, music possesses the power to ease the tension in the heart and dissolve the grip of dark emotions. The heart's enthusiasm expresses itself spontaneously through song, dance, and the rhythmic movement of the body. Since antiquity, the inspiring effect of invisible sound, which moves and unites human hearts, has been perceived as a mystery. 

Rulers utilized this natural inclination toward music, elevating and organizing it. Music was regarded as something serious and sacred, intended to purify human emotions. It was meant to praise the virtues of heroes and thus bridge the gap to the invisible world. In the temple, people approached God with music and pantomimes [

1.text: Enthusiasm that expresses itself brings misfortune.
1.commentary: Someone in a subordinate position enjoys noble connections, which they enthusiastically boast about. This arrogance inevitably attracts misfortune. Enthusiasm must never be an egoistic feeling; it is only justified as a shared disposition that connects people with one another.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Firm as a rock. Not a whole day. Perseverance brings good fortune.
2.commentary: This describes someone who refuses to be deceived by illusions. While others let themselves be blinded by enthusiasm, this person recognizes the first signs of the times with absolute clarity. Thus, they are neither flattering toward those above nor negligent toward those below; they remain as firm as a rock. As soon as the first sign of discord appears, they know how to withdraw in time, without wasting even a single day. Perseverance in such conduct brings good fortune [
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Enthusiasm that looks upward brings remorse. Hesitation brings remorse.
3.commentary: This is the exact opposite of the previous line: where there was independence, here is an enthusiastic gazing upward. If one hesitates too long, that too brings remorse. In approaching others, one must seize the right moment; only then does one hit the mark.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: The source of enthusiasm. He achieves great things. Do not doubt. Friends gather around you as around a hair clasp.
4.commentary: This refers to someone capable of awakening enthusiasm through their own confidence and freedom from doubt. By remaining completely truthful and unwavering, they attract people. By placing trust in others, they win them over for enthusiastic cooperation and achieve success. Just as a hair clasp holds hair together and unites it, this person unifies people through the support they provide.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Persistently ill, yet never dying.
5.commentary: Here, enthusiasm is obstructed. One finds oneself under continuous pressure, which prevents breathing freely. However, this pressure can have its advantages. It preserves a person from wasting their energy in empty enthusiasm. Thus, constant pressure can serve precisely to keep one alive.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Blinded enthusiasm. But if one comes to a change after completion, that is no blame.
6.commentary: Allowing oneself to be blinded by enthusiasm is harmful. However, even if this delusion is already an accomplished fact, if one can still change, one becomes free of blame. Sobriety following false enthusiasm is entirely possible and highly favorable.
6.title: Six at the top means:

17.name: FOLLOWING
17.title: Hexagram 17 隨 - SUI / FOLLOWING
17.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 17 (SUI) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
17.intro:
The upper trigram is Duì, the Joyous, characterized by pleasure; the lower is Zhèn, the Arousing, characterized by movement. Joy in movement leads to following. Duì represents the youngest daughter, while Zhèn represents the eldest son. An older man places himself below a young girl and shows consideration for her. By doing so, he moves her to follow him.

The Judgment

FOLLOWING has supreme success.
Perseverance furthers. No blame.

To achieve following, one must first know how to adapt. Only through service does one learn to rule, for this is the only way to gain the joyful assent of those below, which is essential for following. Whenever anyone seeks to force compliance through cunning, violence, conspiracy, or factionalism, resistance invariably arises, preventing willing compliance.

However, joyful movement can also lead to evil. Therefore, a qualifying condition is added: "Perseverance furthers" - meaning consistency in what is right - and "no blame." Just as one should demand following only under this condition, one must also follow others only under this condition to avoid harm.

The idea of following while adapting to the demands of the time is great and significant, which is why the accompanying judgment is so favorable.

The Image

Thunder in the middle of the lake: the
image of FOLLOWING. Thus the superior man, as darkness
falls, goes indoors for refreshment and rest.

In autumn, electricity retreats into the earth to rest. Thunder in the middle of the lake represents thunder not in motion, but in winter hibernation. Following emerges from this image in the sense of adapting to the demands of the season. Thunder in the middle of the lake points to times of darkness and rest. Thus, after being tirelessly active throughout the day, the superior man allows himself refreshment and rest at nightfall. Every situation turns out well only if one can adapt to it instead of wearing oneself out through misplaced resistance.

The Individual Lines

### Nine at the beginning means:
The standard changes. Perseverance brings good fortune.
Going out of the door to interact with others brings achievements.

Exceptional conditions arise when the relationship between leader and follower changes. The very idea of adaptation and following implies that if one wishes to lead others, one must remain accessible and allow oneself to be guided by the views of subordinates. However, one must maintain firm principles to avoid wavering when facing mere passing opinions. Once ready to listen to others, one must not strictly associate with like-minded people or faction members. Instead, one must step out the door and mingle freely with all kinds of people, whether friend or foe. Only in this way can one achieve anything lasting.

### Six in the second place means:
If one clings to the little boy,
one loses the strong man.

One must be cautious when choosing friends and close relationships. A person keeps either good company or bad company; it is impossible to have both at once. By throwing oneself away on unworthy individuals, one loses connection with spiritually significant people who can foster one's better nature.

### Six in the third place means:
If one clings to the strong man,
one loses the little boy.
Through following, one finds what one seeks.
It furthers one to remain persevering.

Connecting with significant individuals naturally involves a certain degree of loss. One must part ways with what is base and superficial. Yet, one will feel deeply satisfied because one finds exactly what is sought and needed for personal growth. The crucial point is to remain firm. One must know what one wants and avoid being led astray by fleeting inclinations.

### Nine in the fourth place means:
Following creates success. Perseverance brings misfortune.
To walk the path with sincerity brings clarity.
How could this be a blame?

Those with a certain degree of influence often succeed in gathering followers by displaying condescending affability toward subordinates. However, the people who attach themselves are often insincere. They seek personal advantage and try to make themselves indispensable through flattery and subservience. If one becomes accustomed to such partisans and can no longer manage without them, it brings misfortune. Only by remaining completely free from the ego and focusing with conviction solely on what is right and objective does one gain the clarity to see through such people, thereby remaining free of blame.

### Nine in the fifth place means:
Sincere in what is good. Good fortune!

Everyone must have something to follow, something that serves as a guiding star. Anyone who follows the beautiful and the good with conviction will find encouragement in these words.

### Six at the top means:
He finds firm attachment
and is bound fast besides.
The king introduces him to the Western Mountain.

This refers to someone who has already left the turmoil of the world behind: a sublime sage. Yet a follower appears who understands him and will not let him go. Thus, the sage returns to the world once more to assist the follower in his work, creating an eternal bond.

The analogy is drawn from the Zhou dynasty. This dynasty honored meritorious helpers by granting them a place in the ancestral temple of the ruling family on the Western Mountain. In this manner, such a man was integrated into the destiny of the royal house.

18.name: WORK ON WHAT HAS BEEN SPOILED
18.title: Hexagram 18 蠱 - GU / WORK ON WHAT HAS BEEN SPOILED
18.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 18 (GU) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
18.intro: The Chinese character Gu represents a bowl in which worms are breeding. This signifies what is spoiled or decayed. It has come about because the gentle indifference of the lower trigram has joined with the rigid inertia of the upper trigram, causing conditions to stagnate. Since this state is the result of human neglect, it carries an implicit call to eliminate it. Therefore, the meaning of the hexagram is not simply "the spoiled," but rather "what is spoiled as a task" - the "work on what has been spoiled."

dictamen.text: Work on what has been spoiled has supreme success. It furthers one to cross the great water. Three days before the starting point, three days after the starting point.
dictamen.commentary:
What has been spoiled through human error can be repaired through human effort. This state of decay is not an unalterable fate like during a period of stagnation, but rather the consequence of a misuse of human freedom. Therefore, working toward improvement holds great promise because it aligns with the possibilities of the time. However, one must not shrink from the effort and danger - symbolized by crossing the great water - but must take decisive action.

Success, however, requires careful deliberation. This is expressed in the phrase: "Three days before the starting point, three days after the starting point." One must first understand the causes that led to decay before they can be corrected; hence, mindfulness is needed during the time before the starting point. Afterward, one must ensure that the new path is firmly established to prevent a relapse; hence, vigilance is required during the time after the starting point. Decisiveness and energy must replace the indifference and inertia that caused the decay, so that a new beginning may follow the end.

imagen.text: The wind blows at the foot of the mountain: the image of decay. Thus the superior person stirs up the people and strengthens their spirit.
imagen.commentary: When the wind blows at the foot of the mountain, it is thrown back and spoils the vegetation. This contains a call to make improvements. The same applies to base moods and trends: they corrupt human society. To eliminate this corruption, the superior person must renew society. The methods for doing so are also drawn from the two trigrams, though their effects unfold sequentially. Stagnation must be removed by stirring up public opinion (just as the wind acts as a stirring force), and then the character of the people must be strengthened and stabilized, just as the mountain offers rest and nourishment to all growth around it.

1.text: Setting right what was spoiled by the father. If there is a son, no blame remains on the departed father. Danger. In the end, good fortune.
1.commentary: Rigidly adhering to tradition has resulted in decay. However, the corruption is not yet deeply rooted, so it can still be easily corrected. It is as if a son compensates for the decay that crept in under his father. Consequently, no blame rests on the father. Yet, one must not overlook the danger or take the matter too lightly. Only when one remains aware of the risks inherent in any reform will everything turn out well in the end.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Setting right what was spoiled by the mother. One must not be too persistent.
2.commentary: These are mistakes caused by weakness that have brought about decay. Hence the symbol of what was spoiled by the mother. When making amends, a certain delicate consideration is necessary. One must avoid acting too harshly, so as not to cause injury through abruptness.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: Setting right what was spoiled by the father. There will be a little remorse. No great blame.
3.commentary: This depicts someone who proceeds a bit too energetically when correcting the mistakes of the past. This will certainly cause minor inconveniences and friction from time to time. However, too much energy is better than too little. Therefore, even if there is occasional cause for minor regret, one remains free of any serious blame.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Tolerating what was spoiled by the father. To continue down this path brings humiliation.
4.commentary: This shows a situation where someone, out of weakness, fails to confront the decay inherited from the past. Instead, they let it take its course as it begins to manifest. If this continues, humiliation will follow.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Setting right what was spoiled by the father. One meets with praise.
5.commentary: One faces decay resulting from the neglect of earlier times. Alone, one lacks the strength to counter it. However, capable helpers are found, and with their support, a thorough reform is achieved - if not a completely creative new beginning - which is highly praiseworthy.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: He does not serve kings and princes. He sets himself higher goals.
6.commentary: Not every individual is obligated to involve themselves in the affairs of the world. There are those who have already developed inwardly to such an extent that they are justified in letting the world take its course without intervening politically to reform it. Yet this does not mean they may remain idle or purely critical. Only the active cultivation of humanity's higher goals within one's own person justifies such retirement. For even if the sage keeps distant from the daily turmoil, they still create incomparable values for the future of mankind.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

19.name: Approach
19.title: Hexagram 19 臨 - Lín / Approach
19.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 19 (Lín) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.

below.text: Duì, the Joyous of the Lake

19.intro: The Chinese word Lín has a range of meanings that cannot be exhausted by a single English term. The ancient commentaries on the Book of Changes give "becoming great" as its primary meaning. What becomes great are the two strong lines growing into the hexagram from below, expanding the light energy. From this arises the concept of approach, specifically the approach of what is strong and superior toward the lower elements. Ultimately, it signifies the condescension of a higher ruler toward the people, as well as setting to work on affairs. The hexagram is associated with the twelfth month (January-February), because after the winter solstice the light energy is already on the rise.

dictamen.text: Approach has supreme success. Perseverance furthers. When the eighth month comes, there will be misfortune.
dictamen.commentary: The hexagram as a whole points to a time of hopeful progress. Spring approaches. Joy and flexibility bring the high and the low closer together, making success certain. However, resolute and persistent work is required to fully exploit the favor of the time. Furthermore, springtime does not last forever. In the eighth month, the aspects are reversed. Only two strong, light lines remain, and they are retreating rather than advancing (refer to the next hexagram). This turning point must be considered in time. Facing adversity before it manifests, or even before it begins to stir, allows one to master it completely.

imagen.text: Earth above the lake: the image of Approach. Thus the superior man is inexhaustible in his will to teach, and without limits in his tolerance and protection of the people.
imagen.commentary: The earth borders the lake from above, symbolizing the approach and condescension of the higher toward the lower. The superior man's behavior toward others flows from both parts of this image. Just as the lake exhibits inexhaustible depth, the sage is inexhaustible in his readiness to teach. And just as the earth is boundlessly wide, sustaining and nurturing all creatures, the sage sustains and nurtures all people, excluding no part of humanity through boundaries of any kind.

1.text: Joint approach. Perseverance brings good fortune.
1.commentary: The good begins to assert itself and finds a welcoming response in an influential position. This inspires capable individuals to step forward and join the upward movement. However, one must remain careful not to lose oneself in the current of the times, remaining steadfast in what is right: this brings good fortune.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Joint approach. Good fortune! Everything is favorable.
2.commentary: When encouraged from above to advance, and possessing the inner strength and consistency that needs no warning, one achieves good fortune. The future needs to cause no anxiety. Though one knows that all earthly things are transitory and that every rise is followed by a fall, this universal destiny does not cause misgivings. Everything is favorable; hence, one will walk life's paths swiftly, honestly, and boldly.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: Comfortable approach. Nothing that would be favorable. If one comes to grieve over it, one becomes free of blame.
3.commentary: Progress is cheerful, and one gains power and influence. This carries the danger that, trusting in one's position, one might grow comfortable and display a casual, negligent attitude when dealing with people. This is harmful under all circumstances. Yet, a shift in attitude remains possible. If one feels grief over this misguided posture, recognizing the responsibility inherent in an influential position, one frees oneself from error.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Complete approach. No blame.
4.commentary: While the three lower lines represent the rise to power and influence, the three upper lines show the attitude of those in higher positions toward the lower elements to whom they grant influence. Here, a completely open, unprejudiced approach of a superior toward a capable man is shown, drawing him into association regardless of class prejudice. This is highly favorable.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Wise approach. This is right for a great prince. Good fortune!
5.commentary: A prince or anyone in a leading position must possess the wisdom to draw capable, expert people into his circle to manage affairs. His wisdom lies both in knowing how to choose the right individuals and in allowing those he has chosen to act freely without interfering in their work. Only through this restraint will he find the necessary people to meet all demands competently.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Magnanimous approach. Good fortune. No blame.
6.commentary: A sage who has overcome the world and is inwardly finished with life may occasionally find himself in a position to re-enter the worldly sphere and approach others. This brings great good fortune to the people to whom he turns his teaching and help. For the sage himself, this magnanimous self-humbling carries no blame.
6.title: Six at the top means:

20.name: CONTEMPLATION (THE VIEW)
20.title: Hexagram 20 觀 - GUAN / CONTEMPLATION (THE VIEW)
20.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 20 (GUAN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
20.intro:
The Chinese name of the hexagram, with a slight variation in pronunciation, carries a dual meaning. On one hand, it signifies contemplation or viewing; on the other, it means being seen, serving as an exemplar or model. These concepts are suggested by the structure of the hexagram, which can be interpreted as the image of a tower ⛩ common in ancient China. From such towers, one enjoyed a sweeping view of the surroundings, while the tower itself, standing high on a mountain, was visible from afar. Thus, the hexagram represents a ruler who contemplates the laws of heaven above and the customs of the people below, establishing an exalted model for the masses through exemplary governance.

The hexagram is associated with the eighth month (September-October). The light power is retreating, while the dark power is on the rise again. However, this aspect is not central to the overall interpretation of the hexagram.

dictamen.text: Contemplation. The ablution has been performed, but not yet the offering. Full of trust, they look up to him.
dictamen.commentary:
Sacrificial rituals in ancient China began with an ablution and a libation to invoke the deity, followed by the presentation of the offerings. The interval between these two actions is the most sacred - a moment of ultimate inner concentration. When devotion is faithful and sincere, its contemplation transforms and inspires awe in those who witness it.

Similarly, a sacred gravity is visible in nature through the regular operation of natural laws. Contemplating the divine meaning of cosmic events provides the person called to influence humanity with the means to produce similar effects. This requires an inner concentration like that generated by religious contemplation in individuals of great stature and deep conviction. Through this, they perceive the mysterious divine laws of life and realize them within their own personality through the profound seriousness of inner concentration. Consequently, a mysterious spiritual power emanates from their very presence, influencing and subduing people without them ever becoming conscious of how it happens.

imagen.text: The wind blows over the earth: The image of Contemplation. Thus the ancient kings visited all regions of the world, contemplated the people, and provided instruction.
imagen.commentary:
When the wind sweeps over the earth, it reaches everywhere, and the grass must bend to its power. Both dynamics find confirmation in this hexagram. They were practically implemented in the institutions of ancient kings, who made regular journeys to observe their people firsthand, ensuring that no local custom escaped their notice. At the same time, they exerted their influence to reform any customs that were out of harmony.

The entire concept points to the power of a superior personality. Such a person can look across the great mass of humanity and discern their true dispositions, making deception impossible. Conversely, by their sheer presence and the weight of their character, they make an impression that causes others to guide themselves by them, just as the grass bends before the wind.

1.text: Boyish contemplation. For an inferior person, no blame. For a superior person, humiliating.
1.commentary: An uncomprehending contemplation from a distance is depicted here. Someone is actively exerting influence, but their actions are not understood by inferior people. This matters little for the masses; whether or not they understand the actions of the ruling sage, they still benefit from them. However, for a higher individual, this is a disgrace. They must not content themselves with a foolish, thoughtless viewing of prevailing influences, but must examine them in context and strive to understand them.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Contemplation through the crack of a door. Furthers the perseverance of a woman.
2.commentary: Peering through the crack of a door provides a limited view. One looks from the inside out, making the perspective subjectively restricted. Everything is related back to oneself; one cannot empathize with others or understand their motives. This is appropriate for a good housewife, who has no need to understand world affairs. However, for a man who must act in public life, such a narrow, egoistic perspective is naturally detrimental.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Contemplation of my life decides choice of progress or retreat.
3.commentary: This marks the place of transition. One no longer looks outward to receive more or less limited or confused impressions; instead, one directs contemplation inward to find guidance for decisions. This introversion of contemplation overcomes the naive selfishness of someone who views everything solely from their own standpoint. It leads to reflection and, consequently, to objectivity. Yet self-knowledge is not a preoccupation with one's own thoughts, but with the effects that emanate from oneself. Only the real-world effects of one's life provide a clear picture that justifies a decision to advance or retreat.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Contemplation of the light of the kingdom. It is beneficial to exert influence as the guest of a king.
4.commentary: Here, a man is depicted who understands the secrets of bringing a kingdom to prosperity. Such an individual must be placed in an influential position where he can act effectively. He should be treated as a guest, meaning he ought to exert his influence independently and with honor, rather than being used merely as a tool.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Contemplation of my life. The superior person is without blame.
5.commentary: A man in a leading position, to whom others look up, must be constantly ready for self-examination. However, the correct method of self-examination does not consist of idle introspection, but rather of evaluating the effects that emanate from him. Only when these effects are beneficial and exert a positive influence on others will the contemplation of his own life afford the satisfaction of being free from blame.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Contemplation of his life. The superior person is without blame.
6.commentary: While the preceding line represents a man examining himself, here at the highest position, all personal, ego-driven references are eliminated. A sage is shown here who stands outside the turmoil of the world, free from the self, contemplating the laws of life. This is recognized as the supreme achievement, as it renders one entirely free from blame.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

21.name: Biting Through
21.title: Hexagram 21 噬嗑 - Shì Kè / Biting Through
21.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 21 (Shì Kè) of the I Ching.
21.intro: The hexagram represents an open mouth with an obstacle between the teeth (at the fourth position). Consequently, the lips cannot meet. To bring them together, one must energetically bite through the obstacle. The hexagram is also composed of the signs for thunder and lightning, indicating how obstacles are forcefully removed in nature. Energetic biting overcomes the obstacle to union in the mouth. A storm with thunder and lightning overcomes disruptive tension in nature. Legal proceedings and punishments overcome disturbances to harmonious coexistence caused by criminals and slanderers. Unlike Hexagram 6 (Conflict), which deals with civil lawsuits, this hexagram concerns criminal prosecution.

dictamen.text: Biting Through has success. It is favorable to let justice be administered.
dictamen.commentary:
When an obstacle stands in the way of unity, energetic biting through brings success. This applies to all circumstances. Whenever unity cannot be achieved, it is being halted by an intermediary, a traitor, or an obstructing force. One must take decisive action to prevent permanent damage. Such deliberate obstacles do not disappear on their own. Judgment and punishment are necessary to deter or remove them.

However, it is essential to proceed in the right manner. The hexagram is composed of Lí (clarity) and Zhèn (excitement/force). Lí is yielding; Zhèn is firm. Mere firmness and excitement would lead to excessive severity in punishment. Pure clarity and gentleness would be too weak. Combining both creates the proper measure. It is crucial that the decisive individual, represented by the fifth line, is gentle by nature while remaining awe-inspiring due to his position.

imagen.text: Thunder and lightning: the image of Biting Through. Thus the kings of old consolidated the laws through clearly defined punishments.
imagen.commentary: Punishments are the individual applications of the laws, while the laws contain the definition of punishments. Clarity prevails when lighter and heavier offenses are distinctly differentiated during the establishment of penalties. This is symbolized by the clarity of lightning. The consolidation of laws is achieved through the just enforcement of punishments, symbolized by the terror of thunder. This clarity and severity serve to keep people respectful; punishments are not important for their own sake. Obstacles in human society grow large only through ambiguous penal provisions and negligence in execution. The laws are consolidated only through clarity and swift, decisive justice.

1.text: His feet are fastened in the stocks so that his toes disappear. No blame.
1.commentary: If someone meets with punishment at their very first attempt to commit wrong, the penalty is light. Only the toes are covered by the stocks. This prevents them from sinning further and keeps them free from blame. It serves as a warning to halt in time on the path of evil.
1.title: Nine at the beginning

2.text: He bites through tender meat so that his nose disappears. No blame.
2.commentary: Right and wrong are easy to distinguish in this case; it is like biting through tender meat. However, one encounters a hardened offender. Out of anger and excitement, one goes a bit too far. The disappearance of the nose during the bite signifies that one loses their fine sense of discernment due to indignation. Yet this causes little harm, as the punishment itself is just.
2.title: Six in the second place

3.text: He bites on old dried meat and hits something poisonous. Slight humiliation. No blame.
3.commentary: Someone is called to enforce a punishment but lacks sufficient power and authority. Consequently, the offenders do not submit. This involves an old matter - symbolized by salted game - where one encounters difficulties. The old meat is spoiled. By dealing with the matter, one draws poisonous hatred upon oneself, leading to a somewhat embarrassing situation. However, since punishing was a requirement of the time, one remains free from blame.
3.title: Six in the third place

4.text: He bites on dried gristly meat. He receives metal arrows. It is favorable to be mindful of difficulties and to be persevering. Good fortune!
4.commentary: Great difficulties must be overcome. Powerful opponents need to be punished, which is an arduous task. Nevertheless, it succeeds. One must possess the hardness of metal and the straightness of an arrow to master these obstacles. If one remains aware of these difficulties and stays persevering, good fortune is attained. The challenging task succeeds in the end.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place

5.text: He bites on dried lean meat. He receives yellow gold. Perseveringly mindful of danger. No blame.
5.commentary: One must decide a case that is not easy but is nevertheless clear. However, one's own nature is inclined toward benevolence. Therefore, one must gather oneself to act like yellow gold - meaning impartial (yellow being the color of the middle) and true as gold. Only by remaining continuously aware of the dangers stemming from the responsibility one has assumed does one remain free from error.
5.title: Six in the fifth place

6.text: His neck is fastened in the wooden collar so that his ears disappear. Misfortune!
6.commentary:
In contrast to the lowest line, this refers to an incorrigible person. He wears the wooden neck collar as a punishment, but his ears disappear within it. He no longer listens to warnings; he is deaf to them. This obstinacy leads directly to misfortune.

    Regarding "Nine at the beginning," Confucius remarks:
    "The inferior man is not ashamed of unkindness and does not shrink from injustice. If he sees no advantage, he does not move. If he is not intimidated, he does not reform. Yet, if he is corrected in small matters, he takes care in great ones. This is a piece of good fortune for the lesser man."
    Regarding "Nine at the top," Confucius remarks:
    "If good does not accumulate, it is not enough to make a man famous. If evil does not accumulate, it is not strong enough to destroy a man. Therefore, the inferior man thinks that small good deeds have no value and neglects them. He thinks that small sins do no harm and does not give them up. Thus his sins accumulate until they can no longer be concealed, and his guilt becomes so great that it can no longer be absolved."
6.title: Nine at the top

22.name: GRACE
22.title: Hexagram 22 賁 - BÌ / GRACE
22.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 22 (BÌ) of the I Ching.
22.intro: The hexagram shows a fire breaking forth from the secret depths of the earth, flaring up and illuminating the mountain, the heavenly height, making it beautiful. Grace and beautiful form are necessary in any union to ensure it is ordered and lovely rather than chaotic and disordered.

dictamen.text: Grace has success. In small matters, it is favorable to undertake something.
dictamen.commentary: Grace brings success. However, it is not the essential foundation but merely the ornament. Therefore, it should be applied sparingly, only in small matters. In the lower trigram, Fire, a yielding line steps between two strong ones and makes them beautiful; yet the strong lines are the essence, while the weak line is the beautifying form. In the upper trigram, Mountain, the strong line decisively takes the lead, so that here too it is considered the determining factor. In nature, we see the strong light of the sun in the sky. The life of the world depends on it. But this strong, essential element is transformed and given graceful variety by the moon and stars. In human life, beautiful form consists in having fixed, strong orders like mountains, which are rendered pleasing by clear beauty. Contemplating the forms in the heavens grants the ability to understand time and its changing demands. Contemplating the forms in human life gives the possibility to shape the world.

imagen.text: Fire at the foot of the mountain: the image of Grace. Thus the superior man proceeds when clarifying current affairs, but he does not venture to decide controversial issues by it.
imagen.commentary: The fire whose radiance illuminates the mountain and makes it graceful does not shine to a great distance. Thus, while a graceful form suffices to brighten and clarify minor matters, important questions cannot be decided in this manner. They require greater seriousness.

1.text: He makes his toes graceful, leaves the carriage, and walks.
1.commentary: Occupying the initial and subordinate position means one must take the trouble of personal advancement upon oneself. One might have had an opportunity to secure an easy advance covertly - represented by the image of the carriage. But a self-contained person scorns comforts obtained in a questionable manner. He finds it more graceful to go on foot than to ride in a carriage unlawfully.
1.title: Nine at the beginning

2.text: He makes his beard graceful.
2.commentary:
The beard is not something independent. It can only move along with the chin. The image therefore signifies that form is only considered as a consequence and accompaniment of content.

The beard is a superfluous ornament. Cultivating it independently, without regard for the inner content it is meant to adorn, would thus be a sign of a certain vanity.
2.title: Six in the second place

3.text: Graceful and moist. Perseverance brings good fortune.
3.commentary: This represents a highly graceful life situation in which one finds oneself. Grace and a moisture-transfigured radiance surround the individual. While this grace can adorn, it can also cause one to sink. Hence the warning not to drown in moist comfort, but to remain consistently persevering. On this depends good fortune.
3.title: Nine in the third place

4.text: Grace or simplicity? A white horse comes as if on wings: He is no robber, He seeks to woo in due time.
4.commentary: One is in a situation where doubts arise as to whether to continue seeking the grace of outward brilliance or whether it would be better to return to simplicity. The answer already lies within this doubt. An encouragement approaches from without. It arrives like a white winged horse. The white color indicates simplicity. Even if it might seem disappointing at first glance to forego the comforts one could obtain through other means, reassurance is found in the faithful bond with the friend and suitor. The flying horse is the image of thoughts that soar past all boundaries of space and time.
4.title: Six in the fourth place

5.text: Grace in hills and gardens. The roll of silk is meager and small. Humiliation, but ultimately good fortune.
5.commentary: One withdraws from interaction with people of the depths who seek only splendor and luxury, retiring into the solitude of the heights. There, one finds a person to look up to and wish to befriend. However, the ceremonial gifts one has to offer are meager and poor, causing embarrassment. Yet what matters is not the outward gift, but the true intent; therefore, everything turns out well in the end.
5.title: Six in the fifth place

6.text: Simple grace. No blame.
6.commentary:
Here, at the highest stage, all ornament is discarded. Form no longer conceals content but allows it to be fully expressed. The highest grace consists not in the outward decoration of the material, but in its simple, appropriate shaping.

The dark lines are about to ascend, threatening to overthrow the final firm and light line by undermining it with their influence. The base and dark elements do not attack the noble and strong directly; instead, they gradually hollow it out through imperceptible influence until it finally collapses.
6.title: Nine at the top

23.name: SPLITTING APART
23.title: Hexagram 23 剝 - BO / SPLITTING APART
23.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 23 (BO) of the I Ching.
23.intro:
The dark lines are ascending, poised to overthrow the last remaining firm and light line by disintegrating it through their influence. The inferior, dark element does not combat the noble, strong element directly; instead, it gradually hollows it out through an imperceptible influence until it finally collapses.

The hexagram represents the image of a house, where the topmost line signifies the roof. When the roof is shattered, the house collapses. The hexagram is traditionally associated with the ninth month (October-November), a period when the Yin energy grows increasingly powerful and is on the verge of completely displacing the remaining Yang energy.

dictamen.text: Splitting Apart. It does not further one to go anywhere.
dictamen.commentary: This is a time when inferior individuals are advancing, poised to displace the last remaining strong and noble forces. Because this shift is rooted in the natural course of time, it is not advantageous for the superior person to undertake anything under these circumstances. The correct behavior during such adverse times can be inferred from the component attributes of the trigrams. The lower trigram represents Earth, characterized by adaptability and devotion; the upper trigram represents Mountain, characterized by stillness. This suggests adapting to these difficult times and remaining quiet. This is not a matter of human contrivance, but of cyclical conditions that follow celestial laws, exhibiting alternating phases of increase and decrease, fullness and emptiness. One cannot work against these temporal conditions. Therefore, yielding and refraining from action is not cowardice, but wisdom.

imagen.text: The mountain rests upon the earth: the image of Splitting Apart. Thus those above can ensure their position only by giving generously to those below.
imagen.commentary: The mountain rests upon the earth. If it is steep and narrow, lacking a broad base, it must eventually collapse. Its position is secure only when it rises broad and grand from the earth, rather than proud and steep. In the same way, rulers rest upon the broad foundation of the people. They, too, must be generous and magnificent like the earth that sustains everything; only then will they secure their position, attaining the stability of a mountain.

1.text: The bed is split at the leg. The persevering are destroyed. Misfortune.
1.commentary: Inferior elements are approaching, secretly beginning their destructive subversion from below to undermine the very place where the superior person rests. Rulers' loyal supporters are destroyed through slander and all manner of intrigues. The situation is highly detrimental, yet there is nothing to do but wait.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: The bed is split at the frame. The persevering are destroyed. Misfortune.
2.commentary: The power of inferior forces grows, and danger now approaches the individual directly. Clear warning signs appear, and peace is disrupted. While facing this perilous situation, one is also left without support or responsiveness from either above or below. In this isolation, extreme caution is necessary. One must adapt to the times and withdraw in a timely manner. To remain unyielding and stubbornly maintain one's position would only lead to destruction.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: He splits apart with them. No blame.
3.commentary: One finds oneself in the midst of an adverse environment, bound to it by external ties. However, an inner relationship exists with a higher individual. This connection provides the inner stability needed to free oneself from the mindset of those around them. While this places one in opposition to their immediate surroundings, it is not an error.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: The bed is split up to the skin. Misfortune.
4.commentary: Here, misfortune reaches the person's body itself, no longer just their resting place. No warning or additional counsel is appended, as the disaster has reached its peak and can no longer be averted.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: A shoal of fishes. Favor comes through the court ladies. Everything is furthered.
5.commentary: In close proximity to the supreme, strong, and light principle, the nature of the dark element undergoes a transformation. It no longer plots against the strong principle but instead submits to its leadership. Acting as the head of the other weak lines, it leads them all to the strong one, much like a princess presenting her maids to her husband like a shoal of fishes, thereby winning his favor. By willingly subordinating itself to the higher principle, the lower element finds its fulfillment, and the higher principle attains its rightful position. Consequently, everything goes well.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: A large fruit still remains uneaten. The superior person receives a carriage. The house of the inferior person splits apart.
6.commentary: Here, the end of disintegration is reached. Once misfortune has spent its force, better times return. The seed of the good remains; just as fruit falls to the earth, the good grows anew from its seed. The superior person returns to a position of influence and effectiveness, carried by public opinion as if in a carriage. Conversely, the malice of the inferior person backfires, causing their own house to collapse. This reflects a natural law: evil is not only destructive to the good, but in its ultimate consequences, it destroys itself, because evil, which lives only by negation, cannot sustain itself independently. Even the inferior person fares best when kept under proper discipline by a superior person.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

24.name: THE TURNING POINT
24.title: Hexagram 24 復 - FÚ / THE TURNING POINT
24.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 24 (FÚ) of the I Ching.
24.intro: The turning point is indicated by the fact that after the dark lines have pushed all the light lines upward and out, a light line now re-enters the hexagram from below. The time of darkness is over. The winter solstice brings the victory of light. This hexagram is associated with the eleventh month, the month of the solstice (December-January).

dictamen.text: Return. Success. Going out and coming in without error. Friends come without blame. To and fro goes the way. On the seventh day comes the return. It is advantageous to have a destination.
dictamen.commentary:
After a period of collapse comes the turning point. The strong light that was previously expelled enters again. There is movement, but this movement is not forced. The upper trigram, Kūn, has devotion as its inherent character; therefore, it is a natural movement that arises spontaneously. For this reason, the transformation of the old is completely effortless. The old is discarded and the new is introduced; both measures correspond to the time and therefore cause no harm. Associations of like-minded individuals form. But this union takes place in full public view; it corresponds to the requirements of the era, and therefore any selfish, fractional ambition is excluded, ensuring no structural error arises from these associations. Return is grounded in the course of nature. The movement is cyclic, and the path is closed within itself. Therefore, there is no need to rush anything artificially. Everything develops on its own when the time is right. This is the operational meaning of heaven and earth. 

All movements develop in six stages, and the seventh stage brings the return. Thus, the winter solstice arrives in the seventh month after the summer solstice (from which point the year declines), just as sunrise follows the seventh double-hour after sunset. Therefore, seven is the number of the young light, born when six, the number of great darkness, increases by one. This introduces movement into stagnation.

imagen.text: Thunder in the midst of the earth: the image of the turning point. Thus the ancient kings closed the passes at the time of the solstice. Merchants and strangers did not travel, and the ruler did not inspect the provinces.
imagen.commentary: The winter solstice has always been celebrated in China as the resting period of the year - a custom still preserved in the New Year holiday season. In winter, the life force - symbolized by the arousing thunder - is still beneath the earth. Movement is in its earliest beginnings. Therefore, it must be strengthened through rest so that it is not dissipated by premature consumption. This core principle of allowing the returning strength to grow robust through rest applies to all corresponding structural situations. Returning health after an illness, or returning understanding after a disagreement: everything must be treated gently and with care in its initial stages, so that the return may lead to full bloom.

1.text: Return from a short distance. No need for remorse. Great good fortune!
1.commentary: Slight deviations from what is right are unavoidable. One must only turn back in time before going too far. This is of particular importance in character cultivation. Every subtle negative impulse must be eliminated immediately, before it develops further and solidifies. In this way, there is no need for remorse, and everything progresses exceptionally well.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Quiet return. Good fortune!
2.commentary: Turning back always requires a clear decision and is an act of self-mastery. It is made easier when one is in good company. If one can find the humility to set aside pride and align with upright individuals, it brings validation and good fortune.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Repeated return. Danger. No blame.
3.commentary: Some individuals possess a certain inner instability, requiring a continuous recalibration of their will. There is danger in this perpetual turning away from the right path due to uncontrolled impulses and subsequently turning back to it out of a better resolve. However, because this pattern prevents a permanent solidification in wrong ways, the general inclination toward shedding the flaw remains entirely possible.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Walking in the midst of others, one returns alone.
4.commentary: One moves in the midst of a group of low-minded associates but maintains an inner connection with a strong and upright friend. As a consequence, one turns back alone. Although there is no mention of reward or punishment, the outcome is highly favorable; for such a commitment to the right path carries its own intrinsic reward.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Magnanimous return. No remorse.
5.commentary: When the time for return arrives, one should not hide behind trivial excuses, but rather practice introspection and honest self-examination. If an error has been committed, it should be acknowledged with a resolute and magnanimous decision. This is a path that no one will regret.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Missing the return. Misfortune. Disaster from without and from within. If armies are marched in this way, a great defeat will ultimately be suffered, bringing disaster to the ruler of the country. For ten years, one will be unable to attack.
6.commentary: Missing the right moment for return leads to disaster. The internal misfortune is rooted in a misaligned position relative to the universal order, and external misfortune follows as a direct consequence of this structural error. This depicts absolute obstinacy and its inevitable judgment.
6.title: Six at the top means:

25.name: INNOCENCE (THE UNEXPECTED)
25.title: Hexagram 25 無妄 - WÚ WÀNG / INNOCENCE (THE UNEXPECTED)
25.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 25 (WÚ WÀNG) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
25.intro: Above is Qián, heaven; below is Zhèn, movement. The lower trigram, Zhèn, is determined by the strong line it received from above, from heaven. Accordingly, when movement follows the law of heaven, man is innocent and free from guile. This is the genuine and natural state, unclouded by ulterior motives or calculating thoughts. Wherever conscious intent becomes apparent, the truth and innocence of nature are lost. Nature without the guidance of the spirit is not true nature, but degenerate nature. Beginning with the idea of the natural, the sequence of thought extends further, so that the hexagram also encompasses the concept of the unintended and the unexpected.

dictamen.text: Innocence. Supreme success. Perseverance furthers. If someone is not as he should be, he has misfortune, and it does not further him to undertake anything.
dictamen.commentary: Man has received from heaven an originally good nature to guide him in all his movements. By devoting himself to this divine element within, he attains a pure innocence that does what is right with instinctive certainty, completely free from thoughts of reward or advantage. This instinctive certainty brings supreme success and furthers through perseverance. However, not everything instinctive is nature in this higher sense of the word; only that which is right and aligns with the will of heaven qualifies. Without this rectitude, a thoughtless, instinctive way of acting brings nothing but misfortune. Master Kung (Confucius) says regarding this: "He who departs from innocence, where does he go? Heaven's will and blessing do not accompany his deeds."

imagen.text: Thunder rolls under heaven: All things attain the natural state of innocence. Thus the ancient kings, rich in virtue and in harmony with the time, fostered and nourished all beings.
imagen.commentary: When thunder - the life force - stirs again under heaven in spring, everything sprouts and grows, and all creatures receive the childlike innocence of their original being from creative nature. The great rulers of humanity act in the same way: out of the inner wealth of their being, they care for all life and culture, doing everything necessary to foster them at the proper time.

1.text: Innocent conduct brings good fortune.
1.commentary: The first, original impulses of the heart are always good. One can follow them with confidence, assured of finding good fortune and achieving one's purpose.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: If one does not think of reaping while plowing, nor of using the field while clearing it, then it furthers one to undertake something.
2.commentary: One should perform every task for its own sake, as time and place require, without side-glances at success. Then the work prospers, and whatever is undertaken succeeds.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Undeserved misfortune: The cow tied up by someone is the wanderer's gain, the citizen's loss.
3.commentary: Sometimes undeserved misfortune comes from without, caused by someone else - as when a passerby walks off with a tethered cow. His gain is the owner's loss. In all actions, even innocent ones, one must adapt to the proper time; otherwise, unexpected misfortune will occur.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: He who can be persevering remains without blame.
4.commentary: What truly belongs to a person cannot be lost, even if one were to throw it away. Therefore, there is no need for anxiety. One must only be concerned with remaining true to one's own nature without listening to others.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: In an illness that comes through no fault of your own, use no medicine. It will get well by itself.
5.commentary: If an unexpected evil comes from without by chance, one that is not rooted in one's own nature and finds no foothold there, one should not resort to external remedies to remove it. Instead, let nature quietly take its course, and it will heal on its own.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Innocent action brings misfortune. Nothing furthers.
6.commentary: When one is in a situation where progress is no longer timely, the rule is to wait quietly and without ulterior motives. If one acts thoughtlessly to force one's way against fate, success will not be achieved.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

26.name: The Taming Power of the Great
26.title: Hexagram 26 大畜 - Dà Chù / The Taming Power of the Great
