26.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 26 (Dà Chù) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
26.intro:
The Creative is tamed by Keeping Still. This produces a massive accumulation of power, contrasting sharply with Hexagram 9, where the Gentle alone restrains the Creative. While in that previous configuration a single weak line must tame five strong ones, here there are two weak lines - acting as both minister and prince. Consequently, their restraining capability is far more potent. This refers to the structural contrast with Hexagram 9 (The Taming Power of the Small), where a solitary yin line in the fourth position attempts to restrain the surrounding yang lines. 

The hexagram carries a threefold conceptual framework: Heaven positioned within the Mountain yields the idea of holding together or accumulating; Gèn holding Qián still gives the idea of holding back or restraining; finally, because a strong line occupies the top position as the ruler of the sign, representing a sage who is honored and nurtured, it conveys the idea of nurturing or cultivating. This third aspect of cultivation and nourishment focuses specifically on the top strong line, which embodies the sage.

dictamen.text: The Taming Power of the Great. Perseverance furthers. Not eating at home brings good fortune. It furthers one to cross the great water.
dictamen.commentary:
To restrain and accumulate massive creative forces, as depicted here, requires a strong, clear-headed individual who commands the respect of the ruler. Qián signifies immense creative power, while Gèn points to firmness and truth; both indicate light, clarity, and the daily renewal of character. Only through such continuous self-renewal does one remain at the peak of their power. 

In tranquil times, the force of habit helps maintain order, but during great eras of concentrated energy, everything depends on the power of personality. Furthermore, because the worthy are honored - as demonstrated by the strong personality entrusted with leadership by the ruler - it is advantageous not to eat at home, but rather to earn one's bread in public life by accepting office. One is in harmony with heaven; therefore, even difficult and hazardous undertakings, such as crossing the great water, will succeed.

imagen.text: Heaven within the mountain: The image of the Taming Power of the Great. Thus the superior man acquaints himself with many words of antiquity and deeds of the past, in order to strengthen his character.
imagen.commentary: Heaven within the mountain points to hidden treasures. Similarly, a treasure lies buried within the words and deeds of the past, which can be used to fortify and elevate one's own character. This represents the true method of study: rather than restricting oneself to mere historical knowledge, one must continuously make history contemporary by applying its lessons.

1.text: Danger is at hand. It furthers one to desist.
1.commentary: A vigorous advance is desired, but circumstances present an obstacle. One finds oneself held back. Attempting to force progress under these conditions would lead to misfortune. It is therefore better to compose oneself and wait until an outlet opens for the accumulated energies.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: The axle-braces are removed from the wagon.
2.commentary: Here, advancement is blocked, similar to the situation in The Taming Power of the Small (Hexagram 9, Nine in the third place). However, while the obstructing force there is minor, causing a conflict between the forward urge and the restraint - resulting in the wheel-spokes snapping - the restraining force here is absolutely superior. Consequently, no struggle takes place. One submits and removes the axle-braces from the wagon, choosing to wait. Through this restraint, potential energy accumulates for a later, energetic advance.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: A good horse that follows others. Awareness of danger and perseverance further. Practice chariot-driving and armed defense daily. It furthers one to have a destination.
3.commentary: The path opens; the obstruction has ceased. One stands in relation to a strong will moving in the same direction. Progress is achieved like a good horse following another. Yet danger still threatens, and one must remain conscious of it to avoid losing internal firmness. Thus, one must train both in what leads forward and in what protects against unexpected attacks. It is beneficial to have a clear goal toward which to strive.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: The headboard of a young bull. Supreme good fortune!
4.commentary: This line and the following one are the elements that restrain the forward-surging lines below. Before a bull's horns grow, a protective headboard is attached to its forehead. This ensures that once the horns develop, they can no longer inflict harm. Dealing with wild energy before it manifests is an exceptional method of restraint, yielding easy and magnificent success.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: The tusk of a gelded boar. Good fortune!
5.commentary: Here, the restraint of the impetuous forward drive is achieved indirectly. A boar's tusk is inherently dangerous, but if the animal's disposition is altered, the danger disappears. Similarly, one should not combat wildness in people directly, but rather dismantle it by removing its underlying roots.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: One attains the way of heaven. Success.
6.commentary: The period of obstruction has passed. The energy accumulated over long containment breaks through, achieving immense success. This represents a sage who is honored by the ruler, and whose principles now prevail to shape the world.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

27.name: THE CORNERS OF THE MOUTH (PROVIDING NOURISHMENT)
27.title: Hexagram 27 頤 - Yí / THE CORNERS OF THE MOUTH (PROVIDING NOURISHMENT)
27.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 27 (Yí) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
27.intro: The hexagram represents an open mouth: the firm lines at the top and bottom depict the lips, while the open lines between them form the mouth's opening. This image of taking food into the mouth to sustain oneself shifts the core meaning to nourishment itself. The three lower lines illustrate self-nourishment, specifically physical sustenance, while the three upper lines represent the cultivation and nourishment of others on a higher, intellectual and cultural level.

dictamen.text: The Corners of the Mouth. Perseverance brings good fortune. Pay attention to provisioning and how a person seeks to fill their own mouth.
dictamen.commentary:
When providing care and nourishment, one must support the right people and care for oneself in the correct manner. To truly know a person, observe whom they care for and which aspects of their own nature they cultivate and feed. Nature nourishes all creatures. The great person nurtures the capable so that, through them, they can care for all people.

Mencius (VI, A, 14) states: "If you want to know whether someone is capable or incapable, look at nothing else than which part of their nature they deem important. The body has noble and ignoble parts, vital and minor parts. One must not harm the vital for the sake of the minor, nor the noble for the sake of the ignoble. Whoever nurtures the minor parts of their nature is a petty person. Whoever nurtures the noble parts of their nature is a noble person."

imagen.text: Thunder at the foot of the mountain: the image of Providing Nourishment. Thus the superior person is careful in their words and moderate in eating and drinking.
imagen.commentary: "God comes forth in the sign of the Arousing." When the life forces stir anew in spring, all things generate afresh. "He brings them to completion in the sign of Keeping Still." Thus, in early spring, as seeds fall to the earth, all things reach completion. This process illustrates nourishment through alternating movement and stillness. The superior person models the cultivation and refinement of their character on this pattern. Words represent movement directed from the inside out, while eating and drinking represent movement from the outside in. Stillness must moderate both forms of movement. Consequently, stillness ensures that words coming from the mouth do not exceed proper bounds, and nourishment entering the mouth stays within measure, thereby cultivating character.

1.text: You let your magic tortoise go and look at me with corners of the mouth drooping. Misfortune!
1.commentary: The magic tortoise is a creature that requires no earthly food; it possesses such power that it can live on pure air. This image signifies that, by nature and position, a person could live completely free, independent, and self-sufficient. Instead, they renounce this inner autonomy, looking up at others with envy and resentment because those others appear outwardly better off. This base envy, however, only provokes mockery and contempt from the other person, leading to misfortune.
1.title: Nine at the beginning

2.text: Turning toward the summit for nourishment. Deviating from the path to seek nourishment from the hill: Continuing in this way brings misfortune.
2.commentary: The normal course is to provide for one's own nourishment or to receive sustenance legitimately from those who have the duty and right to provide it. When inner weakness leaves a person unable to support themselves, an unsettling restlessness often arises. Bypassing rightful labor, they attempt to secure a living through favor, accepting gifts from those in higher positions. This behavior is unworthy because it deviates from one's true nature. Pursuing this course continuously leads to misfortune.
2.title: Six in the second place

3.text: Turning away from nourishment. Perseverance brings misfortune. Do not act thus for ten years. Nothing is advantageous.
3.commentary: Anyone who seeks sustenance that does not truly nourish reels from desire to consumption, and within that consumption, wastes away with renewed craving. A passionate frenzy aimed solely at satisfying the senses never achieves its goal. One must never act this way - ten years marks a complete cycle. Nothing good comes from it.
3.title: Six in the third place

4.text: Turning toward the summit for nourishment brings good fortune. Scouting around with sharp eyes like a tiger in insatiable desire. No blame.
4.commentary: Unlike the Six in the second place, which describes a person busily intent only on personal advantage, this line represents someone in a high position striving to let their light shine. To achieve this high goal, they need capable assistants, as they cannot accomplish it alone. Eager as a hungry tiger, they search for the right people. Because this zeal serves the public good rather than selfish desires, it is completely free of blame.
4.title: Six in the fourth place

5.text: Deviating from the path. Remaining in perseverance brings good fortune. One should not cross the great water.
5.commentary: A person is conscious of a deficiency. They ought to provide nourishment for the people but lack the independent strength to do so. Therefore, they must deviate from their usual path and seek advice and assistance from a spiritually superior, yet outwardly unassuming individual. Maintaining this attitude with perseverance leads to success and good fortune. However, they must remain fully aware of their dependency. They must not push themselves to the forefront or attempt to undertake massive enterprises, such as crossing the great water.
5.title: Six in the fifth place

6.text: The source of nourishment. Awareness of danger brings good fortune. It is advantageous to cross the great water.
6.commentary: This represents a sage of the highest order, the source of all influences that provide nourishment for others. Such a position carries heavy responsibility. If they remain deeply aware of this burden, they attain good fortune and can confidently undertake great and difficult tasks, such as crossing the great water. These actions bring widespread happiness for them and for everyone.
6.title: Nine at the top

28.name: Preponderance of the Great
28.title: Hexagram 28 大過 - Dà Guò / Preponderance of the Great
28.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete examination and analysis of Hexagram 28 (Dà Guò) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
28.intro: The hexagram consists of four strong lines inside and two weak lines outside. When the strong lines are on the outside and the weak lines are on the inside, the structural configuration is balanced; there is no structural excess, and nothing extraordinary is present. Here, the reverse is true. The hexagram represents a beam that is thick and heavy in the middle but too weak at its ends. This is not a sustainable state. It must change and pass, otherwise disaster threatens.

dictamen.text: Preponderance of the great. The ridgepole sags. It is favorable to have a direction to go. Success.
dictamen.commentary:
The great is in excess. The load is too heavy for the supporting forces. The ridgepole, upon which the entire roof rests, sags because its supporting ends are too weak for the weight. This is a time and a situation requiring extraordinary measures to overcome, as it represents an exceptional period. 

Therefore, one must focus on finding a transition and taking action as quickly as possible; this promises success. Although the strong lines are in excess, they occupy the central positions - meaning at the inner center of gravity - so no violent revolution is to be feared. Forceful measures will achieve nothing. One must untie the knot by gently penetrating into the meaning of the situation, as suggested by the attribute of the inner trigram Xùn. Through this approach, the transition to new conditions will succeed. This requires exceptional capability; therefore, the time of the preponderance of the great is a significant epoch.

imagen.text: The lake rises above the trees: The image of the preponderance of the great. Thus the superior person, when standing alone, remains free of care, and if they must renounce the world, they remain undaunted.
imagen.commentary: Extraordinary times of the preponderance of the great resemble a flood where the lake rises above the trees. However, such conditions are temporary. The correct attitude during these exceptional times is derived from the components of the hexagram: the image of Xùn is the tree that stands firm even when isolated, and the attribute of Duì is a serene joyfulness that remains undaunted even when forced to renounce the world.

1.text: Placing white rushes underneath. No blame.
1.commentary: When beginning an undertaking in extraordinary times, one must exercise exceptional caution. Just as a heavy object intended for the floor is carefully cushioned with white rushes to prevent damage, this caution might seem excessive, but it is not an error. All extraordinary ventures can only succeed through utmost care in their initial steps and foundational layers.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: A withered poplar puts forth a shoot. An older man gets a young wife. Everything is favorable.
2.commentary:
The wood stands near water, which provides the image of an old poplar tree putting forth a new shoot. This represents an extraordinary revitalization of the growth process. A similar extraordinary situation occurs when an older man takes a young woman as his wife. Despite the unusual nature of the circumstances, everything goes well.

From a political perspective, the meaning is that during extraordinary times, it is highly favorable to align oneself with those of lower status, as this offers an authentic opportunity for renewal.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: The ridgepole sags. Misfortune.
3.commentary: This describes a personality that attempts to force its way aggressively through times of structural excess. Refusing advice from others, they find no one willing to support them. Consequently, the burden increases, leading inevitably to bending or breaking. In hazardous times, willful and headstrong behavior only accelerates the collapse.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: The ridgepole is supported. Good fortune. If there are hidden motives, it is humiliating.
4.commentary: Through supportive relations with those below, a responsible leader succeeds in mastering the situation. However, if he were to exploit these connections to secure personal power and status rather than focusing entirely on saving the whole, it would be deeply humiliating.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: A withered poplar puts forth blossoms. An older woman gets a husband. No blame. No praise.
5.commentary:
A withered poplar that puts forth blossoms merely exhausts its remaining strength, bringing itself closer to its end. Similarly, when an older woman takes a husband, no real renewal takes place; the situation remains sterile. Thus, only an oddity persists, even if everything occurs honorably.

Politically, it is implied that if one abandons connections with the lower strata during unstable periods and relies exclusively on relationships with higher classes, an unsustainable condition is created.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: One must wade through the water. It goes over the crown of the head. Misfortune. No blame.
6.commentary: This depicts a scenario where extraordinary conditions have escalated to their absolute peak. Driven by courage, one seeks to fulfill their duty under all circumstances, thereby inviting extreme danger. The water closes over one's head; this is the misfortune. Yet, sacrificing one's life to uphold what is good and right leaves no stain of blame. There are values more vital than mere survival.
6.title: Six at the top means:

29.name: THE ABYSMAL, WATER
29.title: Hexagram 29 坎 - KǍN / THE ABYSMAL, WATER
29.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 29 (KĂN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
29.intro: The hexagram consists of the repetition of the trigram Kǎn. It is one of the eight doubled hexagrams. The trigram Kǎn signifies a plunging inward. A Yang line has plunged between two Yin lines and is enclosed by them, like water in a ravine. It represents the middle son. The Receptive obtained the middle line of the Creative, giving rise to Kǎn. As an image, it is water-specifically water coming from above and moving across the earth in rivers and streams, sustaining all life on earth. Applied to human affairs, it represents the heart and soul enclosed within the body, the light contained within darkness: reason. Because the trigram is repeated, the name of the hexagram carries an additional designation: the Repetition of Danger. This indicates an objective situation to which one must adapt, rather than a subjective attitude. Danger as a subjective attitude implies either foolhardiness or guile. Therefore, danger is also depicted as a ravine-a state in which one finds oneself, like water trapped in a canyon, and from which one emerges just as water does, by acting correctly.

dictamen.text: The Abysmal repeated. If you are sincere, you have success in your heart, and whatever you do succeeds.
dictamen.commentary:
Repeating a danger familiarizes us with it. Water provides the ideal model for proper conduct under such conditions. It flows onward uninterruptedly, filling every space it passes through. It shrinks from no hazardous place or plunge, and nothing causes it to lose its essential nature. It remains true to itself under all circumstances. Similarly, sincerity in difficult situations allows one to mentally penetrate the crisis. Once you master a situation internally, external actions will naturally meet with success. Managing danger requires a thoroughness that resolves everything needing attention, alongside a steady forward movement to avoid perishing by lingering in peril.

When used actively, danger serves an important purpose as a protective measure. Thus, heaven has its perilous height protecting it from any intrusion. The earth has its mountains and waters, whose natural hazards separate lands. Likewise, rulers employ danger as a defense mechanism to guard against external aggression and internal unrest.

imagen.text: Water flows uninterruptedly and reaches its goal: the image of the Abysmal repeated. Thus the superior man walks in lasting virtue and practices the business of teaching.
imagen.commentary: Water reaches its goal by flowing continuously, filling every depression before moving forward. The superior man acts in the same way. He ensures that goodness becomes an established character trait rather than a random, isolated occurrence. Consistency is also paramount when instructing others, as only repetition allows the material to truly become the learner's own property.

1.text: Repetition of the Abysmal. In the abyss, one falls into a pit. Misfortune.
1.commentary: Becoming accustomed to danger easily allows it to penetrate one's inner being. One grows familiar with and habituated to evil. Consequently, the correct path is lost, and misfortune follows as a natural result.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: The abyss carries danger. One should strive to achieve only small things.
2.commentary: When surrounded by danger, one must not recklessly try to escape at all costs, but should initially be satisfied if the peril does not overcome them. One must calmly weigh the circumstances of the time and settle for small gains, since a major success is out of reach for now. A spring also flows sparsely at first, taking time to carve its path into the open.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: Forward or backward, abyss upon abyss. In such danger, pause for now; otherwise, you will fall into a pit in the abyss. Do not act this way.
3.commentary: Every step forward or backward brings danger. Escape is unthinkable. Therefore, one must not be enticed into actions that would only plunge them deeper into peril. Instead, despite how uncomfortable it is to remain in such a state, one must pause until a way out appears.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: A jug of wine, a bowl of rice
4.commentary:
In times of danger, elaborate formalities come to an end. Sincerity of intent is what matters most. Normally, an official requires specific introductory gifts and recommendations before appointment. Here, everything is simplified to the utmost: the gifts are meager, there is no sponsor, and one presents oneself. Yet, there is no need to feel ashamed of any of this, provided there is an honest intention to help one another through the crisis.

Another insight is suggested: the window is the source through which light enters a room. When attempting to enlighten someone during difficult times, one must begin with what is already clear and evident, and proceed simply from there.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: The abyss is not filled to overflowing; it is filled only to the rim. No blame.
5.commentary: Danger arises from aiming too high. Water in a ravine does not pile up; it rises only to the lowest rim to find its way out. Similarly, in times of danger, one only needs to proceed along the line of least resistance to reach the goal. Great deeds cannot be accomplished during such times; escaping the peril is enough.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Bound with cords and ropes, enclosed between thorn-hedged prison walls; for three years one does not find the way. Misfortune!
6.commentary: A person who has lost the right path in extreme danger and is incorrigibly entangled in his sins has no prospect of escaping the peril. He resembles a criminal sitting bound behind thorn-hedged prison walls.
6.title: Six at the top means:

30.name: The Clinging, Fire
30.title: Hexagram 30 離 - Lí / The Clinging, Fire
30.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete examination and analysis of Hexagram 30 (Lí) of the I Ching, featuring Unicode characters and Pinyin.
30.intro: This hexagram is also a double sign. The primary trigram, Lí, means to cling to something, to be conditioned, to depend on something, or to manifest clarity. A dark line clings to bright lines both above and below, creating the image of an empty space between two strong lines, which makes them bright. It represents the middle daughter. The Creative has incorporated the central line of the Receptive, giving rise to Lí. As an image, it represents fire. Fire has no fixed form; it clings to burning objects to radiate light. Just as water descends from heaven, fire flames upward from the earth. While Kǎn represents the soul enclosed within the body, Lí signifies nature in its transfiguration.

dictamen.text: The Clinging. Perseverance brings success. It yields good fortune. Care of the cow brings good fortune.
dictamen.commentary:
The dark clings to the light, thereby completing its clarity. As the light radiates brightness, it requires something enduring within so that it does not consume itself entirely but can shine continuously. Everything luminous in the world depends on something to which it clings to sustain its radiance.

Thus, the sun and moon cling to the sky; grain, grass, and trees cling to the earth. In the same way, the double clarity of the dedicated leader clings to what is right, enabling him to shape the world. When a person, who stands in the world as a dependent and conditioned being, recognizes this limitation and aligns himself with the harmonious and constructive forces of the universe, he achieves success. The cow is the symbol of ultimate docility. By cultivating this docility and voluntary dependence within himself, a person attains clarity without sharpness and finds his true place in the world.

It is a remarkable coincidence, worthy of note, that here, just as in the Zoroastrian religion, fire and the care of the cow are closely linked.

imagen.text: Brightness rises twice: The image of fire.
imagen.commentary: Thus, the great man, by perpetuating this brightness, illuminates the four quarters of the world. Each of the two component trigrams represents the sun in its daily course. This depicts the repeated activity of the sun, indicating the continuous, temporal influence of light. The great man carries forward the work of nature within the human world. Through the clarity of his being, he ensures that light spreads further and further, profoundly penetrating human nature from within.

1.text: The footprints run in all directions. If one is serious and mindful: no blame.
1.commentary: It is early morning, and work begins. After the soul has been closed off from the outside world during sleep, its connections to the world resume. The tracks of impressions run in every direction, and a hurried busyness prevails. At this moment, it is vital to preserve inner composure and not be swept away by the bustle of life. If one remains serious and collected, one gains the clarity needed to handle the numerous impressions rushing in. This composed seriousness is particularly important at the very beginning, for the start contains the seeds of everything that follows.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Yellow light. Supreme good fortune.
2.commentary: The midday of the day is reached. The sun shines with a yellow light. Yellow is the color of the center and of moderation. A yellow light is therefore the image of perfect culture and art, whose highest harmony lies in moderation.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: In the light of the setting sun, people either beat the pot and sing, or they sigh loudly over approaching old age. Misfortune.
3.commentary: Here is the end of the day. The light of the setting sun reminds us of the conditioned and transient nature of life. Faced with this external lack of freedom, people often become internally unfree as well. For some, transience serves as an incentive for unrestrained revelry to enjoy life while it lasts; others allow themselves to be carried away by sorrow, spoiling their precious time by lamenting approaching old age. Both approaches are harmful. To the superior man, an early or late death makes no difference. He cultivates his character, awaits his lot, and thereby secures his destiny.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Its coming is sudden; it flares up, dies down, is thrown away.
4.commentary: The clarity of the intellect relates to life as fire does to wood. Fire clings to wood, but it also consumes it. Intellectual clarity is rooted in life, but it can also destroy it. It all depends on how it operates. Here, the image of a meteor or a straw fire is drawn. An excited, restless character achieves a rapid rise, but lasting effects are missing. Under these circumstances, it is harmful to spend oneself too quickly and consume oneself like a meteor.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Weeping in streams, sighing and lamenting. Good fortune.
5.commentary: Here is the peak of life. Without a warning, one would consume oneself like a flame in this position. If, instead, one abandons fear and hope, recognizes the emptiness of everything, and weeps and sighs out of concern to maintain clarity, good fortune emerges from this sorrow. This represents a genuine internal conversion, unlike the passing mood found in the nine in the third place.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: The king uses him to march forth and punish. It is best then to eliminate the leaders and capture the followers. No blame.
6.commentary: The purpose of punishment is to establish discipline, not to mete out blind retribution. The goal is to cure the evil at its root. In governance, this means removing the ringleaders while sparing the followers. In self-cultivation, it means eradicating bad habits while tolerating harmless ones. Excessive asceticism, like overly harsh punishments, fails to achieve success.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

31.name: INFLUENCE (WOOING)
31.title: Hexagram 31 咸 - XIÁN / INFLUENCE (WOOING)
31.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 31 (XIÁN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
31.intro:
The name of the hexagram means "universal," "pervasive," and, by extension, "to influence" or "to stimulate." The upper trigram is Duì, the Joyous; the lower is Gèn, Keeping Still. Through its persistent, quiet influence, the lower rigid trigram stimulates the upper weak trigram, which responds cheerfully and joyfully to this stimulation. Gèn, the lower trigram, represents the youngest son, while the upper, Duì, represents the youngest daughter. This depicts the universal mutual attraction between the sexes. In this relationship, the masculine element must take the initiative and place itself below the feminine during the courtship.

Just as the first part of the book opens with the hexagrams of Heaven and Earth as the foundations of all existence, the second part begins with the hexagrams of Wooing and Marriage as the foundations of all social relations.

dictamen.text: Influence. Success. Perseverance furthers. To take a maiden to wife brings good fortune.
dictamen.commentary:
The weak is above and the strong is below; hence their forces attract each other, leading to their union. This brings success, for all success relies on the effect of mutual attraction. Maintaining inner quiet while experiencing outer joy ensures that pleasure does not exceed proper limits but remains within the boundaries of what is right. This is the meaning of the warning: "Perseverance furthers." It distinguishes true wooing - where the strong man humbles himself before the weak maiden and shows consideration for her - from mere seduction. This attraction between elective affinities is a universal law of nature. Heaven and earth attract each other, and thus all beings come into existence.

The sage influences human hearts through this attraction, bringing peace to the world. From the attractions that things exert, one can understand the true nature of all beings in heaven and on earth.

imagen.text: A lake on the mountain: The image of Influence. Thus the superior man encourages people to approach him by his readiness to receive them.
imagen.commentary: A mountain with a lake on its summit receives nourishment and stimulation from its moisture. The mountain gains this advantage because its summit is concave rather than protruding. This image suggests that one should keep oneself inwardly humble and free, remaining receptive to good counsel. People soon stop offering advice to anyone who claims to know everything better.

1.text: The influence manifests in the great toe.
1.commentary: Before a movement is actually executed, it first shows itself in the toes. The idea of taking action is already present, but it has not yet manifested outwardly to others. As long as an intention produces no visible effects, it matters little to the outside world, leading neither to good nor to evil.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: The influence manifests in the calves of the legs. Misfortune. Tarrying brings good fortune.
2.commentary: The calf naturally follows the foot in movement. It cannot move forward on its own, nor can it stand still by itself. This represents a movement that lacks independence; because it is not master of itself, it bodes ill. One should wait quietly until prompted to act by a real influence. In this way, one remains free from harm.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: The influence manifests in the thighs. Holds to that which follows it. To continue is humiliating.
3.commentary: Every mood of the heart prompts a movement. Wherever the heart aspires, the thighs run without reflection, holding fast to the heart they follow. In human life, however, moving immediately at the whim of every passing impulse is incorrect and leads to humiliation if continued. This suggests a threefold lesson: one must not blindly run after everyone they wish to influence, but must know how to restrain themselves when necessary. Likewise, one should not immediately yield to every whim of those they serve. Finally, regarding the moods of one's own heart, one must never neglect the power of self-restraint, which forms the very basis of human freedom.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Perseverance brings good fortune. Remorse disappears. If a man is agitated in mind, and his thoughts go hither and thither, only those friends on whom he fixes his conscious thoughts will follow him.
4.commentary: Here, the position of the heart is reached. The stimulation flowing from this center is of the utmost importance. Particular care must be taken that this influence remains constant and good; then, despite the danger arising from the high mutability of the human heart, remorse becomes unnecessary. When the quiet, inherent power of one's personal character is at work, its effects are natural and orderly. All people receptive to the vibrations of such a spirit will be influenced. This influence over others should not manifest as a conscious, deliberate effort to manipulate them. Such deliberate agitation only causes anxiety and leaves one exhausted by the constant back and forth. Furthermore, the resulting effects will be confined only to those individuals on whom one consciously directs their thoughts.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: The influence manifests in the back of the neck. No remorse.
5.commentary: The back of the neck is the least mobile part of the body. When influence manifests here, the will remains firm, and the influence does not lead to confusion. Therefore, remorse does not enter into consideration. What takes place in these deeper recesses of the being - the subconscious - can neither be summoned nor prevented by conscious thought. However, if one remains completely uninfluenceable themselves, exercising an influence on the outside world becomes equally impossible.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: The influence manifests in the jaws, cheeks, and tongue.
6.commentary: The most superficial way of trying to influence others is through mere chatter, without any reality backing the words. Such stimulation, produced solely by the movement of the vocal organs, inevitably remains insignificant. For this reason, nothing regarding good or bad fortune is added.
6.title: Six at the top means:

32.name: DURATION
32.title: Hexagram 32 恆 - HÉNG / DURATION
32.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 32 (HÉNG) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
32.intro:
The strong trigram Zhèn is above, the weak Xùn below. This hexagram is the counterpart to the preceding one: there we find influence, here union as a permanent state. The images are thunder and wind, which are also phenomena naturally paired and permanently connected. The lower trigram indicates gentleness within, while the upper indicates movement without.

Applied to social relations, this represents the institution of marriage as a permanent union of the sexes. While during courtship the young man places himself below the young woman, in marriage - represented by the coming together of the eldest son and the eldest daughter - the husband is the leading and moving force outwardly, while the wife remains gentle and cooperative inwardly.

dictamen.text: Success. No blame. Perseverance furthers. It furthers one to have somewhere to go.
dictamen.commentary:
Duration is a state whose movement is not worn down by obstructions. It is not a state of rest, for mere standstill is regression. Rather, duration is the self-contained, self-renewing movement of an organized, firmly integrated whole that unfolds according to fixed laws, where every end is followed by a new beginning. The end is reached through inward movement - inhalation, systole, concentration. This movement then transitions into a new beginning where the motion is directed outward - exhalation, diastole, expansion.

Thus, the heavenly bodies have their orbits in the sky and can therefore shine permanently. The seasons follow a fixed law of change and transformation, allowing them to exert a lasting influence.

In the same way, the sage finds a lasting meaning in his path, bringing the world to its full realization. By understanding what gives things their duration, one can comprehend the nature of all beings in heaven and on earth.

imagen.text: Thunder and wind: the image of Duration. Thus the superior man stands firm and does not change his direction.
imagen.commentary: The thunder rolls and the wind blows. Both are highly volatile phenomena, seemingly the opposite of duration. Yet their appearance and disappearance, their coming and going, follow eternal laws. Similarly, the independence of the superior man does not mean he is rigid and immovable. He always moves with the times and adapts to them. What remains durable is his fixed direction, the inner law of his being that determines all his actions.

1.text: Seeking duration too quickly brings misfortune through perseverance. Nothing that furthers.
1.commentary: Creating something lasting can only be achieved gradually through long labor and careful reflection. Laozi expresses a similar concept: "If you want to compress something, you must first let it expand properly." Anyone who demands too much all at once acts with headlong haste. Because they attempt too much, they ultimately achieve nothing at all.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Remorse disappears.
2.commentary: The situation is abnormal. The strength of character exceeds the available material power. One might fear being carried away into something beyond one's strength. However, since this is the time of Duration, one succeeds in controlling this inner strength, avoiding any excess and causing all cause for remorse to disappear.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: He who does not give duration to his character meets with disgrace. Persistent humiliation.
3.commentary: When a person is driven by moods aroused by the external world through fear and hope, they lose the inner consistency of their character. Such internal inconsistency leads consistently to painful experiences. These humiliations often come from an unexpected direction. They are not so much the effects of the external world as they are lawful consequences triggered by one's own nature.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: No game in the field.
4.commentary: To get a shot while hunting, one must go about it the right way. If someone persistently stalks game in a place where none exists, they can wait indefinitely and still find nothing. Duration in seeking is not enough. What is not sought in the right way will not be found.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Giving duration to one's character through perseverance brings good fortune for a woman, misfortune for a man.
5.commentary:
A woman should follow one man throughout her entire life, but a man must adhere to his duty at any given time; if he were to constantly adapt himself to the woman, it would be a mistake for him.

Accordingly, a conservative adherence to tradition fits a woman well. A man, by contrast, must remain flexible and adaptable, allowing himself to be guided solely by what his duty demands at the moment.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Restlessness as a permanent state brings misfortune.
6.commentary: Some people remain in constant, hurried motion without ever attaining inner peace. This restlessness not only prevents any thoroughness but becomes a direct danger when it prevails in a position of authority.
6.title: Six at the top means:

33.name: RETREAT
33.title: Hexagram 33 遯 - DÙN / RETREAT
33.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 33 (DÙN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
33.intro:
The power of the dark is ascending. The light retreats to safety before it, so that the dark cannot harm it. This retreat is not a matter of human caprice but a law of natural events. Therefore, in this case, retreat is the correct course of action, allowing one to conserve strength instead of exhausting it.

As a monthly symbol, the hexagram is associated with the sixth month (July-August), during which the forces of winter already begin to show their influence again.

dictamen.text: Retreat. Success. In what is small, perseverance furthers.
dictamen.commentary: Conditions are such that hostile forces, favored by the time, are advancing. In this case, retreat is the correct path, and through retreat one achieves success. Success consists in being able to carry out the retreat correctly. Retreat must not be confused with flight, which seeks nothing but escape at all costs. Retreat is a sign of strength. One must not miss the right moment while still in full possession of power and position. This means understanding how to interpret the signs of the times early on and preparing a temporary retreat instead of engaging in a desperate battle to the death. Thus, one does not simply yield the field to the adversary, but makes their advance difficult by still showing perseverance in details. In this way, the reversal is already prepared during the retreat. Understanding the laws of such an active retreat is not easy. The meaning hidden within such a time is significant.

imagen.text: Mountain under Heaven: the image of Retreat. Thus the superior person keeps the inferior at a distance, not with anger, but with reserve.
imagen.commentary: The mountain rises up under heaven, but it is in its nature to ultimately come to a standstill. Heaven, on the other hand, retreats upward into the distance before it, remaining out of reach. This is the image of how the superior person behaves toward the ascending inferior person. He withdraws from him in his inner disposition. He does not hate him, for hatred is a form of inner involvement by which one binds oneself to the hated object. The superior person demonstrates strength (Heaven) by bringing the inferior to a halt through his reserve (Mountain).

1.text: Retreat at the tail: this is dangerous. One must not attempt to undertake anything.
1.commentary: Since the sign represents something in retreat, the first line is the tail and the topmost line is the head. In a retreat, it is advantageous to be at the front. Here, one is at the back, in direct contact with the pursuing forces. This is dangerous. Under such perilous circumstances, it is not advisable to undertake anything. By keeping still, one most easily escapes the threatening danger.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: He holds him fast with yellow ox-hide. No one can tear him loose.
2.commentary:
Yellow is the color of the middle, indicating correctness and duty. The hide of an ox is firm and unbreakable.

While the superior individuals retreat and the inferior press forward, here an inferior person is depicted who holds so firmly and tenaciously to the superior that they cannot rid themselves of him. Because he wills what is right and is strong in his purpose, he achieves his goal. In this way, the line confirms the words of the Judgment: "In what is small (here meaning: for the inferior person), perseverance furthers."
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: A halted retreat is distressing and dangerous. Keeping people as servants and maids brings good fortune.
3.commentary: When it is time to retreat and one is held back, it is both unpleasant and dangerous, as freedom of action is removed. In such a case, the only way out is to take the people who prevent one from leaving into one's service, so to speak, in order to at least retain the initiative and not fall helplessly under their control. But even if this is a way out, the situation remains far from cheerful. For what can one truly accomplish with such servants?
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Voluntary retreat brings good fortune to the superior person, and downfall to the inferior person.
4.commentary: In retreat, the higher individual parts ways amiably and gladly. The retreat is also easy for him internally because he does not need to violate his convictions. The one who suffers from this is only the inferior person, from whom he withdraws and who must decline without the guidance of the superior person.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Friendly retreat. Perseverance brings good fortune.
5.commentary: It is the task of the superior person to recognize in time when it is appropriate to retreat. When the right moment is chosen, the retreat can be carried out in a perfectly friendly manner without the need for unpleasant confrontations. Yet, despite the courteous external form, absolute firmness of resolve is necessary to avoid being misled by other considerations.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Cheerful retreat. Everything furthers.
6.commentary: The situation is unambiguous. Inner detachment is an established fact. This gives one the freedom to leave. When the path ahead is seen so clearly and without a doubt, a cheerful composure sets in, choosing the right course without any hesitation. Such a clear path always leads to good results.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

34.name: The Power of the Great
34.title: Hexagram 34 大壯 - Dà Zhuàng / The Power of the Great
34.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 34 (Dà Zhuàng) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
34.intro: The great lines, meaning the light and strong ones, are powerful. Four light lines have entered the hexagram from below and are about to ascend further. The upper trigram is Zhèn, the Arousing; the lower is Qián, the Creative. The Creative is strong, while the Arousing provides movement. The union of movement and strength yields the meaning of the Power of the Great. The hexagram is associated with the second month (March-April).

dictamen.text: The Power of the Great. Perseverance furthers.
dictamen.commentary: The hexagram indicates a time when inner worth rises sharply and attains power. However, this strength has already passed its midpoint. Therefore, a danger arises: one might rely purely on power without constantly examining what is right, or become bent on action without waiting for the proper time. For this reason, the caution is added that perseverance furthers. True greatness of power does not degenerate into mere brute force, but remains inwardly aligned with the principles of right and justice. When one understands this point - that greatness and justice must be inseparably linked - the true meaning of all universal events in heaven and earth becomes clear.

imagen.text: Thunder is high in the heaven: The image of the Power of the Great. Thus the superior man does not tread paths That do not accord with established order.
imagen.commentary: Thunder, the electrical force, ascends in spring. This movement aligns with the direction of heaven's own movement. It is therefore an action in harmony with heaven, which generates great power. However, true greatness depends on remaining in harmony with what is right. Therefore, in times of great power, the superior man avoids taking any action that does not accord with the established order.

1.text: Power in the toes. Continuing brings misfortune. This is certainly true.
1.commentary: The toes are at the very bottom and are ready to advance. Similarly, great power at a low station tends to force progress through sheer momentum. If one continues in this manner, it will certainly lead to misfortune. Oriental counsel therefore attaches a warning.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Perseverance brings good fortune.
2.commentary: The underlying situation is one where the gates of success begin to open. Resistance starts to yield, and one advances powerfully. This is the precise point where overconfidence easily sets in if left unchecked. Hence the oracle indicates that perseverance - namely in maintaining inner balance without aggressively exploiting power - brings good fortune.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: The inferior man acts through power; the superior man does not act thus. Continuing is dangerous. A goat butts against a hedge And entangles its horns.
3.commentary: Relying blindly on power leads to complications, much like a goat that butts against a hedge and gets its horns entangled. While the inferior man revels in power when he possesses it, the superior man does not act this way. He remains conscious of the danger of pushing forward under all circumstances, and timely renounces the mere display of force.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Perseverance brings good fortune. Remorse disappears. The hedge opens; there is no entanglement. The power depends on the axle of a large wagon.
4.commentary:
If one works quietly and perseveringly to remove obstacles, success eventually follows

This power is not displayed externally, yet it is capable of moving heavy burdens like a large wagon whose strength resides in its axle. The less power is applied outwardly, the more effectively it operates.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Loses the goat with ease. No remorse.
5.commentary: The goat is characterized by external hardness combined with inner weakness. Here, the situation becomes entirely effortless; no resistance remains. At this point, one can discard the defiant, aggressive disposition and will have no cause for regret.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: A goat butts against a hedge: It cannot go backward, it cannot go forward. Nothing furthers. If one notes the difficulty, this brings good fortune.
6.commentary:
By venturing too far ahead, one reaches a deadlock where it is impossible to move either forward or backward, and any effort only serves to complicate the matter further. Such obstinacy leads to insurmountable difficulties. However, if one recognizes the situation, stops attempting to force a way through, and composes oneself, everything will resolve well over time.

All that is fleeting,
In sin past repeating,
Is gone and past;
Wings start to grow,
The bolt yields at last
To the eternal hall.
6.title: Six at the top means:

35.name: PROGRESS
35.title: Hexagram 35 晉 - JÌN / PROGRESS
35.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 35 (JÌN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
35.intro: The hexagram represents the sun rising over the earth. It is therefore the image of rapid, easy progress, which simultaneously yields wider expansion and clarity.

dictamen.text: Progress: The powerful prince is honored with horses in large numbers. He is received three times in a single day.
dictamen.commentary:
This describes an era when a powerful feudal prince assembles the other princes around the sovereign in obedience and peace. The sovereign rewards him lavishly and draws him into close proximity.

A dual concept underlies this situation. The actual impetus for progress comes from a man in a dependent position whom others look up to as an equal, making them follow him willingly. This leader possesses enough inner clarity not to abuse his vast influence, using it instead for the benefit of his ruler. The ruler, for his part, is free from all jealousy; he rewards the great man generously and keeps him permanently nearby. An enlightened ruler and an obedient servant are the essential conditions for great progress.

imagen.text: The sun rises over the earth: The image of Progress. Thus the superior man himself makes his bright talents shine.
imagen.commentary: The light of the sun rising over the earth is inherently clear. Yet, the higher the sun climbs, the more it emerges from the misty vapors, radiating its original purity over an ever greater area. Similarly, human nature is fundamentally good, but it becomes clouded by contact with the earthly plane. It therefore requires purification so that it can shine in its original, inherent clarity.

1.text: Progressing, but rebuffed. Perseverance brings good fortune. If one meets with no trust, one should remain calm. No blame.
1.commentary: At a time when everything presses for progress, uncertainty still remains as to whether one might meet with a rebuff. In this case, one must simply continue along the right path, which ultimately brings good fortune. It may happen that no trust is extended. Under these circumstances, one should not try to force confidence at all costs; one must remain calm and cheerful, refusing to be provoked to anger. Thus, one remains free of blame.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Progressing, but in sorrow. Perseverance brings good fortune. One then receives great happiness from one's ancestress.
2.commentary: Progress is halted; one finds oneself prevented from connecting with the person in authority with whom one has a relationship. This brings sorrow. However, in such a situation, it is crucial to remain steadfast; then one will experience great happiness from that figure, delivered with maternal gentleness. This good fortune arrives and is well deserved, because the mutual affinity is not based on selfish or partisan motives, but on firm and correct principles.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: All are in agreement. Remorse disappears.
3.commentary: One presses forward in community with others, and their shared agreement lifts one up. This removes any cause for regret, which might otherwise stem from lacking the independence to overcome hostile destiny entirely on one's own.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Progress like a hamster. Perseverance brings danger.
4.commentary: In times of progress, it is easy for strong individuals in the wrong position to hoard possessions. However, such behavior shuns the light. Since times of progress always bring everything hidden into the open, persevering in such actions inevitably brings danger.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Remorse disappears. Take neither gain nor loss to heart. Undertakings bring good fortune. Everything is advantageous.
5.commentary: This depicts a situation where, in times of progress, one occupies a decisive position while remaining gentle and reserved. One might reproach oneself for not energetically exploiting the favor of the moment to secure every possible advantage. Yet, this remorse disappears. One must not take gain or loss to heart; these are secondary matters. It is far more important that one has secured opportunities for successful and beneficial action in this manner.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Progressing with horns is permissible only to discipline one's own territory. Consciousness of danger brings good fortune. No blame. Perseverance brings humiliation.
6.commentary: Progressing with horns - meaning to proceed aggressively - should only be directed against the faults of one's own people during such times. One must remain fully aware that such an aggressive approach always carries risk. By maintaining this awareness, one avoids the errors that otherwise threaten, and one's intentions succeed. Conversely, a stubborn continuation of this overly aggressive attitude, particularly toward outsiders, will bring humiliation.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

36.name: THE DARKENING OF THE LIGHT
36.title: Hexagram 36 明夷 - MÍNG YÍ / THE DARKENING OF THE LIGHT
36.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 36 (Míng Yí) of the I Ching, featuring Unicode characters and Pinyin.
36.intro: Here the sun has sunk under the earth and is therefore darkened. The name of the hexagram literally means "wounding of the bright"; hence, the individual lines frequently speak of wounding. The situation is the exact opposite of the previous hexagram. There, a wise man rules at the top with capable helpers who advance together; here, a dark man holds the position of authority, harming the capable and the wise.

dictamen.text: The Darkening of the Light. In adversity, it furthers one to be persevering.
dictamen.commentary: One must not allow oneself to be swept away helplessly by unfavorable circumstances, nor let one's inner resolve be bent. This is possible if one remains innerly bright while outwardly yielding and adaptable. Through this attitude, even the greatest adversity can be overcome. Under certain conditions, one must indeed conceal one's light to maintain one's will despite difficulties in the immediate environment. Perseverance must live in the innermost consciousness and must not be displayed outwardly. Only in this way can one preserve one's resolve amidst hardships.

imagen.text: The light has sunk into the earth: The image of the Darkening of the Light. Thus the superior man lives with the great multitude: He veils his brilliance and yet remains bright.
imagen.commentary: In times of darkness, it is essential to be cautious and reserved. One should not needlessly provoke overwhelmingly powerful enmity through reckless behavior. In such times, while one should not join in the habits of others, neither should one bring them critically to light. In social interactions during these periods, one must not try to know everything. One must let many things slide without letting oneself be deceived by them.

1.text: Darkening of the light in flight. He drops his wings. The superior man on his wanderings does not eat for three days. But he has a place to go. The host has cause to gossip about him.
1.commentary: With a grand resolution, one wishes to soar above all obstacles. But then one encounters a hostile fate. One retreats and evades. The times are difficult. One must hurry onward restlessly without a permanent dwelling place. If one refuses to make inner compromises and wishes to remain true to one's principles, one falls into want. Yet, one has a fixed goal to strive for, even if the people with whom one stays do not understand and speak ill of him.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: The darkening of the light wounds him in the left thigh. He brings rescue with the strength of a horse. Good fortune.
2.commentary: Here, the lord of light is in a subordinate position. He is wounded by the lord of darkness. However, the injury is not fatal, only hindering. Rescue is still possible. The person affected does not think of himself, but only of saving others who are also threatened. Therefore, he strives with all his might to save what can be saved. Good fortune lies in this dutiful action.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Darkening of the light during the hunt in the south. Their great leader is captured. One must not expect perseverance too quickly.
3.commentary: Seemingly, a stroke of chance is at work. While the strong and faithful man strives to establish order through diligent activity, without any ulterior motives, he happens upon the ringleader of disorder as if by chance and captures him. Thus, victory is achieved. However, one must not be too hasty in correcting the abuses. That would be a mistake, because the abuses have been entrenched for far too long.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: He penetrates into the left side of the belly. One gains the very heart of the darkening of the light and leaves gate and courtyard.
4.commentary: One is close to the head of darkness and thus learns his innermost thoughts. In this way, one realizes that improvement is no longer to be hoped for, and is enabled in time to leave the place of disaster before it strikes.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Darkening of the light as with Prince Jī. Perseverance furthers.
5.commentary:
Prince Jī lived at the court of the dark tyrant Zhòu Xīn. Prince Jī was a relative of the tyrant Zhòu Xīn, which prevented him from withdrawing from the court. This historical relationship serves as the underlying, unnamed context for the entire hexagram situation. Because he was a relative of the tyrant, he could not withdraw from court. He therefore concealed his true convictions and feigned madness. Although he was kept as a slave, he never allowed outward hardships to sway his inner resolve.

This yields the lesson for those who cannot leave their posts in times of darkness: while maintaining invincible perseverance within, they require double caution externally to escape danger.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Not light, but darkness. First he climbed up to heaven, then he plunged into the depths of the earth.
6.commentary: Here the climax of darkness is reached. The dark power was at first placed so high that it could wound all who were good and bright. In the end, however, it perishes from its own darkness, for evil must fall at the exact moment it has completely overcome the good, thereby consuming the very strength to which it owed its existence.
6.title: Six at the top means:

37.name: The Family
37.title: Hexagram 37 家人 - Jiārén / The Family
37.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 37 (Jiārén) of the I Ching, featuring Unicode characters and Pinyin.
37.intro: This hexagram represents the laws operating within the family. The topmost strong line represents the father, the lowest the son. The fifth strong line represents the husband, and the second yielding line represents the wife. On the other hand, the two strong lines in the fifth and third places represent two brothers, while the corresponding weak lines in the fourth and second places represent their wives. Thus, all relationships and dynamics within the family find their essential expression. Each individual line possesses the nature corresponding to its place. The fact that a strong line occupies the sixth place, where a yielding line might normally be expected, clearly indicates the firm authority that must emanate from the head of the family. The line is considered here not merely in its capacity as the sixth, but as the supreme authority. The family demonstrates the inner laws of the household at work, which, when extended outward, keep the state and the world in order. The influence exerted from the interior of the family upon the outside world is illustrated by the image of wind generated by fire.

dictamen.text: The Family. The perseverance of the woman furthers.
dictamen.commentary: The foundation of the family rests upon the relationship between husband and wife. The bond that holds the family together resides in the loyalty and perseverance of the woman. Her place is within (the second line), while the man's place is without (the fifth line). That man and woman occupy their proper places conforms to the great laws of nature. The family requires a firm authority, which is found in the parents. When the father is truly a father and the son a son, when the elder brother fulfills his place as elder brother and the younger his place as younger brother, when the husband is truly a husband and the wife a wife, the family is in order. When the family is in order, all the social relationships of humanity are brought into order. Out of the five cardinal social relationships, three are found within the family: that between father and son (love), between husband and wife (proper conduct), and between elder and younger brother (order). The loving reverence of the son is subsequently transferred to the ruler as loyalty, while the order and affection among brothers are transferred to friends as reliability, and to superiors as proper subordination. The family is the cell of society, the natural soil where the practice of moral duties is made easier through natural affection, creating a foundation within a narrow circle that can then be extended to human relationships at large.

imagen.text: Wind comes forth from fire: the image of the Family. Thus the superior man has substance in his words and duration in his way of life.
imagen.commentary: Heat generates power; this is signified by the wind, which is kindled by fire and comes forth from it. This represents an effect radiating from the inside out. The same principle is necessary in regulating the family. Here, too, the influence must originate from one's own person and extend to others. To exert such an influence, words must possess inner power, which is only possible when they rest on something real, just as a flame relies on its fuel. Only when words are objective and relate clearly to definite circumstances do they carry weight. General discourse and admonitions are completely ineffective. Furthermore, words must be supported by one's entire conduct, just as the wind acts through its duration. Only firm, consistent action will impress others sufficiently for them to adapt and align themselves accordingly. If words and behavior are discordant or inconsistent, no effect is achieved.

1.text: Firm seclusion within the family. Remorse disappears.
1.commentary: The family must form a well-defined unit within which every member knows their place. From the very beginning, children must be accustomed to fixed rules before their will is directed toward other things. If one begins to enforce order too late, when the children's分配 wills have already been spoiled, their grown-up whims and passions offer resistance, leading to cause for remorse. If order is established early enough, occasions for remorse will still arise - as they are inevitable when living together in a larger group - but the remorse disappears repeatedly. Everything adjusts itself. For there is nothing more easily avoided, yet harder to execute, than attempting to "break a child's will" later on.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: She should not follow her whims. She should provide food within. Perseverance brings good fortune.
2.commentary:
The woman should always guide herself by the will of the master of the house, whether it be the father, the husband, or the grown son 

Applied to general circumstances, the advice is not to seek anything by force, but to quietly limit oneself to existing duties.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: When tempers flare within the family, remorse from excessive severity arises. Yet good fortune! When woman and child dally and laugh, it leads in the end to humiliation.
3.commentary: Inside the family, the correct balance between harshness and leniency must prevail. Too much severity against one's own flesh and blood leads to remorse. The best course is to build firm dikes within which individuals are granted full freedom of movement. Nevertheless, in cases of doubt, excessive severity - despite occasional mistakes - is better because it preserves family discipline, whereas excessive weakness leads to disgrace.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: She is the wealth of the house. Great good fortune!
4.commentary: It is the housewife upon whom the prosperity of the family depends. Prosperity always reigns when expenditures and income stand in a healthy relationship to one another. This leads to great good fortune. Applied to public life, this refers to the faithful steward or administrator who furthers the general welfare through sound measures.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: As a king he approaches his family. Fear not. Good fortune!
5.commentary: A king is the image of a fatherly, inwardly rich man. He does not act in a way that causes fear; instead, the entire family can have confidence because love reigns in their interactions
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: His work commands respect. In the end, good fortune comes.
6.commentary: The order of the family rests ultimately on the character of the master of the house. If he cultivates his personality so that it commands respect through the power of inner truth, everything goes well in the family. One must personally shoulder the responsibility when in a leading position.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

38.name: OPPOSITION
38.title: Hexagram 38 睽 - KUÍ / OPPOSITION
38.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 38 (KUÍ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
38.intro: The hexagram consists of the upper primary trigram Lí, the flame that burns upward, and the lower primary trigram Duì, the lake that seeps downward. These movements are in direct opposition to one another. Furthermore, Lí represents the second daughter and Duì the youngest daughter. Although they reside in the same house, they belong to different husbands; therefore, their wills do not align but are directed toward opposite goals.

dictamen.text: Opposition In small matters, good fortune!
dictamen.commentary:
When people live in opposition and estrangement, a great common undertaking cannot be executed because minds diverge too widely. Above all, one must not act abruptly, which would only sharpen the animosity; instead, one must limit oneself to gradual effects in small matters. Here, good fortune can still be expected, as the situation allows for a degree of mutual understanding without ruling it out entirely.

Opposition, which generally appears as an obstacle, also serves important and necessary functions as a polar contrast within a comprehensive whole.

The oppositions between heaven and earth, spirit and nature, man and woman, bring about the creation and reproduction of life through their reconciliation. In the visible world of things, opposition enables differentiation into species, which brings order into the world.

imagen.text: Above, fire; below, the lake: The image of Opposition. Thus amid all fellowship, the superior man retains his individuality.
imagen.commentary: Just as the two elements fire and water never mix even when together but retain their own natures, so the cultured person, despite social interaction and shared interests with people of different dispositions, will never allow himself to be corrupted. Amid all fellowship, he will always preserve his unique character.

1.text: Remorse disappears. If you lose your horse, do not run after it. It will return of its own accord. When you see evil people, guard against mistakes.
1.commentary: Even in times of opposition, one can act in such a way as to remain free from errors, causing remorse to disappear. When opposition begins, one must not try to force unity; this would only achieve the opposite, just as a horse moves further away if you chase it. If it is our horse, we can let it run freely: it will return on its own. Similarly, a person who belongs with us and temporarily distances themselves due to a misunderstanding will return of their own accord if left alone. On the other hand, caution is required when evil people who do not belong with us force themselves upon us, also due to a misunderstanding. Here, the rule is to avoid mistakes: do not attempt to remove them by force, which would only provoke open hostility, but simply tolerate them. They will eventually withdraw on their own.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: One meets his master in a narrow alley. No blame.
2.commentary: Due to misunderstandings, it is impossible for people who naturally belong together to meet in a strictly formal or correct manner. Therefore, a casual meeting under informal circumstances is acceptable, provided an inner alignment and affinity exists.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: One sees the wagon dragged back, the oxen halted, the man's hair and nose cut off. Not a good beginning, but a good end.
3.commentary: Sometimes it appears as if everything has conspired against you; progress is blocked and held back, and one finds oneself insulted and disfigured (cutting off the hair and nose was a severe, degrading punishment in ancient China). Yet one must not lose heart; despite these oppositions, one must hold fast to the person with whom one knows themselves to be aligned. Thus, despite the bad beginning, the end will ultimately be good.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Isolated by opposition, one meets a like-minded companion with whom one can associate in sincerity. Despite danger, no blame.
4.commentary: Finding oneself in a society from which one is separated by an inner opposition leads to isolation. But if in such a situation one meets someone who, by their very nature, belongs to the same sphere and to whom full trust can be given, all dangers of isolation are overcome. Our will succeeds, and we remain free from blame.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Remorse disappears. The companion bites his way through the wrapping. If one goes to him, how could that be a mistake?
5.commentary: One finds a loyal person who was initially misjudged amid the general estrangement. But he bites his way through the separating wraps. For the person to whom this companion reveals his true nature, it is a duty to go to meet him and work together.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Isolated by opposition, one sees his companion as a pig covered with dirt, as a wagon full of devils. First one draws the bow against him, then one lays the bow aside. He is not a robber; he comes to court at the proper time. As one goes, rain falls; then comes good fortune.
6.commentary: Here, the isolation is caused by misunderstandings, rooted not in external circumstances but in internal states. One misjudges his best friends, holding them to be as unclean as a dirty pig and as dangerous as a wagon full of devils. One assumes a defensive posture. But finally, the error is recognized; the bow is laid aside, realizing that the other approaches with the best intentions for a close alliance. Thus the tension dissolves. The union resolves the opposition, just as falling rain relieves the sultry atmospheric tension before a thunderstorm. All ends well, because opposition turns into its exact opposite precisely at its peak.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

39.name: OBSTRUCTION
39.title: Hexagram 39 蹇 - JIĂN / OBSTRUCTION
39.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 39 (JIĂN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
39.intro: The hexagram represents a dangerous abyss lying ahead, while a steep, inaccessible mountain rises behind. Thus, one is surrounded by obstructions. However, the mountain's inherent attribute of keeping still provides a clear indication of how to escape these difficulties. The hexagram delineates obstructions that naturally emerge over time, but which can and must be overcome. Consequently, the entire guidance focuses on surmounting these impediments.

dictamen.text: Obstruction. The southwest furthers. The northeast does not further. It is favorable to see the great man. Perseverance brings good fortune.
dictamen.commentary: The southwest represents the direction of retreat; the northeast signifies the direction of advance. This situation presents obstacles that cannot be directly overcome. In such circumstances, wisdom dictates halting and retreating in the face of danger. This retreat, however, is merely a preparation for surmounting the obstacles. One must unite with like-minded friends and submit to the leadership of a man equal to the situation; success in removing the obstacles will then follow. This requires a steadfast perseverance, precisely when one must apparently take actions that lead away from the goal. This unswerving inner direction ultimately brings good fortune. An obstruction that lasts only for a time is of value for the development of one's personality. This is the value of adversity.

imagen.text: Water on the mountain: the image of Obstruction. Thus the superior man turns inward and cultivates his character.
imagen.commentary: Difficulties and obstructions throw a person back upon themselves. While the base individual seeks blame externally in others and accuses fate, the superior man searches for faults within himself. Through this introspection, external impediments become an opportunity for internal enrichment and cultivation.

1.text: Going leads to obstruction, Coming meets with praise.
1.commentary: When facing an obstruction, one must consider how best to handle it. If danger threatens, we must not blindly forge ahead, as this only leads to complications. Instead, it is correct to withdraw initially - not to abandon the struggle, but to await the proper moment for action.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: The king's servant faces obstruction upon obstruction. But it is not his own fault.
2.commentary: While it is usually best to bypass an obstruction and seek the path of least resistance, there is one case where one must confront the difficulty directly, even if obstacles pile upon obstacles: namely, when the path of duty dictates that one cannot act out of personal choice, but has the obligation to seek out danger in the service of a higher cause. In such a case, one may proceed with complete inner peace, knowing that this difficult situation was not brought about by one's own fault.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Going leads to obstructions; Therefore, he returns.
3.commentary: While the preceding line shows an official who must face danger for the sake of duty, this line illustrates a man acting as a patriarch or leader of his people. If he were to plunge recklessly into danger, it would be useless, because those entrusted to his care cannot advance alone. If, instead, he withdraws and turns back to his people, they welcome him with great joy.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Going leads to obstructions, Coming leads to union.
