Whoever stands still at the beginning, as long as they have not yet abandoned the truth, finds the right path. However, lasting firmness is required to avoid falling into a state of aimless drifting.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Keeping still of his calves. He cannot rescue him whom he follows. His heart is not glad.
2.commentary:
The leg cannot move independently; its movement depends on the movement of the body. If the body is in motion and the leg is suddenly stopped, the continuing momentum of the body causes the person to fall.

The same applies to a person who is in the retinue of a stronger personality. They are carried along. Even if they halt on the path of wrongdoing, they can no longer stop the other person's powerful momentum. Where the master presses forward, the servant cannot rescue him, no matter how good his intentions may be.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: Keeping still of his hips. Making his sacrum stiff. Dangerous. The heart suffocates.
3.commentary:
This refers to enforced quiet. The heart, which is in a state of restlessness, is to be forcibly subdued. However, fire that is violently suppressed turns into acrid smoke that suffocates as it spreads.

Therefore, one must not proceed violently during exercises of meditation and concentration. Instead, quiet must develop naturally from a state of inner composure. If one attempts to force quiet through artificial rigidity, meditation will lead to major difficulties.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Keeping still of his torso. No blame.
4.commentary: Keeping the back quiet, as mentioned in the words for the overall hexagram, means forgetting the ego. This is the highest stage of quiet. Here, this stage has not yet been fully reached. While one is already able to keep the ego with its thoughts and impulses still, one is not yet completely free from them. Nevertheless, keeping the heart still is an important function that eventually leads to the complete elimination of egoistic drives. Even if one does not remain entirely free from the dangers of doubt and restlessness, this mental attitude is no mistake, since it lies on the path to that higher stage.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Keeping still of his jaws. Words have order. Remorse disappears.
5.commentary: In a dangerous situation, particularly when one is not equal to it, it is very easy to indulge in talk and forward jests. Careless talk easily leads to situations that bring much to regret later. However, if one restrains oneself in speaking, words take on a firm form, and then all occasion for remorse disappears.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Noble-hearted keeping still. Good fortune!
6.commentary: Here we find the completion of the effort to attain quiet. One is not quiet in a narrow, petty, or detailed way; instead, a general resignation as a whole brings quiet and good fortune to every single detail.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

53.name: DEVELOPMENT (GRADUAL PROGRESS)
53.title: Hexagram 53 漸 - JIÀN / DEVELOPMENT (GRADUAL PROGRESS)
53.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 53 (JIÀN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
53.intro: The hexagram is composed of Xùn (Wood, Penetration) above or on the outside, and Gèn (Mountain, Stillness) below or on the inside. A tree growing on a mountain develops slowly and in accordance with the proper order, establishing deep roots as a result. This evokes the idea of development, which advances gradually, step by step. The inner qualities of the trigrams also reflect this process: inner stillness provides a shield against rash actions, while outer penetration allows progress and development to take place.

dictamen.text: Development. The maiden is given in marriage. Good fortune. Perseverance furthers.
dictamen.commentary:
The development that leads to a maiden following her husband to his home is a gradual process. Various formalities must be completed before the marriage can be consummated. This gradual progression can be applied to other situations as well, particularly where formal relationships of cooperation are concerned, such as the appointment of an official. In these matters, the proper sequence of development must be allowed to unfold. Rushing into action would lead to undesirable results. The same principle applies when attempting to influence others. True influence relies on a correct process of gradual development achieved through cultivating one's own personality. Any form of sudden, agitational influence fails to produce lasting effects.

The inner life must also follow this same path of development if enduring results are to be achieved.

The outer expression, which must arise from inner peace, is characterized by gentleness and adaptability, yet it remains penetrating.

The very nature of this gradual development requires steadfastness. Only constancy ensures that slow progress does not lose its momentum and fade away.

imagen.text: On the mountain, a tree: the image of Development. Thus the superior man abides in dignity and virtue to improve the customs of the world.
imagen.commentary: A tree on a mountain is visible from afar, and its development influences the landscape of the entire region. It does not shoot up rapidly like marsh plants; its growth is slow and gradual. Similarly, an individual's influence on people can only develop progressively. Sudden impressions or awakenings do not leave a lasting impact. Progress must be thoroughly gradual. To shape public opinion and improve public customs, an individual's personality must first gain weight and influence. This is accomplished through diligent, enduring dedication to one's own moral development.

1.text: The wild goose gradually draws near the shore. The young son is in danger. There is talk. No blame.
1.commentary:
The individual lines all use the gradual flight of the wild goose as a central image. The wild goose is a symbol of marital fidelity, as it is said never to take another mate after the death of its partner.

The opening line marks the first stage of the water birds' journey from the water to the heights, as they reach the shore. This describes the situation of a lonely young person who is just beginning to make his way in the world. Because he lacks connections to welcome or support him, his first steps are slow and hesitant, and he finds himself surrounded by danger. Naturally, he faces a great deal of criticism. Yet, these very difficulties prevent him from rushing ahead blindly, ensuring the success of his eventual progress.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: The wild goose gradually draws near the cliff. Eating and drinking in peace and harmony. Good fortune.
2.commentary:
The cliff represents a safe and stable place upon the shore. The process of development has advanced by one step. The initial uncertainty has passed, and a secure position in life has been found, providing an ample livelihood. This first success, which opens up opportunities for effective action, brings a sense of cheerfulness, allowing one to move toward the future with peace of mind.

It is said of the wild goose that it calls out to its companions when it finds food; this represents peace and harmony in times of good fortune. One does not wish to keep prosperity to oneself but is ready to share it with others.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: The wild goose gradually draws near the plateau. The husband goes forth and does not return. The wife carries a child but does not bring it to birth. Misfortune! It furthers one to fight off robbers.
3.commentary:
A dry plateau is no place for a wild goose. If it flies there, it has lost its way and gone too far. This runs entirely counter to the law of natural development.

The same is true in human life. Misfortune follows when a person does not allow things to develop quietly, choosing instead to plunge prematurely into conflict. One throws his own life away, and his family is ruined in the process. However, this outcome is by no means inevitable; it is simply the consequence of violating the law of natural development. If an individual refrains from actively seeking out conflict and instead limits himself to maintaining his position firmly while repelling unauthorized attacks, everything goes well.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: The wild goose gradually draws near the tree. Perhaps it will find a flat branch. No blame.
4.commentary: A tree is not a suitable resting place for a wild goose. However, if the bird is clever, it will find a flat branch capable of supporting it. In the course of life's development, one often encounters situations that are unsuitable or where it is difficult to maintain one's position without danger. In such moments, adaptability and insight are vital. By remaining flexible, one can discover a safe and viable foothold even in the midst of danger.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: The wild goose gradually draws near the summit. The wife bears no child for three years. In the end, nothing can prevent it. Good fortune.
5.commentary: The summit is an elevated place, and high positions can easily bring isolation. One is often misunderstood by the very person they depend upon: the wife by her husband, or the official by his ruler. This isolation is caused by deceitful people who have insinuated themselves between them. As a result, relationships remain sterile and nothing is accomplished. However, the natural course of development ensures that such misunderstandings dissolve, and the union is ultimately fulfilled.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: The wild goose gradually draws near the cloud-covered heights. Its feathers can be used for the sacred dance. Good fortune.
6.commentary:
Here, life's journey reaches its fulfillment. The work stands completed. Its path rises high into the heavens, like the flight of wild geese that have left all earthly ground behind. They soar upward, preserving the perfect order of their flight and forming precise, elegant lines across the sky.

Even when their feathers fall, they are gathered and used as ornaments in the sacred pantomimes of the temple dances.

Thus, the life of a person who has achieved fulfillment becomes a bright light for the people of the earth, who look up to him as an inspiring example.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

54.name: THE MARRYING MAIDEN
54.title: Hexagram 54 歸妹 - GUĪ MÈI / THE MARRYING MAIDEN
54.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 54 (GUĪ MÈI) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
54.intro:
Zhèn, the eldest son, is above; Duì, the youngest daughter, is below. The man leads and the girl follows him gladly. The text describes a maiden entering her husband's house. There are four hexagrams in total that depict relationship dynamics between spouses. No. 31, Xián, "Influence," describes the mutual attraction felt by a young couple. No. 32, Héng, "Duration," outlines the lasting conditions of marriage. No. 53, Jiàn, "Development," details the gradual, ceremonial steps required to conclude a proper marriage. Finally, Guī Mèi, "The Marrying Maiden," shows an older man followed in marriage by a young girl.

Note: Monogamy is the formal law in China. Every man has only one official wife. This union, which concerns the families far more than the two individuals involved, is concluded under the strictest observation of protocol. However, a man retains the right to follow his more tender personal affections. In fact, it is considered the finest duty of a good wife to assist him in this regard. This arrangement allows the relationship to remain beautiful and transparent. The girl who enters the family by the husband's choice subordinates herself modestly to the mistress of the house as a younger sister. Naturally, these are very delicate and sensitive matters that require great tact from everyone involved. Yet, under favorable circumstances, this provides a solution to a problem that European culture has not successfully resolved. Of course, ideal femininity in China is just as rare as European marriages that perfectly align with Western marital ideals.

dictamen.text: The Marrying Maiden. Undertakings bring misfortune. Nothing that would be furthered.
dictamen.commentary:
A girl who enters a family without becoming the principal wife must behave with exceptional caution and restraint. She must not take it upon herself to displace the mistress of the house, as this would cause disorder and lead to untenable relationships.

This principle applies to all free associations among people. While legally regulated relationships feature a fixed framework of duties and rights, unions based purely on personal affection depend entirely on tactful restraint for their endurance.

Affection as a foundational principle of relationships is of immense importance throughout the world. The union of Heaven and Earth sustains all of nature, and similarly, among human beings, free affection stands as the beginning and end of every true union.

imagen.text: Thunder above the Lake: The image of the Marrying Maiden. Thus the superior man, through the permanence of the end, recognizes the transitory.
imagen.commentary: Thunder stirs the water of the lake, which follows it in shimmering waves. This represents the maiden who follows the man of her choice. Yet every human connection carries the risk that deviations will creep in, leading to endless misunderstandings and difficulties. Therefore, it is essential to keep the end permanently in mind. If people simply let themselves drift, they come together and part as the day dictates. If, on the other hand, they keep a permanent end in view, they will succeed in avoiding the pitfalls that threaten close human relationships.

1.text: The marrying maiden as a concubine. A lame man who can walk. Undertakings bring good fortune.
1.commentary:
The princes of antiquity maintained a strict hierarchy among palace ladies, who were subordinate to the queen just as younger sisters are to the eldest. They often came from the queen's own family, and she would introduce them to her husband herself.

The meaning is that when a young girl enters a family with the full consent of the wife, she does not equal her in public status but steps back modestly. However, if she knows how to integrate herself into the household, she attains a thoroughly satisfying position and finds security in the love of the husband to whom she bears children.

The same dynamic applies to public officials. A prince may have a man with whom he is personally friendly and whom he takes into his confidence. This man must tactfully step back in public behind the official minister of state. Even though he is restricted by this position like a lame man, he can still accomplish much through the goodness of his character.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: A one-eyed man who can see. The perseverance of a solitary person is furthering.
2.commentary: The situation here is that the maiden has bound herself to a man who disappoints her. Husband and wife should work together like two eyes. Here, the maiden is left lonely. The man of her choice has either proven unfaithful or has died. Yet she does not lose the inner light of loyalty. Even if the other eye has gone dark, she maintains her fidelity in solitude.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: The marrying maiden as a slave. She marries as a concubine.
3.commentary:
A girl who finds herself in a low position and cannot obtain a husband may, under certain circumstances, still find a place as a concubine.

This situation arises when a person desires pleasures too intensely that cannot be obtained through normal channels. Consequently, one enters into a situation that is not entirely compatible with one's dignity. No judgment or warning is added; the situation is simply exposed as it is, so that everyone can draw their own lesson from it.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: The marrying maiden delays the term. A late marriage comes in its own time.
4.commentary: The girl is virtuous, refuses to throw herself away, and consequently misses the customary time for marriage. However, this does no harm. She is rewarded for her purity and eventually finds the husband intended for her, even if it happens late.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: The sovereign I marries off his daughter. The embroidered garments of the princess were not as splendid as those of the serving maid. The moon, which is almost full, brings good fortune.
5.commentary:
The sovereign I is Tang the Completer. He decreed that imperial princesses must also be subordinate to their husbands in marriage (see Hexagram 11, line 5). The emperor does not wait to be courted, but gives his daughter in marriage according to his own judgment. Therefore, initiative on the part of the maiden's family is appropriate here.

We see here a maiden of noble birth who marries into modest circumstances and knows how to adapt to her new situation with grace. She is free from the vanity of external adornment, forgets her high rank in marriage, and places herself below her husband, just as the moon, when not yet completely full, does not directly confront the sun.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: The woman holds the basket, but there is no fruit in it. The man stabs the sheep, but no blood flows. Nothing that would be furthered.
6.commentary: During ancestral sacrifices, the woman was required to present the fruits in a basket, while the man had to slaughter the sacrificial animal himself. Here, the rituals are fulfilled only superficially. The woman carries an empty basket, and the man stabs a sheep that has already been slaughtered, merely to keep up appearances. This irreverent, frivolous attitude promises no happiness for the marriage.
6.title: Six at the top means:

55.name: ABUNDANCE
55.title: Hexagram 55 豐 - FÈNG / ABUNDANCE
55.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 55 (FENG) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
55.intro: Zhèn represents movement, while Lí represents the flame, whose essential quality is clarity. Clarity within and movement without produce greatness and abundance. The hexagram depicts a period of high civilization and cultural peak. However, because this represents a maximum or zenith, the text already implies that this extraordinary state of abundance cannot be sustained indefinitely.

dictamen.text: Abundance has success. The king attains it. Be not sad; you must be like the sun at midday.
dictamen.commentary: Bringing about a time of supreme greatness and abundance is not granted to every mortal. It requires a born ruler of humanity to achieve this, because his will is directed toward what is great. The era of such abundance is usually brief. A sage might therefore feel saddened when contemplating the inevitable decline that follows. Yet such sadness does not befit him. Only a leader who is inwardly free from anxiety and sorrow can usher in a time of abundance. He must be like the sun at midday, illuminating and gladdening everything under heaven.

imagen.text: Both thunder and lightning come: the image of Abundance. Thus the superior man decides lawsuits and carries out punishments.
imagen.commentary: This hexagram shares a close relationship with Hexagram 21, Shì Kò (Biting Through), where thunder and lightning also appear together, but in the reverse order. While laws are established in that hexagram, here they are executed and applied. Clarity on the inside enables a thorough examination of the facts, while the powerful shock on the outside ensures the strict and precise execution of justice.

1.text: When one meets his destined lord, they may be together for ten days, and it is no mistake. To go brings recognition.
1.commentary: To bring about an era of abundance, clarity must join with energetic movement. When these two qualities meet in two different people, they are suited to one another. Even if they remain together for a full cycle during this time of abundance, it is not too long and constitutes no error. Therefore, one should go forward to act; it will bring recognition.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: The curtain is of such abundance that the pole stars can be seen at noon. By going forward, one meets with mistrust and hate. If one awakens him through truth, good fortune comes.
2.commentary: It often happens that plots and party intrigues interpose themselves between a ruler who desires great things and the ideal person who could execute them. This causes a darkening effect, much like a solar eclipse. In such moments, instead of the sun, the northern stars become visible in the sky. The ruler is eclipsed by a faction that has usurped power. If one were to attempt energetic action during such a time, it would only arouse suspicion and envy, making any progress impossible. The proper course is to stand firmly in the inner power of truth. This truth is ultimately so potent that it exerts an invisible influence on the ruler, leading to a good outcome.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: The brushwood is of such abundance that the small stars can be seen at noon. He breaks his right arm. No blame.
3.commentary:
This line depicts the progressive eclipse of the sun. At this point, totality is reached, so that even the smallest stars can be seen at noon.

Applied to social affairs, the prince is so completely eclipsed that even the most insignificant people can push themselves forward. Under these conditions, it is impossible for an able man, who could serve as the ruler's right hand, to undertake anything. It is as if his arm were broken. He is not to blame, however, for being prevented from acting in this manner.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: The curtain is of such abundance that the pole stars can be seen at noon. He meets his equal lord. Good fortune!
4.commentary: Here the darkness is already diminishing, allowing complementary elements to find each other. In this case, the necessary balance must also be found: ready action must be joined with the requisite wisdom. Then everything will go well. This line represents the inverse complement of the first line. There, wisdom needed to be reinforced by energy; here, energy must be guided by wisdom.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Lines come, blessing and fame approach. Good fortune!
5.commentary: The ruling man is modest and therefore receptive to the counsel of capable people. As a result, wise advisors enter his circle and bring him the guiding principles for action. This brings blessing, fame, and good fortune to him and to all the people.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: His house is in abundance. He screens his family. He peers through the gate and notices no one anymore. For three years he sees nothing. Misfortune!
6.commentary: This line depicts a man who, through arrogance and self-will, achieves the exact opposite of what he desires. He seeks luxury and splendor for his dwelling, and insists on being absolute master in his own house. By doing so, he alienates his family, leaving him completely isolated in the end.
6.title: Six at the top means:

56.name: THE WANDERER
56.title: Hexagram 56 旅 - LÜ / THE WANDERER
56.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 56 (LÜ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
56.intro: The mountain (Gèn) stands still, while above it, the fire (Li) flames up and does not linger. Therefore, they do not remain together. Strangeness and separation are the lot of the wanderer.

dictamen.text: The Wanderer. Success through smallness. Perseverance is of good fortune to the wanderer.
dictamen.commentary: As a wanderer and a stranger, one must not be brusque or highly ambitious. Since one does not have a large circle of acquaintances, one must not boast. One must be cautious and reserved; in this way, one protects oneself from evil. By being courteous toward others, one achieves success. The wanderer has no fixed abode; the road is his home. Therefore, he must ensure that he is inwardly upright and steadfast, that he stays only in good places, and associates only with good people. Then he will have good fortune and can travel his path unmolested.

imagen.text: Fire on the mountain: the image of the Wanderer. Thus the superior man is clear-minded and cautious in applying punishments and does not protract litigation.
imagen.commentary: When grass burns on the mountain, it gives off a bright light. However, the fire does not linger; it moves on in search of new fuel. It is a rapidly passing phenomenon. It should be the same with punishments and lawsuits. They must be rapidly passing phenomena and must not be dragged out. Prisons should be places that hold people only temporarily, like guests. They must not become permanent dwellings for human beings.

1.text: If the wanderer busies himself with petty things, he brings misfortune upon himself.
1.commentary: A wanderer must not demean himself or get involved with vulgar things along the way. The lower and more defenseless his outward position is, the more he must maintain his inner dignity. For if a stranger thinks he can find a friendly welcome by lending himself to jokes and ridicule, he is mistaken. The only results are contempt and insulting treatment.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: The wanderer comes to an inn. He has his property with him. He gains the perseverance of a young servant.
2.commentary: The wanderer described here is modest and reserved. Inwardly, he does not lose his core self, so he finds a place of rest. Outwardly, he does not lose the goodwill of others, so everyone furthers him, enabling him to acquire property. Furthermore, he attracts a loyal and trustworthy servant, which is of inestimable value to a wanderer.
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: The wanderer's inn burns down. He loses the perseverance of his young servant. Danger.
3.commentary: A violent stranger does not know how to behave. He meddles in affairs and disputes that do not concern him. As a result, he loses his resting place. He treats his servant in an aloof and arrogant manner, thereby losing his loyalty. When a stranger no longer has anyone to rely on, the situation becomes highly dangerous.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: The wanderer rests at a shelter. He acquires his property and an axe. My heart is not glad.
4.commentary: This describes a wanderer who knows how to be outwardly modest, even though he is inwardly strong and aspiring. Therefore, he finds at least a shelter where he can stay. He also succeeds in acquiring property. Yet, he is not safe with his possessions. He must constantly be on guard, ready to defend himself with weapon in hand. Consequently, he does not feel at ease. He remains acutely aware that he is a stranger in a strange land.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: He shoots a pheasant, it falls with the first arrow. In the end, this brings praise and office.
5.commentary:
Traveling statesmen used to introduce themselves to princes by presenting a pheasant as a gift. Here, the wanderer wishes to enter the service of a prince. For this purpose, he shoots a pheasant, bringing it down with his very first shot. Thus, he finds friends who praise and recommend him, and he is finally accepted by the prince, who confers an office upon him.

Circumstances often arise that compel a person to seek a home abroad. If one understands how to meet the situation and introduce oneself properly, one can find a circle of friends and a sphere of activity even in a foreign land.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: The bird's nest burns down. The wanderer laughs at first, then he must cry and lament. Through carelessness, he loses his cow. Misfortune!
6.commentary: The image of the bird whose nest burns down shows the loss of one's resting place. If the bird was careless and imprudent while building its nest, this misfortune can happen. The same applies to the wanderer. If he gives himself up to jest and laughter, forgetting that he is a wanderer, he will later have to weep and lament. For if a person carelessly loses his cow-that is, his modest adaptability-it leads to evil.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

57.name: THE GENTLE
57.title: Hexagram 57 巽 - XÙN / THE GENTLE
57.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 57 (XÙN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.

above.text: Xùn, the Gentle, the Wind, Wood

below.text: Xùn, the Gentle, the Wind, Wood

57.intro:
Xùn is one of the eight double signs. It represents the eldest daughter, its image is wind or wood, and its attribute is gentleness, which nevertheless penetrates just like the wind or like wood with its roots.

The dark element, rigid and immobile in itself, is dissolved by the penetrating light principle, to which it subordinates itself in gentleness. In nature, it is the wind that disperses the gathered clouds, leaving behind a clear and serene sky. In human life, it is the penetrating clarity of judgment that shatters all dark, hidden motives. In the life of the community, it is the powerful influence of a prominent personality who uncovers and disperses all underhanded machinations.

dictamen.text: The Gentle. Success through small things. It is favorable to have a destination. It is favorable to see the great man.
dictamen.commentary:
Penetrating influence produces gradual and inconspicuous effects. It should not work through force or violation, but through continuous, subtle impression. These effects are less conspicuous than those achieved by surprise attack, but they are more lasting and complete. To influence in this manner, one must have a clear objective; only when the penetrating influence works consistently in the same direction can something be achieved.

The small can only achieve something by subordinating itself to a prominent man who possesses the ability to establish order.

imagen.text: Winds following one another: The image of the Gently Penetrating. Thus the superior man spreads his commands and carries out his business.
imagen.commentary: The penetrating power of the wind rests upon its relentlessness. This is what makes it so powerful. It uses time as its instrument. In the same way, the ruler's thoughts must penetrate the soul of the people. This also requires a sustained influence through education and enlightenment. Only when the command has been integrated into the soul of the people does corresponding action become possible. Unprepared action only startles and repels.

1.text: In advancing and retreating, the perseverance of a warrior is favorable.
1.commentary: A gentle nature often leads to indecisiveness. One does not feel the strength to move forward resolutely. A thousand doubts arise, yet one does not wish to withdraw either, drifting indecisively back and forth. In such a case, military decisiveness is the correct approach, doing resolutely what order requires. Resolute discipline is far better than indecisive lack of control.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: Penetrating under the bed. One employs priests and magicians in great numbers. Good fortune! No blame.
2.commentary: At times, one has to deal with hidden enemies or intangible influences that crawl into the darkest corners and suggestively manipulate people from there. In such cases, it is necessary to track these things down into their most secret recesses to determine the nature of the influences - which is the task of the priests - and to eliminate them - which is the task of the magicians. The anonymous nature of such intrigues demands untiring energy, but it brings its reward. Once such uncontrollable influences are brought to light and exposed, they lose their power over people.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: Repeated penetration. Humiliation.
3.commentary: Penetrating reflection must not be pushed too far, otherwise it paralyzes the power of decision. When a matter has been thoroughly thought through, it is time to decide and act. By repeatedly rethinking things, one falls into fresh doubts over and over again, which leads to humiliation because one proves incapable of taking action.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: Remorse vanishes. During the hunt, three kinds of game are caught.
4.commentary: When innate modesty is combined with energetic action, especially due to a responsible position and gathered experience, great success is assured. The three kinds of animals served as sacrifices for the gods, for entertaining guests, and for daily consumption. When game was caught for all three purposes, the harvest of the hunt was exceptionally good.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Perseverance brings good fortune. Remorse vanishes. Nothing that is not favorable. No beginning, but an end. Before the change, three days. After the change, three days. Good fortune!
5.commentary: While in "Work on What Has Been Spoiled" (No. 18) a completely new starting point must be established, here it is only a matter of reforms. The beginning was not good, but a point has been reached where a new direction can be taken. One must change and improve. This must be done with constancy, that is, with a correct and firm attitude, and then it will succeed and remorse will vanish. However, one must note that such improvements require careful consideration. Before making the change, repeated reflection is necessary, and after the change is made, one must carefully observe for a while how the improvements work out in reality. Such thorough work is accompanied by good fortune.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Penetrating under the bed. He loses his property and his axe. Perseverance brings misfortune.
6.commentary: One's insight is penetrating enough. One tracks the harmful influences down into their most secret corners. Yet, one no longer possesses the strength to combat them decisively. In this case, any attempt to penetrate into the personal domains of darkness only brings misfortune.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

58.name: THE JOYOUS
58.title: Hexagram 58 兌 - DUÌ / THE JOYOUS
58.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 58 (DUÌ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
58.intro:
Like Xùn, Duì is one of the eight doubled signs. Duì represents the youngest daughter; its image is the smiling lake, and its attribute is joy. This joy does not stem from the weakness shown in the top line, as it might seem at first glance. The attribute of the soft, dark principle is melancholy rather than joy. Instead, joy comes from having two strong lines within that express themselves outwardly through a gentle medium.

True joy, therefore, relies on inner firmness and strength that manifest outwardly in a soft, gentle manner.

dictamen.text: The Joyous. Success. Perseverance is rewarding.
dictamen.commentary: A cheerful mood is contagious, which is why it brings success. However, joy requires steadfastness as a foundation so that it does not degenerate into uncontrolled unrestrainedness. Truth and strength must dwell within the heart, while gentleness shows itself outwardly in social interactions. In this way, one assumes the right attitude toward both the divine and humanity, thereby achieving something meaningful. Merely intimidating others without gentleness might work for the moment, but never for long. On the other hand, winning people's hearts through kindness makes them willingly take on hardships, and if necessary, they will not even fear death. Such is the power of joy over people.

imagen.text: Lakes resting upon one another: the image of the Joyous. Thus the superior person joins with friends for discussion and practice.
imagen.commentary: A single lake evaporates upward and gradually depletes itself. However, when two lakes are connected, they do not dry up easily because one replenishes the other. The same holds true in intellectual and scholarly pursuits. Knowledge should be a refreshing and vitalizing force. It can only become so through stimulating interaction with like-minded friends, with whom one discusses and practices the application of life truths. In this way, knowledge becomes multi-faceted and takes on a cheerful lightness, whereas the knowledge of the self-taught always retains a certain heaviness and one-sidedness.

1.text: Contented joy. Good fortune!
1.commentary: A quiet, wordless, self-contained joy that desires nothing from the outside and is content with everything remains free from all selfish likes and dislikes. Good fortune lies in this freedom, for it holds the quiet security of a well-anchored heart.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Sincere joy. Good fortune! Remorse vanishes.
2.commentary: One often finds oneself interacting with inferior people, among whom temptations of a lower kind beckon. Joining in such pleasures would surely bring remorse, as a higher person cannot truly be satisfied with base pleasures. If, through this realization, one remains firm in purpose and finds no pleasure in these things, even a dubious environment will not dare to offer ignoble pastimes, knowing they would fail to please. This removes any cause for regret.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: Approaching joy. Misfortune.
3.commentary: True joy must well up from within. When a person is inwardly empty and loses themselves to the outside world, pleasures must be sought from external sources. This is what many welcome as diversion. People who need distraction due to inner instability will always find opportunities to amuse themselves. They attract superficial pleasures through the emptiness of their own being. Consequently, they lose themselves more and more, which is naturally harmful.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Deliberate joy is not at peace. After eliminating mistakes, one has joy.
4.commentary: A person often stands divided between different kinds of pleasure. As long as one remains undecided about which kind of joy to choose, the higher or the lower, internal restlessness prevails. Only when one clearly recognizes that passion brings suffering can a decision be made to cast off the lower element and strive for higher joys. Once this choice is sealed, true inner serenity and peace are found, and the internal conflict is overcome.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Sincerity toward disintegrating elements is dangerous.
5.commentary: Even the best of people face dangerous influences. If one associates with them, their corrosive influence works slowly but surely, inevitably bringing dangers in its wake. However, anyone who recognizes the situation and understands how to see through the danger knows how to protect themselves and remains free from harm.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Seductive joy.
6.commentary: An inwardly vain person attracts the pleasures of diversion and suffers because of them (compare with Six in the third place). When someone is not inwardly anchored, the pleasures of the outside world, from which they do not withdraw, exert such a powerful influence that they are swept away. Here, there is no longer any talk of danger, good fortune, or misfortune. The guidance of life has been surrendered, and what becomes of the person depends entirely on chance and external influences.
6.title: Six at the top means:

59.name: DISPERSION (DISSOLUTION)
59.title: Hexagram 59 渙 - HUÀN / DISPERSION (DISSOLUTION)
59.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 59 (HUÀN) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
59.intro: The wind blowing over the water scatters it, dissolving it into foam and mist. This implies that when life energy becomes stagnant within a person - an internal block symbolized by the dangerous nature of the lower trigram - gentleness can gently scatter and dissolve the rigidity.

dictamen.text: Dispersion. Success. The king approaches his temple. It furthers one to cross the great water. Perseverance furthers.
dictamen.commentary:
The text of this hexagram closely resembles that of Hexagram 45, Ts'ui (Gathering Together). In that hexagram, the focus is on gathering what is scattered, just as water collects into lakes upon the earth. Here, the focus is on dispersing and dissolving the egoism that separates us. Dispersion shows the very path that leads back to gathering, which explains why the texts are so similar.

Overcoming the egoism that divides humanity requires deep spiritual forces. The shared celebration of great religious festivals and worship services - which simultaneously expressed the interconnectedness and social structure of the family and the state - was the means used by the great rulers. Through sacred music and the splendor of ceremonies, they stirred hearts in a collective wave of feeling, awakening a consciousness of the common origin of all beings. In this way, divisions were overcome and rigid isolation dissolved. 

Another powerful means is working together on great common undertakings. By setting a great goal for the collective will, all divisive elements dissolve in the pursuit of that objective - much like passengers on a ship crossing a great river, who must unite in common effort to succeed.

However, only someone who remains free from selfish ulterior motives, standing firm in justice and constancy, is capable of dissolving the hardness of egoism in this way.

imagen.text: The wind drives over the water: the image of Dispersion. Thus the kings of old sacrificed to the Lord and built temples.
imagen.commentary: In autumn and winter, water begins to harden and freeze into ice. When the mild breezes of spring arrive, the rigidity thaws, and the scattered ice floes reunite. The same dynamics apply to the spirit of a people. Hardness and selfishness cause the heart to freeze, and this rigidity isolates it from everyone else. Egoism and greed alienate people. Therefore, a devout reverence must touch the human heart. It must be dissolved in sacred awe of the eternal - shaken by the awareness of the common creator of all beings, and unified by the power of community feelings during the sacred celebration of divine worship.

1.text: He brings help with the strength of a horse. Good fortune.
1.commentary: Here, the focus is on overcoming the first signs of separation before the division is fully complete - scattering the clouds before the storm and rain arrive. In times when subtle shifts in mood occur and mutual misunderstandings begin to take root, one must act quickly and decisively to dissolve these misgivings and dispel mutual distrust.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: At the dissolution, he runs to his support. Remorse disappears.
2.commentary: When you discover within yourself the beginnings of alienation from others, misanthropy, or ill-will, you must actively disperse these inner blockages. You must rouse yourself internally and hasten toward your true support. A person's ultimate support never lies in hatred, but always in a balanced, just, and benevolent view of humanity. By regaining this open, clear perspective on mankind and scattering all melancholic discontent, any reason for remorse vanishes.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: He dissolves his self. No remorse.
3.commentary: At times, the task at hand can become so demanding that you can no longer think of yourself. You must set your own persona entirely aside, dispersing everything that the ego wishes to gather around itself to separate you from others. Only on the foundation of a great renunciation do you gain the strength for great achievements. By placing your goal outside of yourself in a great cause, you can firmly establish this standpoint.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: He dissolves his bond with his group. Supreme good fortune. Dispersion leads to accumulation. This is something ordinary people do not think of.
4.commentary: When working on a task that affects the greater good, you must set all private friendships aside. Only by rising above partisan interests can you achieve something truly decisive. Whoever dares to renounce what is near will win what is distant. However, you must have a vast overview of life's interconnected patterns - the kind of vision only exceptional individuals attain - to truly understand this standpoint.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Loud cries dissolve like sweat. Dissolution! A king dwells without blame.
5.commentary: In times of general dissolution and separation, a great idea serves as the focal point for recovery. Just as a physical illness reaches its turning point and clears through a breaking sweat, a great, inspiring idea acts as a true liberation in times of general stagnation. It gives people something around which they can rally, led by a commanding figure who can dissolve all misunderstandings.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: He dissolves his blood. Departing, keeping at a distance, going out is without blame.
6.commentary: Dissolving one's blood means dispersing whatever might lead to bloodshed and wounds, thereby avoiding danger. This does not imply that a person merely evades difficulties for their own sake. Rather, it means saving one's people - helping them depart before danger strikes, keeping them at a distance from an existing peril, and finding a way out of a crisis that has already engulfed them. In this manner, one does what is right.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

60.name: LIMITATION
60.title: Hexagram 60 節 - JIÉ / LIMITATION
60.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 60 (JIÉ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
60.intro:
A lake occupies a limited space. When more water flows into it, it overflows. Therefore, limits must be set. The image shows water below and water above, with the firmament of heaven acting as a boundary between them.

The Chinese word for limitation originally refers to the firm joints that divide a bamboo stalk. In daily life, it signifies economy, which sets fixed boundaries for expenditure. In the moral sphere, it represents the clear limits that the superior person sets for their actions - the boundaries of loyalty and selflessness.

dictamen.text: Limitation. Success. Bitter limitation must not be persevered in.
dictamen.commentary:
Boundaries are demanding, but they achieve results. By practicing economy in everyday life, one is prepared for times of scarcity. Exercising restraint saves one from embarrassment. Furthermore, limitations are indispensable in maintaining the order of the world. Nature has fixed boundaries for summer and winter, day and night, and these limits give the year its meaning. Similarly, economy ensures that fixed limits on expenditures preserve wealth and prevent harm to the people.

However, moderation is necessary even within limitation. If someone imposes overly bitter restrictions on their own nature, they will suffer under them. If one pushes the limitation of others too far, they will rebel. Therefore, boundaries are necessary even within limitation itself.

imagen.text: Water is above the lake: The image of Limitation. Thus the superior person examines number and measure, And investigates what virtue and correct conduct are.
imagen.commentary: A lake is finite; water is inexhaustible. The lake can hold only a specific measure of the infinite water, and this defines its character. In human life, an individual gains significance through differentiation and the establishment of boundaries. The task here is to clearly define these distinctions, which form the backbone of morality. Unlimited possibilities are not suited for human beings; they would cause life to dissolve into the boundless. To grow strong, one requires the voluntary boundaries imposed by duty. Only by surrounding oneself with these limits and freely adopting the mandate of duty does an individual gain significance as a free person.

1.text: Not going out of the door and courtyard is no blame.
1.commentary:
Often one wishes to undertake a project but faces insurmountable boundaries. In such times, it is essential to understand where to stop. If a person understands this correctly and does not go beyond the limits set for them, they accumulate the energy needed to act decisively when the proper time arrives. Confidentiality is of fundamental importance when preparing significant matters.

Confucius says regarding this: "Where disorder arises, words are the steps that lead to it. If the prince is not confidential, he loses his servant. If the servant is not confidential, he loses his life. If crucial matters are not handled with secrecy in their germinal stage, it harms their fulfillment. Therefore, the superior person is careful to maintain confidentiality and does not go out."
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: Not going out of the gate and courtyard brings misfortune.
2.commentary: When the time for action comes, one must seize the opportunity immediately. Just as water initially gathers in a lake without flowing out, but surely finds an opening once the lake is full, so it is in human life. It is proper to hesitate as long as the time is not yet ripe, but no longer. Once obstacles are removed and action becomes possible, anxious hesitation is a mistake that inevitably brings misfortune, because the opportunity has been missed.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: He who knows no limitation will have to lament. No blame.
3.commentary: When a person is intent only on pleasure and enjoyment, they easily lose their sense of necessary limits. If they give in to extravagance, they will experience the consequences with regret. One should not try to find fault in others. Only when someone recognizes their own mistake can these unpleasant experiences set them free from faults.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Contented limitation. Success.
4.commentary: Every limitation has its value. However, if a restriction still requires constant effort, it demands too much energy. When limitation is natural - just as it is in the nature of water to flow downward - it leads inevitably to success because it represents a saving of energy. The force that would otherwise be exhausted in a futile struggle against the object is applied entirely to the task at hand, and success is assured.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: Sweet limitation brings good fortune. Going brings esteem.
5.commentary: Limitation must be carried out in the right way to be effective. If someone only imposes boundaries on others while exempting themselves, those limits will always be felt bitterly and will cause resentment. If, on the other hand, a leader begins the limitation with themselves, expects little from their people, and achieves results with modest means, good fortune follows. Where such an example is set, it finds followers, so that whatever is undertaken must succeed.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Bitter limitation: Perseverance brings misfortune. Remorse disappears.
6.commentary: If one is too severe in limitation, people cannot endure it. The more consistent one is in such severity, the worse it becomes, for a reaction cannot be avoided in the long run. Similarly, a tormented body avenges itself when one attempts to proceed with overly strict asceticism. Yet, even if this ruthless severity is not something that can be applied permanently and regularly, there are times when it is the only means to guard against guilt and remorse. These are situations where ruthlessness toward oneself is the sole way to save the soul, which would otherwise perish in halfheartedness and temptation.
6.title: Six at the top means:

61.name: INNER TRUTH
61.title: Hexagram 61 中孚 - ZHŌNG FÚ / INNER TRUTH
61.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 61 (ZHŌNG FÚ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
61.intro:
The wind blows over the lake and stirs the surface of the water. Thus, visible effects of the invisible manifest themselves. The hexagram consists of firm lines at the top and bottom, while the center is open. This points to a heart free from prejudice, rendering it capable of receiving the truth. Conversely, the two inner trigrams each have a firm line at their center. This points to the power of inner truth in its effects.

The attributes of the component trigrams are: above gentleness, flexibility toward those below; below joyfulness, obediently following those above. These conditions create the basis for mutual trust, which makes success possible.

The character Fu (truth) actually depicts a bird's claw over a fledgling. It carries the idea of brooding. An egg is hollow. The power of the light element must act formatively and life-givingly from without. Yet, there must already be a germ of life within for life to be awakened. Far-reaching insights can be drawn from these reflections.

dictamen.text: Inner Truth. Pigs and fishes. Good fortune! It furthers one to cross the great water. Perseverance furthers.
dictamen.commentary: Pigs and fishes are the least spiritual animals and therefore the hardest to influence. The power of inner truth must reach a high degree before its influence can extend to such creatures. When dealing with stubborn, difficult-to-influence people, the entire secret of success lies in finding the right way to gain access to them. One must first free oneself completely from personal prejudices. One must, so to speak, let the other person's psyche act upon oneself without bias; this brings one inwardly close to them, enabling understanding and establishing a connection through which the power of one's own personality can win influence. If one encounters no insurmountable obstacles in this way, one can undertake even the most dangerous tasks - such as crossing the great water - and succeed. It is crucial, however, to understand what the power of inner truth rests upon. It is not identical with simple intimacy or secret collusion. Such close collusion can exist even among thieves. While it represents a force in that context as well, it does not lead to good fortune because it is not invincible. Any alliance based solely on shared interests only lasts to a certain point. Where mutual interest ends, the alliance dissolves, and the closest friendship often turns to hatred. Only when the foundation is right and constant does the bond remain so firm that it overcomes everything.

imagen.text: Wind over the lake: The image of Inner Truth. Thus the superior man discusses criminal cases In order to delay executions.
imagen.commentary: The wind stirs the water because it penetrates into every opening. Similarly, when the superior man has to judge the mistakes of others, he seeks to penetrate deeply into their inner motives with understanding, thereby gaining a compassionate assessment of the circumstances. The entire system of ancient Chinese justice was guided by this principle. Complete understanding that knows how to forgive was considered the highest form of justice. This approach to justice was highly effective, for the moral impression was meant to be so powerful that there was no fear of abusing such mercy. It did not stem from weakness, but from superior clarity.

1.text: Being prepared brings good fortune. If there are secret designs, it is disquieting.
1.commentary: The most vital element for the power of inner truth is to be centered and prepared within oneself. From this inner posture arises the correct attitude toward the outer world. If, on the other hand, one tries to cultivate special, secret relationships, it compromises one's inner independence. The more one seeks security in relying on others, the more one becomes anxious and worried about whether these secret bonds will truly hold. As a result, one loses inner peace and the very power of inner truth.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: A calling crane in the shade. Its young answers it. I have a good goblet. I will share it with you.
2.commentary:
This refers to the involuntary influence of one's inner being upon kindred spirits. The crane does not need to show itself on a high hill. Even if it calls from complete concealment, its young hears its voice, recognizes it, and responds. Where a joyful mood exists, a companion will appear to share a cup of wine.

This illustrates the echo awakened in others through genuine sympathy. Wherever a feeling expresses itself truthfully and purely, and wherever an action is a clear expression of one's inner disposition, they exert a mysterious influence at a distance, affecting first those who are inwardly receptive. These circles then expand. The root of all influence lies in one's own inner self. When that self finds true and powerful expression in word and deed, the effect is immense. The result is merely the reflection of what emanates from one's own heart. Any calculated effort to produce an effect would only destroy it.

Confucius says of this: "The superior man abides in his room. If his words are spoken well, he meets with assent at a distance of more than a thousand miles. How much more from nearby! If the superior man abides in his room and his words are not spoken well, he meets with opposition at a distance of more than a thousand miles. How much more from nearby! Words go forth from one's own person and influence people. Deeds are born close at hand and become visible far away. Words and deeds are the hinge and bowstring of the superior man. As hinge and bowstring move, they bring honor or shame. Through words and deeds, the superior man moves heaven and earth. Must one not be careful?"
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: He finds a comrade. Now he beats the drum, now he stops. Now he sobs, now he sings.
3.commentary: Here the source of strength is not within one's own self, but in relationships with other people. No matter how close one is to them, if one's center of gravity rests on others, it is impossible to avoid being tossed between joy and sorrow. Rejoicing to heaven, grieving to death—this is the fate of those who depend on inner agreement with the people they love. This line simply states the law of this condition. Whether this state is felt as a burden or as the supreme happiness of love is left to the subjective judgment of the person involved.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: The moon nearly full. The team horse goes astray. No blame.
4.commentary: To increase the power of inner truth, one must turn toward the higher source from which enlightenment is received, just as the moon receives its light from the sun. However, a certain humility is required, like that of the moon when it is not yet completely full. If the moon faces the sun directly as a full moon, it immediately begins to wane. Just as one must be humble and reverent toward the source of enlightenment, one must also renounce human cliques. Only by going one's way like a horse that runs straight ahead, without looking back at its teammate, does one retain the inner freedom that leads forward.
4.title: Six in the fourth place means:

5.text: He possesses truth that binds together. No blame.
5.commentary: This describes the ruler who holds everything together through the power of his inner being. Only when his strength of character is so broad that he can influence all who belong to his domain is he as he should be. The power of suggestion must emanate from the ruler. It will bind and unite all his followers firmly. Without this central force, any external unity is mere pretense, destined to shatter at the critical moment.
5.title: Nine in the fifth place means:

6.text: Cockcrow penetrating to heaven. Perseverance brings misfortune.
6.commentary: The rooster is reliable. It crows when morning approaches. However, it cannot fly to heaven itself; it only crows. Similarly, one may attempt to arouse faith through empty words alone. This may succeed occasionally, but if pursued continuously, it leads to misfortune.
6.title: Nine at the top means:

62.name: PREPONDERANCE OF THE SMALL
62.title: Hexagram 62 小過 - XIǍO GUÒ / PREPONDERANCE OF THE SMALL
62.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 62 (XIǍO GUÒ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
62.intro: While in the hexagram "Preponderance of the Great" (No. 28), the strong lines are in the majority and are situated on the inside, enclosed between the two weak lines at the beginning and the end, here the weak lines are in the majority and are likewise on the outside, while the strong ones are inside. This is the basis of the exceptional state. When the strong lines are on the outside, we find the hexagrams Yí, Providing Nourishment, and Zhōng Fú, Inner Truth, neither of which represents an exceptional state. When the strong lines are in the majority on the inside, they must force their way through. This creates struggle and exceptional states on a grand scale. Here, however, the weak must of necessity represent the outside. When one holds a decisive position to which one is not intrinsically equal by nature, extraordinary caution is required.

dictamen.text: Preponderance of the Small. Success. Perseverance furthers. Small things may be done; great things should not be done. The flying bird brings the message: "It is not well to strive upward, it is well to remain below." Great good fortune!
dictamen.commentary: Extraordinary modesty and conscientiousness will surely be rewarded with success. However, it is essential that these qualities do not become empty formulas or a subservient attitude, but remain combined with proper dignity in one's personal conduct, preventing self-abasement. One must understand the demands of the time to find the right remedy for its defects and damages. Still, one must not count on great successes, as the necessary strength for them is lacking. Therefore, the message not to strive for high things but to keep to low ones is so important. That this message is brought by a bird follows from the shape of the hexagram. The four strong, heavy lines inside, supported by only two weak lines outside in Dà Guò (No. 28), give the image of a heavy ridgepole. Here, the supporting light lines are on the outside and in the majority; this gives the image of a soaring bird. But the bird should not presume to fly toward the sun; instead, it should descend to the earth where its nest is. It thereby delivers the message proclaimed by the hexagram.

imagen.text: Thunder on the mountain: The image of Preponderance of the Small. Thus the superior man in his conduct places preponderance on reverence. In times of mourning, he places preponderance on grief. In his expenditures, he places preponderance on thrift.
imagen.commentary: Thunder on the mountain is different from thunder on the plain. In the mountains, the thunder is much closer, whereas outside the mountains, it is less audible than the thunder of an ordinary storm. Thus, the superior man derives from this image the call to keep duty closer and more immediate than ordinary people do, even though his behavior might consequently appear petty to outsiders. He is exceptionally meticulous in his actions. In times of mourning, inner grief is far closer to him than outward formality, and in personal expenditures, he is extraordinarily simple and unpretentious. All this makes him an exception compared to the masses. But the essence of this exception is that, outwardly, it always leans toward the side of the lowly.

1.text: The bird meets with misfortune through flying.
1.commentary: The bird should first remain in its nest until it is fully fledged. If it tries to fly before then, it invites misfortune. Extraordinary measures should only be taken when there is no other way. To begin with, one must conform to what is customary for as long as possible; otherwise, one burns through one's strength and achieves nothing.
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: She passes by her ancestor and meets her ancestress. He does not reach his prince and meets the official. No blame.
2.commentary:
Two exceptional cases are mentioned here: In the ancestral temple, where the change of generations occurs, the grandson stands on the same side as the grandfather; hence, he has the closest relations to him. Here, the wife of the grandson is depicted, who passes by the ancestor during the sacrifice and turns toward the ancestress. This extraordinary behavior, however, is an expression of her modesty. She dares more readily to approach the ancestress, to whom she feels related by her gender, so this deviation from the rule is not a mistake.

Another image is that of the official who, as is proper, first seeks an audience with his prince. If he does not meet him, however, he does not try to force anything by violence, but finds his place in conscientious fulfillment of duty by joining the ranks of the officials. This extraordinary restraint is likewise no mistake in exceptional times. (As a rule, every official first has an audience with the prince by whom he is appointed. Here, the appointment comes from the minister.)
2.title: Six in the second place means:

3.text: If one does not take extraordinary precautions, someone may come up from behind and strike. Misfortune!
3.commentary:
At times, extraordinary caution is absolutely necessary. Yet, in precisely such situations, there are straightforward and strong characters who, conscious of being in the right, disdain to take precautions because they consider it petty. Instead, they walk their path proudly and unconcerned. But this self-confidence deceives them. There are dangers that approach from ambush, to which they are not equal.

Still, this is a danger to which one is not unconditionally exposed; it can be avoided if one understands the situation of the times, which demands turning toward the small and insignificant in an extraordinary way.
3.title: Nine in the third place means:

4.text: No blame. Without passing him by, he meets him. Going brings danger. One must be on guard. Do not act. Be constantly persevering.
4.commentary: The hardness of the character is softened by the gentleness of the position, so that no mistake is made. One finds oneself in a situation where one must restrain oneself to the utmost. One must not undertake anything on one's own initiative to meet what is desired. And if one were to go forward to achieve one's goal by force, one would encounter danger. Therefore, one must be on guard and not act, but constantly maintain inner perseverance.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Dense clouds, no rain from our western territory. The prince shoots and hits that one in the cave.
5.commentary:
Since this is a high place, the image of the flying bird has changed to that of flying clouds. But no matter how dense the clouds are, they fly across the sky without shedding rain. Thus, in exceptional times, a born ruler may indeed be present who is called to set the world in order, but he cannot accomplish anything or bring his blessing to the people because he stands alone and has no helper.

In such times, one must search for helpers with whom to accomplish the work. But these helpers must be sought modestly in the obscurity to which they have withdrawn. It is not fame or a great name that matters, but actual achievement.

Through such modesty, one finds the right man and is able to complete the extraordinary work despite all difficulties.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: Without meeting him, he passes him by. The flying bird leaves him. Misfortune! This means disaster and injury.
6.commentary: If one shoots past the mark, one cannot hit it. If the bird does not want to return to its nest but flies higher and higher, it eventually falls into the hunter's net. Anyone who, in extraordinary times, does not know how to stop in small things but restlessly presses on, invites misfortune from both gods and men because he distances himself from the natural order.
6.title: Six at the top means:

63.name: AFTER COMPLETION
63.title: Hexagram 63 既濟 - JÌ JÌ / AFTER COMPLETION
63.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete investigation and analysis of Hexagram 63 (JÌ JÌ) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
63.intro: This hexagram represents the fully developed form of Hexagram 11, Peace (Tài). The transition from chaos to order is complete, and everything is now precisely in its proper place. The strong lines occupy strong positions, and the weak lines occupy weak positions. While this is an exceptionally favorable aspect, it also invites deep reflection. At the exact moment perfect equilibrium is achieved, any subsequent movement can cause the state of order to collapse back into decay. The single strong line that moved to the top, bringing absolute order to every detail, naturally draws the other lines to follow its course. As a result, the hexagram suddenly shifts back into Hexagram 12, Standstill (Pǐ). Therefore, this sign characterizes the conditions of a peak moment, which demands the utmost caution.

dictamen.text: Success in small matters. Perseverance furthers. Good fortune at the beginning, disorder at the end.
dictamen.commentary: The transition from the old era to the new is already complete. In principle, everything is settled, and success can now only be achieved in minor details. However, maintaining the right attitude remains critical. Everything appears to run smoothly on its own accord. This easily tempts one to slacken, lose momentum, and let things drift without attending to specific details. Yet, this indifference is the root of all trouble and inevitably leads to decay. This principle illustrates the typical course of history. However, this pattern is not an inescapable law. Those who understand it can avoid its consequences through continuous constancy and vigilance.

imagen.text: Water above Fire: The image of the condition After Completion. Thus the superior man takes misfortune into account and guards against it in advance.
imagen.commentary: When water hangs in a kettle over a fire, the two elements interact and generate power (as seen in the creation of steam). However, the resulting tension demands caution. If the water boils over, the fire is extinguished and its productive energy is lost. If the heat is too intense, the water evaporates into the air. These elements, though interacting to produce energy, are inherently antagonistic. Only extreme care can prevent damage. Similarly, there are periods in life where all forces are balanced and work together, making everything seem in perfect order. Only the sage recognizes the hidden dangers in such times and knows how to avert them through timely precautions.

1.text: He brakes his wheels. He gets his tail in the water. No blame.
1.commentary: In times following a great transition, everything presses forward, driven by an urge for progress and development. However, this initial rushing forward is not beneficial and leads inevitably to loss and collapse by overshooting the mark. A strong character refuses to be swept up in the general frenzy and stops his course in time. While he will not remain entirely untouched by the unfortunate consequences of the general push, the impact only catches him from behind - much like a fox that has already crossed the water and only gets its tail wet. This cannot cause him essential harm because his behavior was correct.
1.title: Nine at the beginning means:

2.text: The woman loses her carriage curtain. Do not run after it; on the seventh day you will get it.
2.commentary:
When a woman rode in a carriage, a curtain shielded her from the gaze of the curious. If this curtain was lost, proceeding would violate social propriety. Applied to public life, this means that when one wishes to achieve something, the authorities fail to extend the trust required for personal protection, so to speak. Especially in times after completion, rulers can become proud and self-assured, neglecting to welcome unrecognized talent with due attention.

This situation usually breeds opportunistic striving. When trust is not offered from above, people find alternative ways to gain it and push themselves into the spotlight. The text strongly advises against such unworthy behavior: "Do not search for it." Do not throw yourself away on the outside world. Instead, wait quietly and independently develop your personal worth. Times change. Once the six stages of the hexagram have passed, a new era begins. What truly belongs to you cannot be withheld permanently; it comes to you on its own. One must simply know how to wait.
2.title: Six on the second place means:

3.text: The Illustrious Ancestor disciplines the Devil's Country. After three years he conquers it. Inferior people must not be employed.
3.commentary: The Illustrious Ancestor is the dynastic title of Emperor Wǔ Dīng of the Yīn dynasty. After stabilizing the internal affairs of the empire with a firm hand, he waged prolonged colonial wars to subdue the northern border regions inhabited by the Huns, from which constant raids threatened. The situation described is one where colonial expansion begins with a certain historical necessity after a period of completion, when a new power has risen and internal order is established. Prolonged struggles must generally be expected in these endeavors. However, a correct colonial policy is critical. One must not treat these hard-earned territories as a welfare institution for individuals who have made themselves impossible at home but are deemed good enough for the colonies. Such an approach ruins success from the very start. This applies to large and small enterprises alike, for expansionist drives and their inherent dangers affect every growing enterprise, not just rising states.
3.title: Nine on the third place means:

4.text: The finest garments turn to rags. Be careful all day long.
4.commentary: In times of cultural peak, disruptions occasionally occur that reveal internal flaws within society, initially causing widespread alarm. However, because the general situation remains favorable, these damages can easily be patched up and hidden from the public. Everything then fades from memory, and an illusion of untroubled peace returns. To the thinking person, however, such incidents serve as serious warnings that must not be ignored. Only by paying attention can one avert disastrous consequences.
4.title: Six on the fourth place means:

5.text: The neighbor in the East who slaughters an ox does not attain as much real happiness as the neighbor in the West with his small offering.
5.commentary: Religious attitudes are also influenced by the spiritual atmosphere of times after completion. Elaborate forms and increasingly lavish external pomp tend to replace simple, ancient rituals. Yet, this display of magnificence lacks inner sincerity. Human whim replaces conscientious alignment with the divine will. While humans look at outward appearances, the divine looks at the heart. Therefore, a massive but cold religious service does not carry as much blessing as a simple, pious offering.
5.title: Nine on the fifth place means:

6.text: He gets his head in the water. Danger.
6.commentary: A final warning is added here at the conclusion. After crossing a body of water, one can only get their head wet by turning back toward the water carelessly. As long as one moves forward without looking back, this danger is avoided. However, there is a tempting urge to stop and look back at the overcome danger. Such vain self-contemplation brings no luck. It leads directly into danger, and if one does not resolve to move forward relentlessly, they will fall victim to it.
6.title: Six at the top means:

64.name: BEFORE COMPLETION
64.title: Hexagram 64 未濟 - WEI JI / BEFORE COMPLETION
64.description: Richard Wilhelm's complete study and analysis of Hexagram 64 (WEI JI) of the I Ching with Unicode characters and Pinyin.
64.intro: This hexagram indicates a time when the transition from disorder to order is not yet complete. The turning point is already prepared, as all the lines of the upper trigram relate to those of the lower trigram. However, they are not yet in their proper places. While the preceding hexagram resembles autumn, which forms the transition from summer to winter, this hexagram is like spring, leading from the stagnation of winter into the fertile season of summer. The Book of Changes concludes with this hopeful outlook.

dictamen.text: Before Completion. Success. But if the little fox, when he has almost completed the crossing, gets his tail in the water, there is nothing that would be advantageous.
dictamen.commentary: The conditions are difficult. The task is great and full of responsibility. It is nothing less than leading the world back from confusion to order. Yet, it is a task that promises success, because there is a goal available that can unite the divergent forces. However, one must proceed softly and cautiously at first. One must proceed like an old fox walking on ice. In China, the caution of the fox walking on ice is proverbial. He constantly listens for the cracking and carefully, providently selects the safest spots. A young fox, not yet knowing this caution, goes boldly ahead, and it happens that he falls in just when he is almost across the water, getting his tail wet. Then, of course, the entire effort was in vain. Accordingly, in times before completion, deliberation and caution are the fundamental conditions for success.

imagen.text: Fire is above Water: The image of the condition before transition. Thus the superior man is careful in differentiating things, so that each finds its proper place.
imagen.commentary: When fire, which naturally presses upward, is above, and water, whose movement is downward, is below, their effects diverge and remain without relation. If one wishes to achieve an effect, one must first investigate the nature of the forces involved and find their proper place. By putting these forces to work in the right position, they achieve the desired effect, and completion is attained. To handle external forces correctly, however, it is essential above all that one occupies the right standpoint oneself. Only from there can one act effectively.

1.text: He gets his tail in the water. Humiliating.
1.commentary: In times of disorder, it is tempting to press forward as quickly as possible to achieve something visible. But this enthusiasm leads to nothing but failure and humiliation as long as the time to act has not yet arrived. In such a period, it is wise to spare oneself the disgrace of failure through restraint. (Note the difference between this situation and the first line of the preceding hexagram.)
1.title: Six at the beginning means:

2.text: He brakes his wheels. Perseverance brings good fortune.
2.commentary: Here, too, the time for action has not yet come. But the required patience must not be a lazy waiting, just living from day to day. That would lead to no permanent success. Instead, one must develop the inner strength that enables forward progress. One must, so to speak, have a carriage ready to make the transition, but must still brake its wheels. Patience in the highest sense is restrained strength. Therefore, one must not fall asleep or lose sight of the goal. If one remains strong and steadfast in purpose, everything turns out well in the end.
2.title: Nine in the second place means:

3.text: Before completion, an attack brings misfortune. It is advantageous to cross the great water.
3.commentary: The time of transition has arrived, but one lacks the strength to complete it. Attempting to force it would be disastrous, precisely because a collapse would then be inevitable. What should be done instead? One must create a new situation, enlist the abilities of capable helpers, and take the decisive step forward together with them - crossing the great water. Then completion will become possible.
3.title: Six in the third place means:

4.text: Perseverance brings good fortune. Remorse disappears. Shock to discipline the devil's land. For three years, rewards are given with great realms.
4.commentary: Now is the time of battle. The transition must be completed. One must make oneself completely strong in purpose; this brings good fortune. All doubts that may arise during such serious times of struggle must be silenced. It is a matter of a fierce battle to shock and discipline the devil's land, the powers of decay. But the struggle also has its reward. Now is the time to lay the foundations of power and dominion for the future.
4.title: Nine in the fourth place means:

5.text: Perseverance brings good fortune. No remorse. The light of the superior man is true. Good fortune!
5.commentary: The victory is won. The power of steadfastness has not been put to shame. Everything has gone well. All doubts are overcome, and success has justified the deed. The light of a noble personality shines forth anew, prevailing among people who believe in it and gather around it. The new era, and with it good fortune, has arrived. Just as the sun shines twice as beautifully after the rain, or as a forest greens with renewed freshness from the charred ruins after a fire, the new era stands out all the more brilliantly from the misery of the old.
5.title: Six in the fifth place means:

6.text: In true confidence one drinks wine. No blame. But if one gets his head wet, he loses it in truth.
6.commentary:
Before completion, on the border of the new era, one is together with one's own in full mutual confidence, spending the time of waiting over wine. Since the new era is already directly at the door, this is no blame. One must only mind the right measure. If one pours wine over his own head in sheer high spirits, he loses the favorable position through intemperance.

Note: Just as the hexagram "After Completion" represents the gradual transition from a time of ascent across the cultural peak to a period of stagnation, the hexagram "Before Completion" represents the transition from chaos to order. This sign stands at the end of the Book of Changes. It points out that within every end lies a new beginning. Thus, it gives hope to humanity. The Book of Changes is a book of the future.
6.title: Nine at the top means:
